**Surah al-Mu'min**

It is also called Surah Ghafir and Surah al-Ṭawl. As narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Masruq, and Samura ibn Jundub, it is Meccan. Abu Hayyan reported a consensus (ijmaʿ, scholarly agreement) on this. It is also reported from al-Hasan that it is Meccan except for the verse ﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ [Ghafir: 55], because the five daily prayers were revealed in Medina, while the prayer in Mecca consisted of two rak'ahs without fixed times. You know that the correct view is the opinion of the majority, that the five prayers were revealed in Mecca, and that it is not necessarily intended by the glorification in the verse to refer to prayer. It has also been said that it is Meccan except for the verse ﴿Indeed, those who dispute about the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 35] and what follows, which is Medinan. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-ʿAliyah and others that it was revealed concerning the Jews when they mentioned the Dajjal. However, this is not a explicit statement that it was revealed in Medina. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said: "When they say a verse was revealed concerning such-and-such, they sometimes mean the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), and sometimes they mean that the matter is included within the verse even if it was not the occasion, as when you say: 'This verse is meant to refer to such-and-such.'" Al-Zarkashi said in al-Burhan: "It is known from the custom of the Companions and the Successors that when one of them said 'This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such,' he meant that it includes this ruling, not that this was the cause of its revelation. This is a kind of deriving a ruling from the verse, not a kind of transmitting what occurred." Yes, what is related from Abu al-ʿAliyah later, if Allah wills, is close to an explicit statement on this.

Its verses number eighty-five in the Kufan and Syrian reckonings, four in the Hijazi, and two in the Basran. It has also been said to be eighty-six, or eighty-eight. The connection between its beginning and the end of Surah al-Zumar is that when Allah, glorified is He, mentioned there what the state of the disbeliever and the state of the believer will lead to, He, exalted is He, mentioned here that He is the Forgiver of sin and the Acceptor of repentance, so that this would be an invitation to the disbeliever to faith and to abandon what he is engaged in. Between these two surahs there are several aspects of connection, and it is sufficient that in each of them is mentioned the conditions of the Day of Resurrection and the conditions of the disbelievers on it, both in the gathering place and in the Fire, with what is mentioned. In this surah, more of that has been detailed than in the other.

In Tanasuq al-Durar, the reason for placing the seven Ḥawāmīm after Surah al-Zumar is the correspondence of the openings, in beginning with ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾. In the codex of Ibn Masʿud, the beginning of al-Zumar is "Ḥā Mīm," and this is a noble connection. Then the Ḥawāmīm were arranged because they share the opening with "Ḥā Mīm" and the mention of the Book. Moreover, it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Jabir ibn Zayd that they were revealed consecutively after al-Zumar in the order they have in the codex. Many reports have come concerning their virtue. Abu ʿUbayd related in his Fada'il from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "Everything has a core (lubab), and the core of the Qur'an is the Ḥawāmīm."

He and Ibn al-Ḍurays, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥakim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman related from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "The Ḥawāmīm are the brocade of the Qur'an." Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Daylami related it from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) report. Al-Daylami and Ibn Mardawayh related from Samura ibn Jundub as a marfuʿ report: "The Ḥawāmīm are a garden from the gardens of Paradise."

Muhammad ibn Nasr and al-Darimi related from Saʿd ibn Ibrahim that he said: "They used to call the Ḥawāmīm the brides." Ibn Nasr and Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: 'Allah gave me the seven long surahs in place of the Torah, He gave me the surahs from al-Ra's to al-Ṭawāsīn in place of the Gospel, He gave me what lies between al-Ṭawāsīn and the Ḥawāmīm in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the Ḥawāmīm and the Mufaṣṣal, which no prophet before me recited.'"

Al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab related from Khalil ibn Murrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Ḥawāmīm are seven, and the gates of Hell are seven. Each Ḥā Mīm comes and stands at one of these gates, saying: 'O Allah, do not admit through this gate whoever believed in me and recited me.'" Reports about some verses of this surah also indicate its virtue.

At-Tirmidhi, al-Bazzar, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever recites Ḥā Mīm up to ﴿to Him is the final return﴾ and the Verse of the Throne in the morning will be protected by them until evening, and whoever recites them in the evening will be protected by them until morning.'"

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾: with the alif pronounced emphatically and the mīm vowelless. Ibn ʿĀmir, in the transmission of Dhakwan, and Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr recite with clear imalah (inclination of the vowel). Nafiʿ, in the transmission of Warsh, and Abu ʿAmr recite with intermediate imalah (bayna bayna). Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa recite with a fatḥah on the mīm, reading it as indeclinable (mabni) because two unvowelled letters came together, and the fatḥah is for lightness, as in أين (ayna) and كيف (kayfa). It is also permitted that this is in the accusative by an implied اقرأ (read). It is not declined because it is a proper noun and feminine, since it means the surah; or because it is a proper noun with a resemblance to foreignness, since فاعيل (fāʿīl) is not among the patterns of Arabic word-forms, and this occurs only in the language of non-Arabs, like قابيل (Qabil) and هابيل (Habil). This is reported from Sibawayh. In al-Kashf, it is stated that the better explanation is definiteness and compounding.

Abu al-Sammal recited with a kasrah on the mīm, according to the original principle of joining two unvowelled letters, as in جير (jīr). Al-Zuhri recited it with a ḍammah (ruf'), and the apparent reading is that it is i'rab (grammatical inflection). So it is either a subject (mubtada') or the predicate of an omitted subject. Discussion of its meaning is like the discussion of its counterparts. It is pluralized as ḥawāmīm and ḥāmīmāt. As for the second, Ibn ʿAsakir recited in his History:

This is the Messenger of Allah in good deeds, he came with Yasin and Hamimat.

As for the first, several reports about it have already been mentioned, and I do not think anyone denies the authenticity of all of them, or claims that the word ḥawāmīm in them is a distortion by foreign narrators. Also, Abu ʿUbaydah recited:

I swear by the seven that were lengthened, and by the hundreds that came after them,
And by the eights that were doubled and repeated, and by the ṭawāsīn that were recited,
And by the ḥawāmīm that were made sevens, and by the mufaṣṣal that were detailed.

Al-Jawaliqi, al-Hariri, and Ibn al-Jawzi held that it is not said ḥawāmīm. In al-Ṣiḥaḥ, it is reported from al-Farrāʾ that the common people's saying "al-ḥawāmīm" is not from the speech of the Arabs. The author of Zad al-Masir related from his teacher Abu Mansur al-Lughawi that it is an error to say: "I recited al-ḥawāmīm," and the correct form is "I recited ālu ḥā mīm." In the hadith of Ibn Masʿud: "When I come upon Āl Ḥā Mīm, I come upon gardens, soft and fragrant, in which I take delight." On this is the verse of al-Kumayt ibn Zayd in al-Hāshimiyyāt:

We found among you in Āl Ḥā Mīm a verse, which a pious man among us and an Arabic speaker interpreted.

And al-ṭawāsīn and al-ṭawāsīm, with a mīm instead of the nūn, are so according to them, and what you have heard suffices for refuting them. Yes, what they said is heard and accepted, like what we have said, but it should be known that ʾĀl in their saying ʾĀl Ḥā Mīm is not, as al-Khafaji said, in the sense of the well-known āl, which means family. Rather, it is a word mentioned before what cannot properly take a dual or plural form, from compound names and the like, such as تأبط شرا (Ta'abbaṭa Sharran). When they wanted to form its dual or plural, and it is a sentence where this is not possible, since nothing like it is known in Arabic speech, they added before it the word āl or dhā. So it is said: "The āl of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran came to me," or "the dhā of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran came to me," meaning the two men or the men named by this name. So āl Ḥā Mīm means "the Ḥawāmīm," and āl means "possessor of." What is meant is that to which this expression is applied and used, and this is a metaphor for spiritual companionship. In the speech of al-Raḍī and others there is an indication of this, though they did not explicitly explain it, so keep it in memory. It is related in al-Kashf that the better course is to pluralize it as dhawāt Ḥā Mīm, that is, not ḥawāmīm or ḥāmīmāt. Its meaning is "the surahs accompanied by this expression, namely Ḥā Mīm."

Revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

The grammatical discussion of it is like the discussion at the opening of Surah az-Zumar, except that here (tanzil, "revelation") may be the predicate (khabar) of Ha-Mim. Perhaps the specification of the two attributes (al-'Aziz and al-'Alim) is due to the inimitability (i'jaz) of the glorious Qur'an and the kinds of knowledge (ulum) that the scope of understanding (nitaq al-afham) is too narrow to encompass. Or it is in the manner of the specification of the two attributes mentioned earlier, for it is the nature of an eloquent speaker that his knowledge of things be that of one who is wise (hakim). However, it has been said that (al-'Alim) is used instead of (al-Hakim) for variety (tafannun).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 3:

The words of the Most High, ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty﴾, are attributes (sifat) of the Glorious Name, like ﴿the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾. The attributes ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, and the Possessor of bounty﴾ are mentioned to encourage (hope, al-targhib), and ﴿severe in punishment﴾ is mentioned to instill fear (al-tarhib). Together they urge (al-hath) toward the purpose of ﴿the revelation of the Book﴾, which is what is mentioned after it: monotheism (tawhid) and belief in the Resurrection, which necessarily entails belief in what is other than these two and turning to Allah the Most High. The first two of these, although they are active participle forms (ism fa'il), were not intended to indicate renewal (tajaddud) or restriction to a particular time, but rather permanence and continuity (thubut wa-al-istimrar). Therefore their genitive construction with what follows them is a pure genitive (idafa mahda), which gives them definiteness, so it is correct to describe with them the most definite of the definites (a'raf al-ma'arif). As for ﴿the Possessor of bounty﴾, the matter is very clear.

Yes, the matter of ﴿severe in punishment﴾ is problematic, for shadid is an assimilated adjective (sifa mushabbaha). Sibawayh stated explicitly that whenever a construction whose genitive is not pure (idafa ghayr mahda) is added to a definite noun, it is permissible to intend by its genitive a pure construction, so that it becomes definite and the definite noun may be described by it, except for what belongs to the category of the assimilated adjective, for that does not become definite. From here al-Zajjaj held that ﴿severe in punishment﴾ is a substitute (badal). It is objected that placing the substitute between the attributes creates a clear incongruity, because the attribute indicates that the described noun is intended, whereas the substitute is the opposite, so it is as if the intention were resumed after having been treated as unintended. The answer is that this difficulty appears clearly only according to the view of Sibawayh and the rest of the Basrans, who hold that the assimilated adjective never becomes definite at all by being added to a definite noun. As for the view of the Kufans, who hold that it is like other attributes and may become definite by addition, and that a definite noun may be described by it, as in "I passed by Zayd, good of face" (marartu bi-Zayd hasan al-wajh), then there is no difficulty. And according to the first view it is said regarding what has been mentioned: shadidan is interpreted as mushaddid, an active participle from ashaddahu (he made it severe), like adhin meaning mu'adhdhin (muezzin), so it is given its ruling. Or it is said: it is defined by al- (the definite article), and the original is "the severe is His punishment," but the genitive was omitted because there is no ambiguity with other than an attribute, since it occurs among the attributes. The possibility that it is a substitute alone is not to be considered, as you have heard, and in order to harmonize with the attributes accompanying it which are unaccompanied by it, and what is presumed is treated as existing. They have altered much of their speech from its rules for the sake of harmony, to the point that they said: "ma ya'rifu sahadaliyhi min 'anadaliyhi" (he does not know his two testicles from his two...), meaning: he does not know his male organ (dhakar) from his two testicles (unthayayhi), so they made dual what is singular for the sake of what is dual.

[Page 42]

It has also been permitted that all the mentioned followers (tawabi') are substitutes. He deliberately made ﴿severe in punishment﴾ indefinite and unspecified, to indicate extreme severity and that there is nothing more calamitous than it, and bitter, to increase the warning. In al-Kashf, making all of them substitutes involves a great incongruity, especially in substituting ﴿the Mighty﴾ for ﴿Allah﴾, the comprehensive Name encompassing all the attributes, the proper noun by explicit text. And where is this from the excellence of the opening?

Makki went to the permissibility of ﴿the Forgiver of sin and the Accepter of repentance﴾ alone, without what precedes them, being two substitutes, and that they are then indefinite. You know what is in this from what has preceded. Abu Hayyan said: the substitute of correction (badal al-bada') according to those who affirm it may be repeated. As for the substitute of the whole from the whole (badal kull min kull), the substitute of part from the whole (badal ba'd min kull), and the substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), I know of no explicit statement from any of the grammarians either permitting or prohibiting their repetition. However, in the words of some of our companions there is what indicates that a substitute from a substitute is permissible, but not multiple substitutes for one substituted noun. The apparent meaning of al-Khafaji's words is that the grammarians explicitly stated the permissibility of multiplicity, where he said: "The rarity of substitutes in derived nouns does not affect the view of substitution, nor does the fact that an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one unless it is described, nor does the fact that the grammarians did not mention the multiplicity of substitutes, as is said, because the grammarians explicitly stated the opposite regarding all of them." Al-Damamini has a lengthy discussion of this at the beginning of his commentary on al-Khazrajiyya, which this place cannot contain; if you want it, look into it. End of quotation.

In my view, substitution here is not valid in any sense, whether of the whole or of a part. ﴿The repentance﴾ (al-tawb) may be a verbal noun (masdar) like al-awb meaning "return," and it may be a collective noun (ism jam') for tawba (a single act of repentance), like tamr (dates) and tamra (a single date). ﴿The bounty﴾ (al-tawl) is excess of reward and favor, or that together with the abandonment of deserved punishment, as is said, and this is better than restricting it to the abandonment of punishment, even though it occurs after ﴿severe in punishment﴾. The claim that reward is promised and so becomes like what is obligatory, and therefore is not bounty, is not valid, since the promise of it is not an obligation. Ibn Abbas interpreted it as breadth and wealth; Qatada as blessings; Ibn Zayd as power.

The placing of the conjunction (waw) between ﴿the Forgiver of sin﴾ and ﴿the Accepter of repentance﴾ serves to indicate that the sinner who repents is gathered between two mercies: that Allah, glorified is He, accepts his repentance and records it for him as an act of obedience among the acts of obedience, and that He makes it an erasure of the sin, as if he had never sinned, as if it were said: "the one who combines forgiveness and acceptance." This is what al-Zamakhshari said. Its basis, as in al-Kashf, is that these are successive attributes without the conjunction, indicating the absolute general sense arising from mere sequence. So when one of the combined items is specified by the conjunction, it indicates that what is meant and considered is specifically that, and what precedes it, in order to preserve the speech of an eloquent speaker from being meaningless. Thus the conjunction here indicates that He, glorified is He, combines forgiveness and the acceptance of repentance for the penitent in particular. This does not contradict the fact that He, mighty and majestic, may forgive one who has not repented.

As for what is said, that the placement (of the conjunction) indicates that the meaning is as Abu al-Shaykh reported in al-Azamah from al-Hasan: "the Forgiver of sin for one who does not repent, and the Accepter of repentance for one who repents," this is not accepted. The difference that they mention between the positions of the two verbs, namely the forgiveness of sin and the acceptance of repentance from it, which requires that forgiveness relates to one group and acceptance to another, since they made the object of the first the sin remaining in the records without accountability, and the object of the second the sin removed and erased from them, existing together with the sequence, has no bearing on the conjunction. Then the aforementioned explanation applies on the principles of both the People of the Sunna and the Mu'tazila, so there is no basis for rejecting it on grounds that are not damaging. The preference for what is less favored is a matter of choice. The placing of ﴿the Forgiver﴾ before ﴿the Accepter﴾ is by the principle of clearing before adorning (al-takhliya qabl al-tahliya); so understand this.

Regarding the certainty of the acceptance of the repentance of a disobedient person, there are two opinions among the People of the Sunna. In al-Bahr: the apparent meaning of the verse is that the repentance of one who is disobedient in a matter other than disbelief, like the repentance of one who is disobedient in disbelief, is certainly accepted. In the singling out of the attribute of punishment, being submerged among His attributes that indicate mercy, there is evidence of the abundance of mercy and its precedence. So, glorified is He, what a God He is, how merciful and how generous He is! ﴿There is no god but Him﴾, therefore total turning toward His obedience in His commands and prohibitions is obligatory, ﴿to Him is the final return﴾, so it is to Him alone, not to anyone else, glorified is He, neither independently nor in partnership, and He will recompense each of the obedient and the disobedient. The sentence ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is either a new independent sentence or a circumstantial clause (hal). It has also been said that it is an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, or of ﴿severe in punishment﴾.

[Page 43]

Among the verses is what necessitates admonition, and what is in them. Abd ibn Humayd reported from Yazid ibn al-Asamm that a man who was powerful and was from the people of Syria had gone astray, and that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, missed him and asked about him. He was told: "He has persisted in drinking wine." So Umar summoned his scribe and said to him: "Write: From Umar ibn al-Khattab to so-and-so son of so-and-so. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, the One besides whom there is no god. (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ha Mim. ...up to His words, may He be exalted:) ﴿To Him is the final return﴾." The letter was concluded, and he said to his messenger: "Do not deliver it to him until you find him sober." Then he instructed those around him to supplicate for him for repentance. When the letter reached him, he began reading it and saying: "My Lord has promised me that He will forgive me, and has warned me of His punishment." He kept repeating it to himself until he wept. Then he departed (in repentance) and departed in the best manner. When Umar learned of his repentance, he said: "This is how you should act when you see your brother has slipped in a lapse: support him, steady him, pray to Allah, exalted is He, that He accept his repentance, and do not be helpers of Satan against him."

﴿Only those who disbelieve dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾. It was revealed, as Abu al-'Aliyah said, concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sulami, one of the mockers. By "disputing" is meant disputing in falsehood, through attacking the signs, aiming to refute the truth and to extinguish the light of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is based on His words, exalted is He, after this: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾ (40:5). It is mentioned there as a likening of the state of the disbelievers of Makkah to the disbelievers of the factions before them. Otherwise, disputation concerning the Qur'an, for clarifying its obscure points, resolving its difficulties, debating the people of knowledge in deriving its meanings, and refuting the people of deviation from it, is among the greatest struggle (jihad) in the way of Allah, exalted is He.

As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), which 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) hadith: "Indeed, disputing about the Qur'an is disbelief," it points to this, since he mentioned "disputing" in an indefinite and denounced form, which indicates that a type of it is disbelief and misguidance, while another type is not like that.

The verification, as in al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), is that disputing about a thing requires that the thing be either doubtful to the disputants or to one of them, or denied in the same way. Whatever the case, it is blameworthy, except when it is from one who affirms the Oneness of Allah against one who has left the religion, or from one who verifies the truth against one who has deviated into innovation. In that case it is praiseworthy in relation to one of the two parties. As for what has been said, that inquiry concerning it for clarifying the ambiguous and the like is disputing "for it" (ʿan-hā) and not "about it" (fī-hā), since the verb jādala takes ʿan when it means preventing and defending against a thing, and fī when it means the opposite, as the Imam (al-Razi) mentioned, and also takes bi (ب), as in His words: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ (16:125), there is discussion in this.

As for His words, ﴿in the signs of Allah﴾ rather than "in it" with a pronoun referring to the Book, it indicates that disputing any single sign of it is sufficient for disbelief, so how much more so for one who denies it entirely and says about it what he says. It also indicates that each sign of it is a sign that it is from Allah, exalted is He, who is described by those attributes. Therefore it shows the severity of the obstinacy of the disputant in disbelief, and that he disputed the clear matter that has no concealment.

From what has been mentioned, the connection of this verse with what precedes it becomes evident, and the link of His words, ﴿So let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ (40:4), with it. That is: when you know that these people are extremely obstinate in disbelief, having lost this world and the Hereafter by disputing the signs of Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing, and persisting in that, then do not be swayed by their enticement through the widening of their provision and their being granted respite, for their end is destruction, as was done to those before them who were similar to them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 5:

What is pointed to by His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ ... etc. And al-taqallub (the movement about) is leaving one land for another. The intended "lands" (bilad) are the lands of al-Sham (Syria) and Yemen, since the verse concerns the disbelievers of Quraysh, who used to move about these lands for trade. They had the winter journey to Yemen and the summer journey to al-Sham. There is no harm in intending what encompasses that and other things. Zayd ibn Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr read ﴿فلا يغرك﴾ (fa-la yaghurrak, "so let it not deceive you") with idgham (assimilation, the merging of two identical consonants) and a fatha on the ra, which is the dialect of Tamim. The fakk (unmerged form) is the dialect of the Hijazis. He began with the people of Noah because he, peace be upon him, was according to what is in the sea the first messenger on earth, or because they were the first people who denied their messenger and became extremely arrogant. ﴿And the factions after them﴾, i.e., those who banded together and united against the messengers, peace be upon them, from the people of Noah onward, such as ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿Every nation plotted against their messenger﴾ of those nations. ʿAbdullah read ﴿بِرَسُولِها﴾ (bi-rasulihā, "against its messenger," feminine), observing the wording of ﴿ummah﴾. ﴿To seize him﴾, i.e., so that they could carry out against him what they wished: imprisonment, torment, killing, or other things. So al-akhdh (seizing) is a kinaya (metonymy) for the power described. Some interpreters explained it as capture, which is close to what was mentioned. Qatada said: that is, to kill him. ﴿And they argued with falsehood﴾, with what has no reality. It has been said that this is their saying: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10]. The more appropriate view is that it is everything they say to deny the message and to beautify their own position. Explaining it as the devil is nothing. ﴿To refute﴾, i.e., to remove ﴿thereby﴾, that is, by falsehood, ﴿the truth﴾, the established matter from which there is no escape. It has been said: that is, by their disputation with falsehood. ﴿So I seized them﴾ with destruction that uprooted them. ﴿So how was My punishment?﴾ For you pass by their dwellings and see their traces. This is an affirmation containing astonishment at what befell them for the listeners. It is also permissible that it refers to the lack of consideration on the part of these people. He used the kasra (vowel) instead of the ya' of possessive suffix in ʿiqab because it is a fasila (verse-end). Scholars differed about what the seizing mentioned is caused by. It has been said: the whole of the denial, the intention to seize, and the disputation with falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari preferred that it is caused by the intention to seize. In al-Kashf he said: this is because His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and they argued with falsehood, to refute﴾ is the denial itself, and seizing resembles seizing, whereas denial only necessitates the deserving of the otherworldly punishment referred to after this. It cannot be denied that both necessitate both, but since the suitability of seizing to seizing is more complete, and denial is more evidently connected to the otherworldly punishment, he made it connected to seizing, to signal complete suitability. Then, contentious disputation has no purpose other than harm, so it strengthens the intention from this aspect. Rather, denial also strengthens it. The purpose of introducing His saying ﴿does not dispute﴾ and mentioning the factions is to allude to this meaning. Then the explicit statement of His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿every nation plotted against their messenger﴾ indicates clearly what he preferred, so there is no need to excuse it by saying that he only considered this and not what the discourse was directed at, namely the false disputation, for consolation. End. Fairly speaking, what Jar Allah did shows regard for the meaning and a verbal correspondence, except that the apparent reading is that it is a consequence of the whole, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 6:

﴿And thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieved﴾. That is, just as the decree of His Exalted Majesty to destroy those who formed factions against the prophets was carried out, so too was His decree, glorified is He, to destroy these who formed factions against you, namely the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿That they are the companions of the Fire﴾. It is also permitted that it be in the nominative position, as a substitute (badal) for "كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ" (the word of your Lord): a substitute of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull) if by "the word" is meant His saying, or His decree, glorified is He, that they are among the companions of the Fire; and a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) if by it is meant the more general sense. By "those who disbelieved" are meant those factions. The meaning is: just as their destruction by the uprooting punishment in this world was decreed, so too was their destruction by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter decreed, because of their disbelief. The first explanation is more apparent from the context. The expression with the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah), together with its addition to his pronoun (ﷺ), and "كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ" (the word of your Lord) was explained, with reference to him, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And it was a due right upon Us to help the believers﴾ [al-Rum: 47] and similar verses. In the Codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) the reading is "وكَذَلِكَ سَبَقَتْ" (and thus has preceded), which, it is said, is an explanation of meaning and not a recitation (qira'ah). Ibn Hurmuz, Shayba, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "كَلِماتٌ" (words) in the plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 7:

﴿Those who bear the Throne﴾. It is a great body; the legs of the Kursi and what is beneath it, in relation to it, are like a ring in a desert.

It is related in some reports that God Most High created the Throne from a green jewel, and between two of its legs is the fluttering of a swiftly flying bird for eighty thousand years. Some have mentioned regarding its vastness that if its concave surface were lightly wiped with all the waters of the world, they would fall short of covering it. The people of the hay'a (astronomy) and those who agree with them claim that it is spherical, that it is the muhaddad (the ninth sphere, the sphere that limits the others) and the falak al-aflak (the sphere of spheres), and that it is like the rest of the spheres, not described by heaviness or lightness. The apparent meaning is that "bearing" is in its literal sense, and its bearers are great angels.

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh related, with a sound chain, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been permitted to narrate about an angel whose feet have passed through the lowest seventh earth, while the Throne is upon his shoulders, and he is saying: 'Glory be to You, where You were and where You will be.'"

Abu Dawud and a group related, with a sound chain, from Jabir, with the wording: "I have been permitted to narrate about an angel of the angels of Allah Most High, one of the bearers of the Throne, the distance between the lobe of his ear and his shoulder being a journey of seven hundred years." According to some reports, they are eight. Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Harun ibn Rabab, who said: The bearers of the Throne are eight, responding to one another with a melodious voice; four of them say: "Glory be to You and praise, for Your forbearance after Your pardon," and four of them say: "Glory be to You and praise, for Your pardon after Your power."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Abu Qubayl that he heard Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) say: The bearers of the Throne are eight, the distance between the brow of one of them and the back of his eyes being a journey of five hundred years. Some reports say that today they are four, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be eight.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Wahb, who said: The bearers of the Throne are four; when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be strengthened with four others: one of them in the form of a human, who intercedes for the children of Adam regarding their provision; one of them in the form of an eagle, who intercedes for the birds regarding their provision; one of them in the form of a bull, who intercedes for the livestock regarding their provision; and one of them in the form of a lion, who intercedes for the predators regarding their provision. When they bear the Throne, they fall to their knees from the greatness of Allah Most High, and they are taught: "There is no power and no strength except in Allah," so they rise and stand on their feet.

There is also a report from Wahb, likewise, that they bear the Throne on their shoulders, which is what the apparent sense of the earlier report of Abu Hurayrah indicates.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Hibban ibn Atiyyah, who said: The bearers of the Throne are eight; their feet are fixed in the seventh earth, their heads have passed beyond the seventh heaven, and their horns are as long as their height, with the Throne upon them.

In some reports, they are humble and do not lift their gaze; in others, they are unable to raise their eyes because of the radiance of the light. And they, according to what Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Umamah, speak in Persian, i.e., when they speak other than glorification; otherwise the apparent meaning is that they glorify in Arabic. However, Allah Most High knows best the soundness of this report. In some reports from Wahb, they have no speech except to say: "Holy is Allah, the Mighty, whose greatness has filled the heavens and the earth."

What will come after this in the verse, God willing, its apparent sense refuses restriction: ﴿and those around it﴾, i.e., those who are around the Throne, who are angels in extreme multitude, whose number none knows but Allah Most High.

It has been said: Around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels circling it, glorifying Allah and proclaiming His greatness; and behind them are seventy thousand rows standing, having placed their hands upon their shoulders, raising their voices with tahlil and takbir; and behind them are one hundred thousand rows who have placed their right hands upon their left, and none of them is there but glorifying with what the other does not glorify with.

It is mentioned regarding their multitude that the creatures of the land are a tenth of the creatures of the sea; the total is a tenth of the creatures of the air; the total is a tenth of the angels of the lowest heaven; the total is a tenth of the angels of the second heaven, and so on up to the seventh heaven; the total is a tenth of the angels of the Kursi; and the total is a tenth of the angels surrounding the Throne. There is no comparison between this total and what Allah Most High knows of His hosts, glory be to Him: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord but He﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

The bearers of the Throne and those surrounding it are called the Karubiyyun, the plural of Karubiyy, with a fatha on the kaf, a damma on the unpointed ra, and a light (not doubled) pronunciation; doubling it is an error. Then a waw follows, then a single ya, then a doubled ya, from karuba meaning qaraba (to draw near). Some have doubted its being heard from the Arabs, but Abu Ali al-Farisi affirmed it and cited as evidence the verse:

Karubiyyah among them, bowing and prostrating.

In it is an indication of intensity in nearness, by the pattern fa'ul and the ya added for intensity. It has also been said that it is from al-karb, meaning severity and grief, and it seems their description by this is because they are the most fearful of the angels.

Some have claimed that the Karubiyyun are the bearers of the Throne and that they are the first angels to exist, and such a matter is not known except by transmission. From al-Bayhaqi it is related that they are the angels of punishment, and this seems to be another usage of karb in the sense of severity and grief. Ibn Sina said in the Risalah al-Malaikah: "The Karubiyyun are those who dwell in the high wilderness of bewilderment, standing in the most noble station in throngs, looking with a gaze at the most splendid sight; they are the angels brought near and the spirits made free. As for the working angels, they are the bearers of the Throne and the Kursi and the inhabitants of the heavens." End of quotation.

Some have said that bearing the Throne is a metaphor for its management and its preservation from anything that might harm it or from any of its states, which none knows but Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They made the qarinah (indicator) rational, because the Throne is "spherical" in its natural place and therefore has no need of bearing. This is attributed to the philosophers and most of the theologians. Likewise, they held that the hafif (surrounding movement) and the tawaf (circumambulation) around the Throne are a kinayah (allusion) or majaz (metaphor) for nearness to the Lord of the Throne, glory be to Him, their high rank with Him, and their mediation in the execution of His command, Mighty and Majestic. The truth is the literal sense in both places, and the rational indicator mentioned is within the realm of prohibition.

Ibn Abbas and a group read "al-'Urush" with a damma on the ayn. It was said: it is the plural of 'arsh, like suqf and saqf, or a dialect form of al-'arsh. The first relative pronoun is the subject, the second is coordinated with it, and the predicate is the words of the Most High: ﴿glorify the praise of their Lord﴾. The clause is a resumptive statement intended to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by explaining that the angels who are in the highest place are persistent in supporting those who are with him among the believers, in their victory, and in seeking what makes them happy in both abodes. That is, they declare Allah Most High free of everything unbecoming to His exalted majesty, such as corporeality and the Throne's being a carrier of Him, Mighty and Majestic, while being engaged in praising Him, Majestic in His glory, for His blessings which have no end.

﴿And they believe in Him﴾, with true and complete faith. The explicit statement of this, despite being unnecessary to mention at all, serves to show the virtue of faith, to display the honor of its people, and to indicate the cause of their supplication for the believers, as His words express: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾. For sharing in faith is the strongest and most complete bond, and the most compelling motive for sincere advice and compassion, even if the kinds differ and the places are distant. In it, according to what has been said, is an indication that the bearers of the Throne and the dwellers of the earth are equal in faith in the unseen, for had there been direct observation, it would have been necessary from the bearing, according to the customary norm, or because the Throne is a transparent body that does not block sight at all, he would not have said "they believe," because faith is the heartfelt assent, that is, knowledge or what stands in its place, together with acknowledgment, and it occurs only regarding a report and its content, from a scientific or probable belief arising from proof or the word of the truthful; as if he acknowledged the truthfulness of the informant or the proof.

As for direct vision, it makes explanation unnecessary. In this there is an allusion to the refutation of the anthropomorphists (mujassimah). A similar case in this regard is his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Do not prefer me over the son of Matta." Thus it has been said. It should be known that the fact that the bearers of the Throne do not see Him, Mighty and Majestic, with the senses, does not entail that the believers will not see Him, Most High, in the Hereafter.

﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾, according to the intention of speech, i.e., they say: "Our Lord..." etc. The clause has no place in the i'rab, either as an explanation of "yastaghfiruna," or in the nominative position as an apposition to that clause, based on the permissibility of this in clauses, or in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yastaghfiruna."

Their seeking forgiveness on this view has been explained as their intercession for the believers and their urging them to repentance through what they pour into their hearts. It is also permitted that the seeking of forgiveness in His words ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those in the earth﴾, explained as deferring punishment, granting provision, enjoying what He created of abundant benefits, and the like, may be meant. Although this does not specifically concern the believers, they are its foundation, so singling them out here is an indication of that. The more apparent view is that the clause is an explanation.

"Mercy and knowledge" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it is transferred from the subject. The original would be: "Your mercy and Your knowledge encompassed all things," and it was changed to what is in the glorious wording, for the sake of intensifying the description of Him, Mighty and Majestic, with mercy and knowledge, in that His essence, glory be to Him, is made as though it were the very essence of mercy and knowledge. Along with this is an allusion to their generality, because the relation of all things to Him, Most High, is equal, and so equality in their encompassment by both is required. The description of Him, Most High, with perfect mercy and knowledge serves as a preface to His words, glory be to Him: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾ ... etc. The causation of forgiveness by mercy is evident. As for its causation by knowledge: the meaning is, "Forgive those whom You know to have repented," i.e., from sins in general, based on the view that this is what is understood from the unrestricted term, "and followed Your way," which is the path of truth that Allah Most High laid down for His servants and to which Islam calls, i.e., Your all-encompassing knowledge that comprehends what is hidden and what is manifest requires that. In it is also an alert to their purification from the turbidity of showing off and desire, for that is known to Allah Most High alone.

The aforementioned preface includes an allusion that the vast mercy and the comprehensive knowledge require that these people attain the great success and the highest portion of good pleasure. In it is a hint at the meaning of:

If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive abundantly, and what servant of Yours does not commit wrong?

For even if the servant exerts himself to the utmost in fulfilling his duties to Allah Most High, he is still deficient. To this refers the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Nor I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." The mention of mercy first is because it is the one intended in itself here. In beginning the supplication with "Our Lord" there is an appeal that is not hidden, and for this reason beginning supplications with it is frequent. His words, Most High: ﴿And protect them from the punishment of the Hellfire﴾, i.e., preserve them from it, are an explicit statement after an allusion for emphasis, since the supplication for forgiveness entails that. In it is an indication of the severity of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 8:

﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You promised them﴾. That is, You promised them them (the Gardens). The second object (al-maf'ul al-akhar, the second object of the verb) is therefore understood, and the intended meaning is "You promised them entry into them." The repetition of the address ("Our Lord") is for the sake of increasing entreaty (al-isti'tf, supplication for compassion). Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read «jannat 'Adnin» in the singular, and likewise it is in the codex of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud). ﴿And whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their offspring﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in "admit them" (adkhilhum). That is, admit with them those (others), so that their joy is complete and their delight is multiplied. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj permitted that it be conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿You promised them﴾, meaning "You promised them and You promised whoever was righteous..." etc. It was said: the intended promise here is the general promise. It has been objected that on this view the conjunction has no sound basis, so the intended promise is the specific promise to them in the words of the Most High: ﴿We shall join their offspring with them﴾ (al-Tur: 21). The apparent reading is conjunction with the first (clause), and the supplication of admission is explicit in it, while in the second it is implicit. The apparent meaning is that by righteousness is meant the righteousness that qualifies one for entry into the Garden, even if it is below the righteousness of those who are followed (by them). Ibn 'Abla read «salua» with a damma on the lam; it is said: ṣalaha, so he is ṣalīḥ, and ṣaluha, so he is ṣāliḥ. 'Isa read «dhurriyyatahum» in the singular. ﴿Indeed, You are the Almighty﴾, that is, the Overpowering, to whom no decreed matter is impossible, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who does only what wisdom dictates, the manifest wisdom, among which is the admission into the Gardens of those whose admission has been requested. The sentence is therefore a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it.

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 40, verse 9]

﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾, i.e., from their punishments, according to what is reported from Qatadah. The term "evil deeds" (sayyi'at) is applied to punishment because punishment is itself evil. It is also permissible that it means the commonly known sense, namely sins. In that case the sentence contains an elided noun, i.e., "and protect them from the recompense of evil deeds," or it is a metonymy by which the cause is named for the effect. In either case, this is not a repetition of ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾. Rather, it is a generalization after a specification, since it includes worldly and otherworldly punishment absolutely. Or the first supplication is for those who were followed, and this one is for the followers. It is also permissible that "evil deeds" means the commonly known sense without an elided noun, and that "protect" (taqi) means "keep them from sins," i.e., "protect them from sins in this world." Protecting them from sins means keeping them from committing them, and this is a supplication for protection from the cause of punishment after the supplication for protection from its effect, which is punishment. It has been objected that on this reading it would be more appropriate to place this supplication before the other. ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day﴾, i.e., the Day of accountability, ﴿You have indeed had mercy on him﴾. On the last interpretation it may be said: "And whoever You protect from evil deeds on the Day of action," i.e., in this world, "You have indeed had mercy on him in the Hereafter." This interpretation is supported by the claim that "that Day" (yawma'idhin) most naturally refers to the world, because "idh" indicates past time. But there is clear objection to this. ﴿That﴾ refers to the mercy understood from His mercy, or to the protection understood from the act of protecting, or to both together. The masculine form of the demonstrative is appropriate on the first two possibilities, and the singular form on the last possibility is likewise clear. ﴿It is the great triumph﴾, i.e., the attainment, ﴿the great﴾, which leaves no further object of desire for any desirer.

This is the place to note that al-Zamakhshari held that the intended sense of "those who repented" is those who repented of sins in general. He said that "evil deeds," with an elided noun, are minor sins or major sins from which repentance has been made, and he mentioned that protection from them is expiation or the acceptance of repentance. He also said that these forgiven people are repentant and righteous, like the angels in purity, and that seeking forgiveness for them is like intercession, whose benefit is an increase in honor and reward. Therefore it does no harm that they are promised forgiveness, since God does not break His promise. It has been objected that there is no benefit in mentioning mercy and emphasizing it if the one forgiven is like the angels, peace be upon them, in purity, and there is no need for seeking forgiveness, let alone emphasis on it. It has also been objected that what he said about evil deeds is impermissible, because the removal of the punishment for a major sin after repentance is obligatory in his school, and what is obligatory to do cannot be requested by supplication without being pointless and ugly according to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school). The same applies to the removal of the punishment for a minor sin, so it is not fitting to request it by supplication. And it cannot be that this is for an increase in benefit, because that would not be called forgiveness. al-Tayyibi relates this from the Imam (al-Razi), then says: "In that case it must be said that the intended sense of repentance is repentance from polytheism, as al-Wahidi said: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾, i.e., Your religion, Islam." If you say: "If repentance from sins were not intended, it would suffice to say: ﴿So forgive those who believe﴾, to match the preceding phrase," I reply: God knows best. This is close to placing an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun, without a prior word. Its explanation is that the verse ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent…﴾ comes separately from His words ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾. Therefore the verse explains the manner of seeking forgiveness, not the state of those for whom forgiveness is sought. Their distinguishing description is known by taste. As for the purpose of shifting from the pronoun, and why it was not said "forgive them" but rather "for those who repent," it is that the angels, just as they gave reasons for forgiveness with respect to the One who bestows goodness, may He be exalted, by His all-encompassing knowledge and wide mercy, they also gave as the reason for the recipient of the overflow repentance from polytheism and following the way of Islam. If you say: "This repentance is valid only for one whose polytheism preceded his Islam, not for one born Muslim who remained so," I reply: The verse was revealed in the time of the Companions, and most of them had moved from polytheism to Islam. If it had been said, "Forgive those who did not commit polytheism," they would have been excluded. So the Companions, may God be pleased with them, were given precedence in accordance with the general rules of all rulings. End. By my life, there is indeed ample room for discussion in this, a great deal of room.

In *al-Kashshaf*, al-Zamakhshari chose what he chose over what al-Wahidi said, that repentance means repentance from polytheism, because repentance when mentioned without qualification refers to repentance from sins in general. Moreover, on al-Wahidi's reading there is repetition, since the one who repents from polytheism is a Muslim, and "the one following the way" has been interpreted in that statement as him. And when the bearers of the Throne and those around it, peace be upon them, stipulate the righteousness of the follower, namely the offspring, in light of the statement of God, ﴿With faith, We will join their offspring with them﴾ [al-Tur 52:21], then what about the one followed? You know that righteousness is among the most distinguishing qualities of the believer. The supplications of Abraham and Joseph, peace be upon them, for joining the righteous are sufficient evidence of this. As for the claim that they do not need the supplication, the answer is that it is not necessary that it be for need. Do you not see our saying: "O God, bless our master Muhammad," and what is reported in it of virtues? That which is known to be granted by God, may He be exalted, is fitting to request, because supplication in itself is an act of worship, and it brings to the one who supplicates and to the one for whom he supplicates a nobility that does not fall short of the attainment of the basic reward. Furthermore, if the protection from evil deeds means expiation, then the question arises as to which evil deeds are expiated. There is no doubt that the texts indicate that repentance expiates all evil deeds, and that minor sins are expiated so long as major sins are avoided. Therefore, it is necessary to specify it with this, as has been mentioned. And if its meaning is that they are pardoned and not held to account for them, as is the statement of al-Wahidi and the preferred view of the Imam and those who follow him, then one should consider which of the two meanings of protection is more apparent. Also, the statement of God, ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have indeed had mercy on him﴾, and what it indicates of emphasis, is like the saying "whoever reached the pasture of al-Summan has indeed reached it."

Its following with His words, glorified be He, ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, concerns those who fell short, or the forgiven, and is more apparent. From this explanation it has become clear that this view is apparent in this context, and that it agrees with the principles of both groups. There is nothing in it to indicate that God pardons major sins without repentance or that He does not pardon them, so its permissibility is not contradicted by other evidences. And so on to the end of what he said. This is a good statement, although in parts of it there is some dispute, such as the hadith about repetition and the claim that righteousness in the verse is among the most distinguishing qualities of the believer. It may be preferred that the intended meaning of repentance is repentance from sins in general rather than repentance from polytheism only, on the grounds that what is understood from ﴿and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ is that each of them is protected from that. It is known that the threat must be carried out against some sinful believers and that they will be punished in the Fire. Therefore, a supplication to protect each believer from punishment would be impermissible.

They have explicitly stated the prohibition of saying, "O God, forgive all the believers all their sins," for this reason. This does not apply if the supplication is for righteous repentant believers. The reading of the genitive construction as referring to a specific known thing, namely that by "the punishment of the Blazing Fire" is meant punishment of an eternal kind, is clearly not to be relied upon. The objection that the supplication would be for something already known to occur, if repentance is taken to mean repentance from sins in general, is answered by the alternative reading, namely repentance from polytheism, since in that case the supplication is not necessarily for something known, because the meaning would be: "forgive those who repented from polytheism their sins which they did not repent of," and the forgiveness of those sins is not known to occur. This has been answered by what is in *al-Kashshaf*. Moreover, the claim that forgiveness for the repentant is known to occur is itself disputed, as we indicated at the beginning of the surah. Yes, this requirement is clearly present in their words, ﴿and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You promised them﴾. Similar to this is what is reported in the supplication after the call to prayer: "and raise him to the praiseworthy station which You promised him." This has been answered by something other than what was indicated here, namely that the prior promise does not require the promised thing to be attained without an intermediary supplication.

In sum, there is no harm in understanding repentance as repentance from sins in general, and saying so does not commit one to any of the principles of the Mu'tazilah. So reflect, and be fair.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 10:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ begin a description of the state of the disbelievers after they have entered the Fire. ﴿They will be called out to﴾ while they are in the Fire, and they will have come to loathe their own selves (al-ammara, "the commanding self") for the evil that they fell into by following its desires, to the extent that they will bite their fingertips out of loathing. This is what ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from al-Ḥasan.

In some reports, they will loathe themselves when Satan says to them: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]. It was also said: they will loathe themselves when they know that they are among the companions of the Fire. The one calling out is the guardians (of Hell) or the believers, who say to them, magnifying their regret: ﴿The loathing of Allah is greater than your loathing of yourselves﴾. This (clause) is the object of the calling out, because it includes the meaning of speech, as if it were said: they are called out to, being told: "The loathing..." Or it is the object of an implied saying introduced by the fa' of explanation, meaning: they are called out to, and it is said to them: "The loathing..." Making it the object of the calling out, by dropping the preposition and connecting the verb directly to the clause, is not sound.

The word maqt ("loathing") is a verbal noun whose genitive complement, the glorious Name, is in the construction of a verbal noun with its agent. Likewise, the second maqt is annexed to the pronoun of address.

There is either a tanazuʿ (grammatical "dispute" over a shared element between two verbs) in the sentence, or the object of the first is omitted without a dispute, meaning: the loathing of Allah toward you or toward your selves is greater than your loathing of your selves. The lam is either the lam of emphasis or the lam of oath. Maqt is the strongest hatred. The later scholars (khalaf) interpret it, when it is attributed to Allah the Exalted, as the strongest denial.

﴿When you were invited﴾, that is, when the prophets and their deputies were inviting you ﴿to faith﴾, and you refused to accept it, ﴿and you disbelieved﴾. This is a cause for the judgement, or for what is judged. The word ﴿when﴾ (idh) is connected to "greater". The use of the present tense indicates continuous, renewed occurrence, as if it were said: the loathing of Allah the Exalted toward your selves is greater than your loathing of them, because you were invited again and again to faith, and so disbelief was repeated from you. The time of the two loathings is one, according to what is most apparent, and it is the time of their loathing of their selves that we have just mentioned.

It is also permissible that it be a cause for their loathing of their selves, with idh connected to the second maqt. So they loathed their selves because they were invited to faith many times and disbelieved. The present tense is used as in the previous case, and the time of the two loathings is likewise. The real cause is their persistence in disbelief despite repeated calls to faith. It is also permissible that it be a cause for the loathing of Allah, with idh connected to it. What is in favour of this and against it will be known shortly, Allah willing.

The apparent practice of a group of the great scholars is to prefer that idh be temporal, not causal. It was said: it is a temporal adverb of the first maqt, and the meaning is: the loathing of Allah the Exalted toward you in the world, when you were invited to faith and disbelieved, is greater than your loathing of yourselves today while you are in the Fire, or while you are certain that you are among its people. So the time of the two loathings differs. That the time of the first is the world and the time of the second is the Hereafter is transmitted from al-Ḥasan, and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from Mujahid. Many scholars objected to this, saying it requires separating the verbal noun from what is in its complement by a foreign element, namely the predicate. In the Amali of Ibn al-Hajib, he says there is no harm in it, because adverbs have wide latitude.

It was also said: it is an adverb of another verbal noun indicated by the first, or of a verb indicated by that, as in al-Bahr.

In al-Kashf: in this there is that the implied element must have its own complements if it is independent and the breach is wide. If it is made a badal (substitute), then its deletion and the working of the deleted verbal noun is not excluded from separation by the predicate, and it is not foreign in every respect. Estimating the verb, that is, "your loathing of Allah when you are invited", is further and further removed. It was also said: it is an adverb of the second maqt. It was objected that they did not loathe their selves at the time of the invitation, but rather on the Day of Resurrection.

It was answered that the speech on this view is of the kind of the saying of the Commander (Ali, may Allah honour his face): "I was eaten on the day the red bull was eaten," and the saying of ʿAmr ibn ʿAdas al-Tamimi to his divorced wife Dakhtanus bint Laqit, when she asked him for milk, and she had no provisions: "The summer wasted the milk." This is by way of metaphor, treating the occurrence of the cause, which is their disbelief at the time of the invitation, as the occurrence of the effect, which is their loathing of their selves when they witness what befell them because of it. It was also said: the meaning according to this is "when it becomes clear that you were invited to faith, which saves, and to the truth which deserves acceptance, and you refused." Or the meaning of "their selves" is their kind among the believers, for they used to loathe the believers in the world when they were invited to faith. This is the most remote of the interpretations.

Makki said: idh is governed by an implied verb "remember," and the meaning is bewilderment and reproach. Some scholars approved of this, but I consider it contrary to what is apparent. The author of al-Kashf claimed that in it there is clear incongruity, and he gave a reason whose point has not become clear to me, so reflect.

The explanation of ﴿your loathing of your selves﴾ as the loathing of each one of them for himself is the apparent meaning. It is also permissible that it means the loathing of some of them for others. It was said: the followers loathe the leaders because they led them into disbelief, and the leaders loathe the followers because they followed them, so they bore burdens like their burdens. So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 11:

﴿They said: "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ These are adjectives of the two verbal nouns (masadir) of the two verbs, and the implied sense is: "You caused us to die a death, two (deaths), and You gave us life a life, two (lives)."

It is also permitted that the two verbal nouns are "two deaths" (mawtatayn) and "two lives" (hayatayn), and these are either verbal nouns of the two verbs mentioned, with the augmentation removed, or verbal nouns of two other verbs which the mentioned ones indicate. For causing to die (al-imatah) and causing to live (al-ihya') necessarily point to death and life, so it is as if they said: "You caused us to die, so we died two deaths, two," and "You gave us life, so we lived two lives, two," in the manner of his saying:

"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but the stripped or the scraped."

That is, it has left, so nothing remains except the stripped... etc. The meaning of this has been disputed. It is said: by the first causing to die they meant creating them dead; by the second, their causing to die at the completion of their terms; by the first giving of life, their being given life through the breathing of the spirit into them while they were in the wombs; and by the second, their being given life through the returning of their spirits to their bodies for the resurrection. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas, and by a group including al-Hakim, who declared it sound, from Ibn Mas'ud; and by 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir from Qatadah. It is also related from al-Dahhak and Abu Malik. They made this comparable to the verse [al-Baqarah: 28]: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life again?﴾

If causing to die is literally the making of a thing devoid of life, whether or not it was preceded by life, then the matter is clear. If it is literally the transforming of life into non-existence after it was existent, as is apparent from their statement, where they said: the form of the verbs and the form of the intensive (tafil) are both coined for "making into" (tasyir), that is, transferring from one state to another, then in applying it to what is counted as the first causing to die there is obscurity, since that requires that life preceded, and there is no preceding in what has been mentioned. It has been justified that this is by way of metaphor (majaz), as they established regarding "the narrowness of the mouth of the well and the breadth of its bottom." They said: when the Maker chooses one of two permissible options, while He is equally able to do either, He has diverted the made thing, which was permissible, from the other; so His diverting it from it is like transferring it from it. That is, the verbal form (af'al) or the intensive form (taf'il), which indicates "making into," is used metaphorically for transferring from one state to another state, by way of its necessary consequence, which is diverting from what is within the realm of possibility. Following from this is making the possible, whose willing is permitted, equivalent to the actual. Likewise, the command in the narrowness of the mouth of the well, for example, is made, by its issuing, to be at the second state, equivalent to commanding its transfer from something else. For this reason, one of the eminent scholars made it equivalent to a metaphor by implication (isti'arah bil-kinayah), so it is a metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) entailing a metaphor by implication. Thus what is meant by causing to die there is diverting, not transferring.

Some have stated that it is necessary to affirm the generality of metaphor, lest there be a combination of literal and metaphorical meaning in the verse, or the use of a homonym in both its meanings, on the assumption that the form is shared between diverting and transferring. Whoever permits what has been mentioned does not need to hold this.

In al-Kashshaf, Jar Allah preferred that one of the two causings to die is what is mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you were dead and He gave you life﴾, and applying it to that is by way of metaphor, and it is a metaphor used in the Qur'an. The manner of the figurative usage has been mentioned. The verification of this rests on one point: giving life means making a thing living. So when the earthly or seminal material is endowed with life, it is correctly said that it has become possessed of life in the literal sense, since there is no need for a literal preceding death, but only for a preceding absence of life. Thus there is giving life in the literal sense. As for causing to die, if the opposition between death and life is taken as the well-known opposition (al-taqabul al-mashhuri), it requires that it be preceded by life, so causing to die before it is not valid literally. If the real opposition (al-taqabul al-haqiqi) is taken, it is valid. But the apparent usage, according to the customs of the Arabs and non-Arabs, is that it is the well-known kind. End.

By the well-known and the real kinds he meant what they mentioned concerning opposition by privation and possession (al-'adam wal-malakah). For they said: the two opposites by privation and possession are two matters, one of which is existential and the other the absence of that existential quality in a subject receptive of it. If its receptivity is considered according to its individual person at the time of its being qualified by the privative matter, then it is the well-known privation and possession, like beardlessness, for it is the absence of a beard in what by its nature at that time should have a beard, for a child is not called beardless. If its receptivity is considered more generally, without being restricted to that time, like the absence of a beard in a child, or if its receptivity is considered according to its species, like blindness in one born blind, or according to its nearer genus, like blindness in the scorpion, or its more remote genus, like the absence of voluntary motion in a mountain, for its remote genus, namely body, which is above the inanimate, is receptive of voluntary motion, then it is the real privation and possession. But there is some obscurity in basing the requirement of being preceded by life and its absence upon that, and especially if the expression in the past form is added, as is not hidden from the one who reflects.

Then the causing to die twice and the giving of life likewise was explained by His saying: ﴿So we confess our sins﴾, namely that they had denied the resurrection and so disbelieved, and following that came countless sins, for whoever does not fear the consequence will run wild in disobedience. When they saw that causing to die and giving life had recurred upon them, they knew that God, exalted is He, is able to restore them just as He is able to originate them, so they confessed their sins which they had committed, namely the denial of the resurrection and the sins that followed from it.

Al-Suddi said: by the first causing to die they meant their being caused to die at the completion of their terms; by the first giving of life, their being given life in the grave for questioning; by the second causing to die, their being caused to die after this giving of life until the Hour; and by the second giving of life, their being given life for the resurrection. It was objected to him that this speaker would then be committed to three givings of life, so it should have been said in the revealed text "You gave us life three times." If he claims that the well-known life, which was in this world, is not counted because of its rapid passing and the cessation of its effects and rulings, then he is committed to not counting the causing to die after it.

Some of the verifiers, in defending this view, said: the purpose of the disbelievers in this statement is their acknowledgment of what they used to deny in this world and what they used to reject when the prophets called them to faith in God and the Last Day. For their saying here is like an answer to the call in His saying: ﴿They will be called out: "The hatred of God is greater..."﴾. It is as if they answered: "The prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, called us, and we used to believe that there is no life after death. Now we acknowledge the two deaths and the two lives because of the hardships and conditions of both that we have endured." So the sin confessed is the denial of the resurrection, and for this it is made consequent upon the statement. They mentioned the two causings to die only in order to mention the two givings of life, since both lives were denied by them, unlike the life well known. The station of this verse is other than the station of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you were dead and He gave you life﴾, for this, as you have heard, is to explain the acknowledgment and confession on their part in the Hereafter of what they denied in this world, while that is to explain the favour which calls for the thanks of the benefactor, or to explain the proofs in order to turn them away from disbelief.

What favours this view is that the usage of applying causing to die to both causings to die is evident. It was criticized by al-Kashshaf, which said: there is no indication in the wording that shows the first giving of life is excluded, though applying it to that is more evident, and the contrast calls for its inclusion. It suffices for the confession to establish one of the two givings of life other than the first. It has also been said: they only said "You gave us life twice" because they are two kinds: the giving of life for resurrection and a giving of life before it. Then the giving of life for resurrection is of two parts: a giving of life in the grave and a giving of life at the Hour. But He did not mention its division, because they were deniers of both its parts.

It was objected that mentioning the second causing to die, which is in the grave, is evidence that the division is intended, and that the meaning is a personal multiplicity, not a generic one. Yes, this may serve as support for what Jar Allah chose. It has been related from a group of the early generation that although the givings of life are three, it omitted mention of the second, because it is included in the giving of life for resurrection. This was said by the author of al-Kashshaf, who then said: on this view, the causing to die according to the choice of Jar Allah is a causing to die before life and a causing to die after it, and the causing to die in the grave has been omitted just as its giving of life has been omitted. And you may say that causing to die is a single kind, unlike giving of life, so plurality was observed in giving of life personally and not in causing to die; and he mentioned the second causing to die because it is denied by them, like the two lives, and it must be acknowledged; not for the sake of indicating that plurality in giving of life is personal. The truth is that this is a valid aspect, but His saying, exalted is He: ("two") is apparent in the sense of a single occurrence, so for this reason whoever preferred the first aspect preferred it, even though causing to die in it is not evident, on the way that this is a metaphor used in the Qur'an. So reflect.

The Imam said: most of the scholars have argued from this verse for the establishment of the punishment of the grave, because they established for themselves two deaths. One of the two deaths is witnessed in this world, so there must be the establishment of another life in the grave, so that the death that follows it becomes a second death, and this indicates the occurrence of a life in the grave. He extended the discussion in verifying this and defending it. But the fair-minded person holds that the punishment of the grave is established by the sound hadiths and not by this verse, because of the strength of the aspect narrated from the one you heard first concerning it. It has been said that it is the aspect; but I think that al-Zamakhshari's choice of it is due to a Mu'tazili subtlety. Ibn Zayd said concerning the verse: what is meant is their being given life as particles (nasam) when the covenant was taken from them from the loins of Adam, then their being caused to die after that, then their being given life in this world, then their being caused to die, then their being given life. This is explicit that the givings of life are three, and he applied the term giving of life to the third, and the most probable assumption is that he meant by it the giving of life for resurrection. It has been said: the repetition in their speech is like its occurrence in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then return the gaze twice (karratayn)﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], where it is intended to mean repetition and multiplication. So it is as if they said: "You caused us to die time after time and You gave us life time after time, so we know Your great power, and that the restoration is not beyond You, just as other things are not beyond You. So we confess our sins which we committed in denying that." On this view, you need not regard the death in the loins of Adam, then the giving of life for the covenant, then the causing to die, then the giving of life by the breathing of the spirit in the wombs, then the causing to die at the completion of the term in this world, then the giving of life in the grave for questioning or other purposes, then causing to die in it, then giving life for resurrection. It is not hidden that, with what is in it, this is complete only if the statement were "You caused us to die two deaths or two times, and You gave us life two lives or two times," for example, not what is in the revealed text, for "two" there is a description of both "two deaths" and "two lives," and it is a safeguard against the possibility that multiplication is intended, as was said regarding ﴿two gods, two (ithnayn)﴾ [al-Nahl: 51]. Basing the matter on the view that number has no concept (mafhum) is not free from debate. Among the strangest things said about this is what is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: that the disbeliever in this world is alive in body but dead in heart, so the two states are taken into account; there is then a causing to die and a giving of life for the heart and the body in this world, then their being caused to die at the completion of their terms, then their being given life for resurrection. Something like this is related so that one may be informed of his condition.

﴿So is there any way out?﴾ That is, any kind of exit from the Fire, meaning: is there any way to a quick or slow exit, or from one place in it to another, or to the world or to something else,

﴿from a path?﴾ a route among the routes, so that we may take it. Such an expression is used in despair. It is not intended as a question; they said it out of extreme despair, as an excuse or in bewilderment. For this reason they were answered by mention of what brought them to ruin, and it is:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ ... and so on. [The question is] without an answer concerning the exit, either negation or affirmation, even if the interrogation is on its apparent meaning, and what is intended is a request for exit, like ﴿Send us back, that we may act righteously﴾ [As-Sajdah: 12] and similar to it. It would be said: ﴿Be silent therein⁠﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 108], or something similar to that, so it is said.
