It is also permitted that they requested the return so that they might act in accordance with the requirement of that acknowledgment, but with a sense of its improbability and a perception of despair regarding it. The answer is a way of making them despair, by explaining that they were persistent in polytheism, so they were recompensed with the continuation of punishment and abiding in the Fire, as His Exalted judgment requires. That is an answer negating the path to exit in the most emphatic manner. I see no harm in this view, and it is likely to be the most immediately apparent. The meaning: ﴿That﴾ is the torment you are in, ﴿because⁠﴾, that is, due to the fact that the matter is that when ﴿Allah is called upon⁠﴾, that is, worshipped by Him, Glorified is He, in the world, ﴿alone⁠﴾, that is, singled out and solitary. It is then an accusative of circumstance, interpreted as a indefinite derivative noun; or it is to be taken as "He was made one alone" as an absolute object of a verb implied by the verb, in the manner of ﴿And He caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. The whole sentence is also a circumstantial clause, its verb omitted and the verbal noun put in its place. There is another discussion concerning this, detailed in the commentary on "al-Wafdah," and some of it has already passed.

﴿You disbelieved⁠﴾ in His Oneness, Exalted is He, that is, you denied and rejected that. ﴿And if partners are associated with Him, you believe⁠﴾ in the associating, that is, you acquiesce and affirm it. In the use of ﴿idha⁠﴾ and the past form in the first conditional, and ﴿in⁠﴾ and the present form in the second, there is an indication, which is not hidden, of the wretchedness of their state. Since that is so, ﴿the judgment belongs to Allah⁠﴾, who does not judge except with truth and does not decide except by what wisdom requires, ﴿the Most High, the Great⁠﴾, who is characterized by the utmost of knowledge and the furthest limit of greatness, so there is nothing like unto Him in His essence, attributes and acts. For this reason His dominion is severe against those who associate partners with Him, and His wisdom requires their eternal abiding in the Fire, so there is no way for your exit from it, ever, since you were polytheists. The Kharijites' use of this verse for their corrupt claim is utterly baseless, and it suffices in refuting them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family﴾ [An-Nisa': 35], and the verse, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Judged by it are two just men among you⁠﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95].

﴿He it is who shows you His signs﴾, which indicate His great affairs that necessitate His being alone in divinity (ulluhiyyah), so that you may infer from them that and act in accordance with what they require. So when He alone is called upon, you believe, and when partners are associated with Him, you disbelieve. These signs are what is observed of the effects of His power, exalted and majestic is He.

*In everything there is a sign of Him, indicating that He is One.*

﴿And sends down﴾ with tashdid (gemination of the letter nun), and it is also read with takhfif (lightening), from al-inzal. ﴿for you provision from the sky﴾, i.e., a cause of provision, which is rain. Its being singled out for mention, although it is among those signs, is because it is distinguished by the description of being one of the effects of His mercy and of the great blessings that necessitate gratitude. The use of the present tense in both verbs indicates the renewal and continuity of the showing and the sending down. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the object is for what has passed more than once. ﴿And none is mindful﴾ by means of those signs, which are as if fixed in the intellects, yet are overlooked due to their obviousness, because of being absorbed in imitation and following desire, ﴿except one who turns back﴾, i.e., who returns from denial by turning toward them and reflecting upon them. For the one who is certain of something does not look at what contradicts it. Thus whoever does not turn back is far removed from remembrance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 14:

﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾: worship Him, the Mighty and Majestic, sincere to Him in religion, free from shirk. ﴿Though the disbelievers dislike it﴾: your sincerity [in worship] and it is hard for them.

The apparent meaning of the words of al-Kashshaf is that "So call upon..." etc. is caused by (musabbab 'an) the turning in repentance (al-inabah), and that there is in it an iltifat (shift of grammatical person, from third to second) where he said: "Then He said to those who turn in repentance" [p. 55]. The original wording would be "let that penitent one call upon [Him]," in the sense of "if the turning in repentance is sound," in the manner of "we have indeed come to Khurasan." Many have agreed that it is an address to those who were mentioned.

In al-Kashf, the verification is that His words, exalted is He, ﴿And none will be reminded﴾ etc., are an i'tiraḍ (parenthetical insertion), and His words, glorified is He, ﴿So call upon Allah﴾ are caused by His words, exalted is He, ﴿It is He who shows you﴾, on the basis that it is an address that includes both the believer and the disbeliever, because they were both mentioned earlier, not for the disbelievers alone, in the manner of ﴿[the aversion] of you toward yourselves﴾, since it is not among what they were called to on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is "so call upon Him." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun so that it would settle more firmly, and to indicate that His being the true object of worship is what requires that He alone be worshipped. The benefit of the i'tiraḍ is that these verses and their indication of His, glorified is He, being exclusively the object of worship apply to the one who turns in repentance, not to the stubborn opponent.

As for his words in al-Kashshaf, "Then He said to those who turn in repentance," it is an indication that the benefit of placing the i'tiraḍ first is that benefiting from the verses, in this case, is as if it were caused by the turning in repentance in meaning, since the causing of the earlier by the later was the turning in repentance. This is the correct view, and the explanation of ﴿though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ by his words "even if that enrages your enemies" does not contradict it, for it serves to alert that the carrying out of that command happens only after their repentance, as if that had already occurred and the opposition between them and the disbelievers had taken place. This is a verification worthy of acceptance, but in the interpretation of al-Kashshaf's words there is clear strain.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 15:**

﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ is a *ṣifah mushabbahah* (a quasi-adjectival form), and it is put in the genitive construct with its agent, from *rufiʿa al-shayʾu* (with *ḍamm*), meaning that a thing rose high. It is also permissible that it be a *ṣīghat mubālaghah* (intensive form) of the pattern of active participles, with its genitive complement being the object, though this is distant. (*Al-darajāt*) means the ascents of the angels, peace be upon them, until they reach the Throne. That is, He is the Exalter of the degrees of His angels and their ascents to His Throne.

Ibn Jubayr explained it as "the heavens." There is no harm in this, for the angels ascend from heaven to heaven until they reach the Throne. However, he made *rafīʿ* an active participle with its complement being the object, and said: that is, the raising of one heaven above another, and the Throne is above them all. You have already heard that this has a distance to it. Describing Him, exalted is He, by this is an indication, by way of *idmāj* (incidental inclusion), of His might, glory be to Him, and His sovereignty, may His majesty be exalted.

It is also permissible that it be a metonymy (*kināyah*) for the exaltedness of His station and authority, may His station and authority be exalted, just as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, is a metonymy for His dominion, may His majesty be glorified. No consideration is given to whether He, glory be to Him, has a throne or not. Metonymy, although it does not negate the intention of the literal meaning, does not necessitate that the literal meaning be intended. Ibn Zayd said: that is, the one of great attributes. It seems to be an explanation of the resulting metonymic meaning. It was also said: they are the degrees of His reward, which He bestows upon His friends, exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Salam. This is more appropriate to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere in devotion to Him﴾. The first meaning is more appropriate to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He sends down the Spirit by His command﴾, because it includes mention of the angels, peace be upon them, who are those sent down with the Spirit, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. Whichever is the case, ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, and the clause ﴿He sends down﴾ are three predicates. It was said that they are predicates of *huwa* (He), which precedes in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is He who shows you﴾ and so on. Abu Hayyan considered this unlikely because of the long separation. It was also said that *huwa* is omitted, and the clause is like a reason for specifying worship and sincerity of religion for Him, exalted is He. It contains an explanation of the sending down of spiritual provision after the explanation of the sending down of physical provision in ﴿He sends down for you provision from the sky﴾. The intended meaning of the Spirit, according to what is related from Qatadah, is revelation, and according to what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, is the Qur'an. This flows in the hearts as the spirit flows in the bodies. Al-Dahhak explained it as Jibril, peace be upon him, and he, peace be upon him, is the life of hearts in terms of the knowledge that descends with him.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted that it means everything with which Allah, exalted is He, bestows favour upon His rightly guided servants in conveying faith and noble intellectual matters. This, as you see, is far-fetched. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by His command﴾: it was said that it is an explanation of the Spirit, and it was interpreted as that which encompasses command and prohibition. It was preferred over the word revelation to indicate that the specificity of the life of hearts through revelation is from two aspects, that of emptying (*takhallī*) and adorning (*taḥallī*), which are achieved through compliance and abstention.

Page 56

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that *amr* is interpreted as decree (*qaḍāʾ*). Then *min* is made initial (*ibtidāʾiyyah*), related to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *al-rūḥ* (the Spirit), meaning: arising from His command. Or it is a qualifier of it, according to the view of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its clause, meaning: the one who is from His command. Some of them interpreted it as the angel and made *min* initial, related to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause or qualifier, as mentioned above. The angel being the source of revelation is because he receives it from Him. As for the one who interpreted the Spirit as Jibril, peace and blessings be upon him, he said: *min* is causal (*sababiyyah*), related to *yulqī* (He sends down). The meaning is: He sends down the Spirit for the sake of conveying His command ﴿to whom He wills of His servants﴾, and they are those whom He, glory be to Him, chose for His messages and the conveyance of His rulings to them. The renewing continuity (*istimrār tajaddudī*) understood from *yulqī* is evident, for the sending down (*ilqāʾ*) has not ceased from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until the end of the time of our Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. It is in the sense of continuity until the Hour, by the establishment of one who carries out the call, according to what Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, sends to this community, at the head of every hundred years, one who renews its religion for it." That is, by reviving what has been obliterated of acting upon the Book and the Sunnah and commanding according to their requirements. The matter of that renewal, according to what Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted, does not need what has been mentioned.

*Rafīʿ* was read in the accusative (*naṣb*) as a mode of praise. ﴿That he may warn﴾ is a cause (*ʿillah*) for the sending down. Its hidden pronoun refers to Allah, exalted is He, or to the one, or to the Spirit, or to the command. Its return to the one to whom it is sent, who is the Messenger, is closer both in wording and meaning, due to the nearness of the referent and the strength of the attribution, for he is the one who warns people in reality without intermediary. Abu Hayyan preferred that it returns to Him, exalted is He, because He, glory be to Him, is the one spoken of. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the Day of Encounter﴾ is an object of *li-yundhira*, or a time adverb, and the object of warning is omitted, meaning: to warn of the punishment or the like on the Day of Encounter,

The phrase ﴿يَوْمَ هم بارِزُونَ﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in grammar an appositive) for ﴿يَوْمَ التَّلاقِ﴾. *Hum* is the *mubtada'* (subject) and *barizun* the *khabar* (predicate), and the clause is in the position of a genitive after the noun *yawm*, which is governed by the preposition-like prefix of the clause. It was said: this is an analysis according to the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) that it is permissible to add a future time-adverb such as *idhā* to a nominal clause, as in "I will come to you when Zayd is going." Sibawayh does not permit this, and requires an implied verb after the adverb, with the noun being in the nominative by virtue of that verb. It is also permissible that *yawm* be an adverb (*zarf*) for the words of Allah Most High: ﴿لا يَخْفى عَلى اللَّهِ مِنهم شَيْءٌ﴾ ("Nothing about them is hidden from Allah"). The apparent reading is the substitute construction. This clause is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) explaining and confirming their emergence, and removing what some of the doubters in this world used to suppose, namely that they could hide, which is a false supposition. It is also permissible that it be a second predicate (*khabar thani*) for *lahum*.

It was said: it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun in ﴿بارِزُونَ﴾. And ﴿يَوْمَ التَّلاقِ﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, so named, said Ibn Abbas, because creatures meet on it. Muqatil said: because the Creator and the created meet on it. al-Tabarsi related this from Ibn Abbas. al-Suddi said: because the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet on it. Maymun ibn Mihran said: because the oppressor and the oppressed meet on it. al-Tha'labi related that it is because every person meets his deeds. Some of the eminent scholars preferred what Muqatil said, and said: it is the best of the opinions, because it applies the unrestricted term to what occurs in many places, such as ﴿فَمَن كانَ يَرْجُو لِقاءَ رَبِّهِ﴾ ("Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord"),

﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us"),

﴿وقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَرْجُونَ لِقاءَنا﴾ ("And those who do not hope for meeting Us say").

The author of al-Kashshaf said: the first opinion, which was related from Ibn Abbas first, is more fitting, because the discourse runs on its literal sense, and because it negates what might be supposed of equality between the Creator and the created, and because each of the two substitutes has its own benefit in intensifying the terror: the first portrays the meeting of creatures of differing kinds, and the second portrays the emergence before the Owner of their affairs in a manner that leaves no doubt for anyone. As for verses such as ﴿لِقاءَ رَبِّهِ﴾ (al-Kahf 110), they are used with another meaning. ( وبارِزُونَ ) derives from *baraza*, and its root meaning is "to be in the open" (*bi-raz*), that is, in open ground (*fada'*). The intended meaning is "visible," with nothing concealing them, not a mountain, a hill, or a building, because on that day the earth will be a level plain (*qa' safsaf*), and they will not have garments; rather they will be naked and uncovered, as came in the two *Sahihs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Ibn Abbas: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Indeed you will meet Allah barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised.'" It was said: the meaning is "those who come out of their graves," or "their deeds and their inner secrets will be manifest." It was said: "their souls will be manifest, not veiled by the coverings of the bodies while still attached to them." This last view is not accepted without a sound report from the Infallible (the Prophet ﷺ). The meaning of Allah's words ( مِنهم ), as has been said, is "of their conditions and their deeds."

It was said: "of their persons," and the generality was preferred, meaning: nothing is hidden from Him, exalted is His majesty, of their persons, their deeds, and their conditions, whether apparent or hidden, past or future.

Ubayy read ﴿لِيُنْذِرَ يَوْمُ﴾ with *yundhira* in the active voice and *yawm* in the nominative as the subject, metaphorically. al-Yamani, as mentioned by the author of al-Lawami', read ﴿لِيُنْذَرَ﴾ in the passive, with ﴿يَوْمُ﴾ in the nominative as a deputy for the subject. al-Hasan and al-Yamani, as mentioned by Ibn Khalawayh, read ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ with the feminine *ta'* (second person). It was said: the subject in it is the pronoun of address referring to the Messenger ﷺ. It was said: the pronoun refers to the Spirit, because it is feminine.

Allah Most High's words ﴿لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ﴾ ("Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer") are a quotation of what is asked on that day and of what is answered, with an implied speech verb coordinated with what precedes it from the negated resumptive clause, or it is a resumptive clause that comes as an answer to a question arising from the description of their emergence and the manifestation of their states, as if it were said: "What will happen then?" and it was answered: "It will be said: ﴿لِمَنِ المُلْكُ﴾..." etc.

Allah Most High's words ﴿اليَوْمَ تُجْزى كُلُّ نَفْسٍ﴾ mean: of souls, both righteous and wicked, ﴿بِما كَسَبَتْ﴾ ("for what it earned"), that is, of good or evil, ﴿لا ظُلْمَ اليَوْمَ﴾ ("no injustice today"), by reducing the reward or increasing the punishment, ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ ("indeed Allah is swift in reckoning"), that is, His reckoning is swift, since He, glorified is He, is not preoccupied by one matter from another, so He reaches the account of souls for what each deserves quickly. It was related from Ibn Abbas that when He, Most High, begins to reckon them, the people of Paradise do not speak except in Paradise, and the people of Hell do not speak except in Hell. As a completion of the answer, it was brought to explain the summary contained in it, and the closing phrase serves to give the reason for what precedes it.

The one who utters this, both question and answer, is one and the same.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Allah Most High will gather the creatures on the Day of Resurrection in one level place, a white earth like a silver ingot, in which Allah Most High was never disobeyed and in which no error was ever made. The first thing He will say is that a caller will call out: ﴿لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ﴾ ﴿اليَوْمَ تُجْزى كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِما كَسَبَتْ لا ظُلْمَ اليَوْمَ إنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾. The first of the disputes with which they will begin is that of blood..." and the hadith continues. According to al-Hasan, the one asking is Allah Himself, exalted and majestic. It was said: he is an angel. It was said: the questioner is Allah Most High or an angel, and the answerer is the people.

al-Tayyibi, in explaining the statement of al-Kashshaf, stated that the words of Allah Most High ﴿اليَوْمَ تُجْزى﴾ ... etc. are a reason (*ta'lil*), so the questioner and the answerer must be Allah, exalted and majestic. When He, glorified is He, asked ﴿لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ﴾ and answered Himself ﴿لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ﴾, the situation became the place for a question and a demand for an explanation.

The Lord's words, "Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned" (Q. 40:17), are an answer to the question. This means that sovereignty belongs to Allah alone because He alone is able to requite every soul for what it has earned. He has perfect justice, so He wrongs no one. He has complete control, so no matter does not distract Him from another, and He therefore hastens the reckoning. Had "For Allah, the One, the Subduer" been the answer given by the people of the gathering, this resumptive clause would not have been appropriate. End of quotation from al-Alusi. There is much in it to be examined.

The truth is that the words of Allah, the Exalted, "Today every soul will be recompensed..." etc., if they are from the speech of the one answering, as the apparent meaning of the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud indicates, after the people have spoken, it is also permitted that they are not part of the completion of the answer, but are rather a report of what Allah, the Exalted, will say on that day after the question and answer. In any case, the restriction of sovereignty to Allah, the Exalted, on that day is only with regard to the apparent state of affairs, namely the cessation of causes, the removal of intermediaries, and the manifestation of this to the disbelievers and the ignorant. As for the reality of the matter, it always testifies to this. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi held that the question and answer are from Allah Himself and will occur between the two blasts, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, annihilates the creation. A similar view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

'Abd ibn Humayd in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A caller will call out before the Hour: 'O people, the Hour has come upon you.' The living and the dead will hear it. Allah, glory be to Him, will descend to the lowest heaven and say: 'Whose is the sovereignty today? To Allah, the One, the Subduer.'" The context clearly indicates that this is the Day of Resurrection, so perhaps, if the hadith is sound, it occurs twice.

The meaning of souls being recompensed for what they have earned is that they will be requited with good if they earned good, and with evil if they earned evil. It has been said that souls acquire, through beliefs and deeds, states that necessitate their pleasure and their pain, but they do not perceive them in this world. When the Resurrection comes and the obstacles are removed, they will experience their pain and their pleasure. The apparent meaning of this view is that it speaks of spiritual pleasure and pain, and we do not deny that these will occur on that day. But we say that the recompense is not confined to these two, rather it will also be with bodily pleasure and pain. Therefore, restricting the interpretation of the verse to this alone is deficient.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 40, verse 18:**

﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day﴾: the Day of Resurrection, as Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said. The meaning of *al-Azifah* is "the near one." It is said: *azifa al-shukhus* ("the departure drew near") when its time came near and grew short. Originally it is an active participle (*ism fa'il*), but it was then transferred from that usage and made a proper noun for the Resurrection, because it is near in relation to what has passed of the duration of the world, or in relation to what remains, since every coming thing is near. It is also permissible that it remains in its original sense, so that it is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "the imminent Hour." Some scholars supposed the omitted noun to be *al-khutta* (with a dammed *kha'* and a shadda on the unmarked *ta'*), which means the matter or the great affair that deserves to be written down and inscribed because of its strangeness. By this is meant the difficult events that occur on the Day of Resurrection, and their nearness, because every coming thing is near. By "the Day" is meant the time in general, or it is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim said: "*Yawm al-Azifah*" is the Day of death and the arrival of the appointed term.

This interpretation is preferred because it is further from repetition, more fitting to what follows it, and the description of its nearness is more evident.

﴿When the hearts are at the throats﴾: this is a substitute (*badal*, a grammatical apposition) for "the Day of the Imminent." *Al-Hanajir* is the plural of *hanjarah* or *hunjur*, like *hulqum* (throat), in both wording and meaning. It is, as al-Raghib said, the top of the Adam's apple from the outside, a piece of flesh between the head and the neck. The expression is a metaphor (*kinayah*) for intense fear or extreme anguish. It is also permitted that it be taken literally: the hearts of the disbelievers reach their throats on the Day of Resurrection, yet they do not die, as would be the case in this world.

﴿Choking with grief﴾ (*kazimin*) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the owners of the hearts, according to the sense, since mention of the hearts indicates mention of their owners. It is of the same type as ﴿And We shall remove whatever rancour is in their breasts﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]. It is as if it was said: "When their hearts are at their throats, choking upon them." It comes from *kazama al-qirbah*, meaning when one fills a water-skin and seals its mouth. The meaning is: holding themselves back over their hearts, lest they come out with the breath, for the one who stops a water-skin holds it upon the water, lest it spill out because it is full. There is great emphasis in this.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *al-qulub* (the hearts) hidden in the predicate, that is, ﴿at the throats﴾. According to the view of those who permit a circumstantial clause to come from the subject, it may be a circumstantial clause from *al-qulub* itself.

The plural is used in the manner of rational beings (*jam' al-'uqala'*), because the hearts are treated as if they were rational beings, since they are described with their attributes, as in His saying: ﴿So their necks remain bowed to it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4]. The meaning is: while the hearts are choking upon distress and affliction. From this it is known that ﴿at the throats﴾ cannot be a locative complement (*zarf*) of ﴿choking﴾, because the meaning would be corrupted and it would require an omitted element while being in no need of it. Likewise, according to the reading *kazimun* applied only to the first (subject), it becomes necessary that ﴿at the throats﴾ be a predicate and *kazimun* be another predicate. By this, the view that the circumstantial clause refers to the hearts is preferred.

Al-Kawashi supposed "they are choking" (*hum kazimun*) so as to agree with the circumstantial status of the owners. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the object of *andhir-hum* ("warn them"), meaning: warn them while appointing their choking, or while being close to choking.

﴿They will have no close friend (*hamim*) who would be concerned for them, nor an intercessor who would be obeyed﴾: *hamim* means a close, sympathetic friend. It is said: *ihtamma Fulan li-Fulan* ("so-and-so became angry for so-and-so") when he became incensed, as if he is the one who becomes incensed in protection of his relatives. The close intimates of a man are called *hammatuhu*, and from this *al-hamim* has been interpreted as "friend." ﴿Nor an intercessor who would be obeyed﴾: that is, nor an intercessor who would intercede. The clause is in a position of genitive or nominative as a qualifier of "intercessor." The intended meaning is the negation of the attribute and of the qualified noun, not the attribute alone, so as to indicate that there is an intercessor, but he is not obeyed. The statement is of the type: "You do not see the lizard entering a hole in it." He did not confine himself to negating the benefit of the intercessor, but added to it what he added, so that the negation of the qualified noun stands in place of evidence for the negation of the attribute. That addition therefore removes the supposition of the existence of the qualified noun, since its non-existence was made a settled, well-known matter, with no dispute about it, because evidence should be clearer than what it proves. This is like saying to one who reproaches you for staying away from the raid: "I have no horse to ride, and I have no weapon to fight with." Let this be understood.

If the pronouns mentioned from the words ﴿and warn them﴾ up to this point refer to the disbelievers, as is apparent, then placing ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ in the position of their pronoun serves to record wrongdoing against them and to give the reason for the ruling. If, however, the pronouns are general, referring to them and to others, then this is not a case of placing an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun, but rather a statement of a ruling specifically for the wrongdoers. The wrongdoers meant are those who are complete in wrongdoing, and they are the disbelievers, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 19:

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾, i.e., the treacherous glance, such as a glance at one who is not a mahram and furtively stealing looks at him, and other than that. So "khaa'innah" is an attribute of an implied noun (mawsuf muqaddar), and making the glance "treacherous" is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), or a explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah), or an implicit metaphor (kinayah) with an imaginative element (takhyil), by making the glance like a thing that is stolen from the one being looked at; for this reason the word "stealing" (istiraq) was used for it. It is also permissible for khaa'innah to be a verbal noun (masdar), like kadhibah, 'aqibah and 'afiyah, meaning: He, glorified is He, knows the treachery of the eyes. It was said: it is an attribute added to its described noun, as in the line of poetry:

"And if you give drink to the noble people, [you make] the wicked among us [drink]"

meaning: He, glorified is He, knows the treacherous eyes. But this does not fit with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what the breasts conceal﴾, meaning: and that which the breasts conceal of inner thoughts; or the concealing of the breasts for what they conceal of that. Because harmony (mula'amah) is required to be observed in the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan), and what suits the treacherous eyes is the concealed breasts. As for what was said regarding the impropriety of this, that the station of hyperbole requires that the stealing of the glance be intended, [this] is added to it as a first indication; it does not undermine the stated reasoning, since there is no obstacle to its being on a sought-after matter with indications. Then, were it not for the indication, it would be permissible to make the eyes a preparation for the attribute; so the indication is what prevents it. This sentence, according to the Kashshaf, is connected to the beginning of the speech, being one of the predicates of "huwa" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the One who shows you﴾, in the sense of: He is the One who shows you... etc. And He knows the treachery of the eyes. He did not make it a reason for negating intercession, in the sense of: they have no intercessor, because God, exalted is He, knows the treachery from them, secretly and openly. It was said: because it is not suitable as a reason for negating it, but rather for negating its acceptance, for God, exalted is He, is the Knower, not the intercessor, and the intended meaning is the negation of intercession. The reason for placing this predicate in this position is what it contains of transition (takhallus) to condemning their gods, although placing it before ﴿the One who shows you﴾ has no basis, since it is connected to what precedes it most strongly, as has been indicated. Likewise regarding ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, because of its connection to what precedes and the command to the penitent to be sincere, and because of what it contains of the abruptness (nabw) of placing a verbal negative clause between the subject and its nominal, definite predicate. As for its placement between the three conjunctions, it is like between the staff and its bark, so there is no place more deserving of it than this, and lexical distance does not harm in such a case, as is not hidden. Some thought it harmful: so some of them said: the sentence is connected to the whole of His saying, exalted, glorified is He: ﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day﴾ to its end, because when He, glorified is He, commanded the warning of that Day and what occurs in it of severe distress and grief, and mentioned that the wrongdoer finds no one to protect him from that nor anyone to intercede for him, He, majestic and exalted, mentioned His awareness of everything that proceeds from the servant and that he will be recompensed for what he did, so that he would be wary of that Day, when he knows that God, exalted is He, is aware of his deeds. Abu Hayyan went to this view.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿Swift in reckoning﴾, because the swiftness of His reckoning of creation is only due to His knowledge, which needs no deliberation or thought, nor anything that reckoners need. He, may God have mercy on him, related from a group that it is connected to His saying, exalted: ﴿Nothing among them is hidden from God﴾. Then he said: this is a good view, strengthened by the fit between the two meanings, and weakened by the distance and the number of intervening elements. Some made it connected to the negation of accepting intercession contained in His saying, exalted: ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾, for "yuta'" (obeyed) in the negation means accepting his intercession, on the basis that it is a reason for that: meaning, the intercession of an intercessor for them is not accepted, because God, exalted is He, knows from him the treachery, secretly and openly; and it is not a reason for the negation of intercession, so as to refute what was said. What is in it is not hidden. By my life, the Jarallah (al-Zamakhshari) in a situation like this is not to be matched.

﴿Allah judges with truth﴾. That is, the One who has these attributes judges a judgment joined with truth, not with falsehood, since He, glory be to Him, is free of any need for injustice. The placing of the subject first (taqdim al-musnad ilayhi) is for the sake of *taqwa* (God-consciousness). It has also been permitted that it is for exclusivity (*hasr*, restriction). The benefit of shifting from the pronoun to the proper name, and of using the all-comprehensive name after the mention of the attributes, is what is indicated: the intended referent is the One described by those attributes.

﴿And those whom they call upon besides Him do not judge anything﴾. This is a mockery of their gods, because an inanimate object (*jamad*) is not described as judging or not judging. Some have considered it to be of the type of *mushakala* (rhetorical correspondence, using a word because of its counterpart), and its original form is: "they do not have power over anything." The first reading was preferred, and it was said that this is because mockery is more forceful, since the intended purpose is not to argue for their unfitness to be deities.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi', according to one transmission from him, and Hisham, read *tad'una* ("you call") with the second-person *ta'* (*iltifat*, shift of grammatical person). It has also been permitted that it is under an implied *qul* ("say"), in which case it is not an *iltifat*, even though it was expressed in the third person before it, because it is not against what the context requires, since it is the beginning of a speech built upon addressing them.

﴿Indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. This affirms His knowledge, exalted is He, of the treachery of eyes and what the breasts conceal, and His judging with truth, and it is a warning to them concerning what they say and do, and an allusion to the condition of what they call upon besides Him, mighty and majestic is He. In it is an indication that the judge should be all-hearing and all-seeing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 21:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and observed what was the end of those before them?﴾ That is: what was the condition of those who denied the messengers, peace be upon them, before them, such as ʿAd and Thamud? The verb ﴿yanzurū﴾ (observe) is in the jussive mood (jazm) on the basis that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿yasīrū﴾ (travel). Abu Hayyan permitted that it be in the subjunctive (naṣb) as a response (jawab) to the negation, as in his saying:

*Have you not asked, so that the ruins would inform you?*

It was objected that this cannot be interpreted as "that they did not travel and [therefore] observe." It was answered that the interrogative is a rebuking interrogative (istifham inkari), which carries the sense of negation, so it becomes a response to a negation of a negation.

﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾, meaning in capability and ability to act. The separate pronoun (ḍamīr munfaṣil) ﴿hum﴾ is an emphatic (taʾkid) for the attached pronoun before it. It was also permitted that it be a separator pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl), and it is not necessary that it occur between two definite nouns, for al-Jurjani permitted the present tense to follow it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats﴾ (Al-Buruj: 13). Yes, the more common usage is that it is so. Moreover, the comparative adjective (afʿal al-tafḍil) that follows it and is governed by the "than" (min) that introduces the one surpassed is definite in form, since the article (al) does not enter it, and in meaning, because what is intended is the most excellent with respect to a specific excellence.

Page 61

The clause ﴿kānū﴾ and so on is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) clause, answering the question of how their affairs turned out. Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿minkum﴾ (than you) with the second-person pronoun, as a shift (iltifat).

﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿quwwa﴾ (strength): that is, and greater in traces upon the earth, like well-built fortresses and fortified cities. God, exalted is He, has related of a people among them that they used to hew houses out of the mountains.

It was also permitted that it be conjoined to ﴿ashadd﴾ (stronger), with an elided element assumed, meaning "and greater in traces," so that it includes powerful traces and others. But this is a departure from the apparent meaning without a significant need. It was also said that what is meant by these traces is the traces of their footprints upon the earth, due to the greatness of their bodies, but this is not valid at all.

﴿So God seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from God.﴾ That is: they had no protector from God, exalted is He, who would shield them and prevent His punishment from them ever. The phrasing indicates permanence, and what is meant is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation. The second ﴿min﴾ is extra (zāʾida), and the first ﴿min﴾ is connected to ﴿wāqin﴾ (protector). The prepositional phrase is placed first for emphasis and for the rhyme (fāṣila), since it was said that the name of God, exalted is He, does not occur as a rhyme-ending. It was also permitted that the first ﴿min﴾ be substitutive (badaliyya), meaning: they had no protector in place of the One possessing the attributes of perfection, and by this is meant their associate-gods. And that it be initial (ibtidaʾiyya), as a warning that the seizing was in the utmost severity, for if the protection did not come from Him, glory be to Him, there would be no remaining protection for them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 22:

﴿That﴾ seizing [is] ﴿because﴾ that is, because of the fact that ﴿their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾ with miracles and clear rulings ﴿but they disbelieved﴾ immediately after their messengers came to them with that. ﴿So Allah seized them﴾ ﴿Indeed He is Strong﴾ capable of whatever He wills, mighty and majestic, to the utmost degree of capability ﴿severe in punishment﴾ no punishment is considered great beside His punishment, glory be to Him. This is an explanation of the generality in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, if the ba' there is causal (sababiyyah); and it is an explanation of the cause of the seizing if it is for accompaniment (mulabasah), i.e. their being seized while accompanied by their sins, not repenting of them. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 23:

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are his miracles, peace be upon him, ﴿and a clear authority﴾, a compelling, manifest proof. It has been said that what is meant by this is the same as what is meant by the signs, and that the difference between the two descriptions is treated as if it were a difference between two entities, so the second is conjoined to the first. It has also been said that what is meant is some of his signs that have a particular importance, such as the staff, and that it is conjoined to them to magnify its importance, just as Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, are conjoined to the angels.

This has been objected to on the ground that such a construction is only used when the second item is specified by a proper name or something similar. But with its indefiniteness, there is room for doubt. Al-Tabarsi related that what is meant by the signs are the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), and by the authority the miracles that indicate his prophethood, peace be upon him. It has also been said that the signs are the miracles, and the authority is the holy power (al-quwwah al-qudsiyyah) that he was given, peace be upon him, and its manifestation is through the appearance of its effects, such as his undertaking the call without concern. Isa read «sultanin» with a damma on the lam.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 24:

﴿To Pharaoh and Haman﴾ — Haman was Pharaoh's minister. The Jews claimed that Pharaoh had no minister called Haman, and that Haman was a tyrant who came long after Pharaoh, after a vast span of time and an age of aeons. This denial came to them from the disorder that befell their books and the historical records of Pharaoh, owing to the long lapse of time and the many trials they suffered, so that their souls and their books were largely annihilated.

﴿And Qarun﴾ — It is said that he was one of the people of Moses, peace be upon him. It is also said that he was someone else, and that he was the commander of Pharaoh's armies. Their being mentioned among Pharaoh's followers is due to their standing in disbelief and because they were the most famous of his followers.

In the mention of the story of the sending to Pharaoh and those with him, and the detailed account of what took place, there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and an explanation of the end of those who were the strongest of those before him and the nearest to them in time; this is why this was singled out for mention. And there is no remoteness in the idea that Pharaoh and his armies were stronger than ʿAd. ﴿So they said: "A sorcerer, a liar"﴾ — that is, they, meaning Moses, peace be upon him, are saying he is a sorcerer in respect of the miracles he displayed, ﴿a liar﴾ in his claim that he is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾, and the command of God Most High reached them, [Pharaoh and his people] being unconcerned with their saying, "a sorcerer, a great liar." ﴿They said﴾ out of rage, fury, and inability to counter [him]: ﴿Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women.﴾ That is, return upon them what you used to do to them at first, so that you may prevent them from supporting Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. So the command to kill and to spare occurred twice. The first time was when the soothsayers (kahanah) and astrologers (munajjimun) reported, in Pharaoh's statement, a boy from the Children of Israel who would strip him of his kingdom. The second time is this one, and the pronoun in (they said) refers to Pharaoh and those with him. It has been said that Qarun did not make this statement, but they overpowered him. ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, in loss, from the expression "the animal strayed" (dallat al-dabbah) when it is lost. The meaning is that it benefits them nothing, so the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing. The lam in (the disbelievers) is either the lam of prior reference (lam al-'ahd), and the explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to censure them for disbelief and to indicate the cause of the ruling; or it is the lam of genus (lam al-jins), and those mentioned are included in it primarily. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion placed amid what is related of their falsehoods, to hasten the clarification of the invalidity of what they displayed of lightning and thunder, and its complete collapse.

Pharaoh said, ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾. Whenever he intended to kill him, his people restrained him by saying: "He is not the one you fear. He is weaker and lesser than that, and he is only a sorcerer who is opposed by a sorcerer like himself. If you kill him, you will create doubt among the people, and they will believe that you were unable to counter him with proof." The apparent meaning is that the accursed one (may Allah curse him) was certain that he (peace be upon him) was a prophet, but he had in him deceit and trickery, and he was a killer and a shedder of blood even over trivial matters. So how would he not kill one who was better than him, given that Moses was the one who would overthrow his throne and demolish his kingdom? Rather, he feared that if he intended to kill him, he himself would be hastened to destruction. Therefore his saying ﴿Leave me﴾ ... etc. was a deception toward his people and a way of giving them the impression that they were the ones restraining him, whereas what restrained him was only the terror of fear in his own soul. This is indicated by his saying ﴿and let him call upon his Lord﴾, because its outward sense is contempt for Moses (peace be upon him) by calling upon his Lord (glorified is He), as one says: "Call upon your helper, for I will take vengeance upon you." Its inner meaning is that his limbs were trembling from the supplication of his Lord; therefore he spoke this at the very start of his speech and showed that he did not care about the supplication of his Lord. This is only like one who says: "Leave me, I will do such-and-such, and if it does not happen, so be it." Otherwise, what is it for one who claims to be their lord except that he should give weight to what Moses (peace be upon him) claims, and so utter it mockingly or in earnest?

﴿Indeed I fear﴾ that if I do not kill him, ﴿he will change your religion﴾, meaning that he will alter your state which you are in, of worshipping me and worshipping idols. The accursed one had commanded them to carve idols and to make them intercessors for them with him, just as the disbelievers of Makkah used to say: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18]. For this meaning they attributed the gods to him in their saying: ﴿and leave you and your gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 127]. So this is an attribution of honour and distinction. This is what some of the exegetes adopted. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Al-din (religion) means authority (sultan)," and from this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"If you should settle among a tribe of the Banu Asad, in the authority of 'Amr, and Fadak comes between us,"

meaning: indeed I fear that he will change your authority and make you humble. ﴿Or that he will cause to appear﴾, if he is not able to change your religion entirely, ﴿corruption in the land﴾. This refers to lawlessness, which removes security and brings to a halt farming and livelihoods, and people perish through killing and loss. Thus the corruption he meant is the corruption of your worldly affairs. So the resulting meaning, as established at first, is: indeed I fear that he will corrupt for you the matter of your religion by altering it, or corrupt for you the matter of your worldly life by disruption; and these are two matters, each of which is bitter. Something similar is said regarding the second meaning of "religion." It is related from Qatadah that the accursed one meant by "corruption" the obedience to Allah (exalted is He).

[Page 63]

The people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr read "wa-an," with the connecting waw (al-waw al-wasilah, the conjunctive waw).

Al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans other than Hafs read ﴿yuzhir﴾ (يُظْهِرَ) with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and ﴿al-fasad﴾ (الفَسادُ) in the nominative (marfu'). Mujahid read ﴿yazzahhar﴾ (يَظَّهَّرُ) with a shaddah on the za' and the ha', and ﴿al-fasad﴾ in the nominative. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿yuzhar﴾ (يُظْهَرُ) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ha', in the passive voice (mabni lil-maf'ul), and ﴿al-fasad﴾ in the nominative.

﴿And Moses said﴾ when he heard what the accursed one had spread of talk about killing him, ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge (isti'adhah) in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾. He, peace be upon him, said this addressing his people, according to what many scholars have held. That is because the previous statement from Pharaoh was an address to his people by way of consultation and deliberation, not in the presence of Moses, peace be upon him. So the apparent meaning is that Moses, peace be upon him, also addressed his people, not Pharaoh and those present with him, with this. What supports this is the saying of the Exalted in [al-A'raf: 128], ﴿Moses said to his people, "Seek help in God"﴾, in this very same story. And the Exalted's saying here, (and your Lord), is also supportive, even though Pharaoh and those with him do not believe in His lordship. Their not believing in it (that He is so in reality) does not detract from its being supportive, because support depends on what is apparent. The statement is introduced with "indeed" (inna) for emphasis and to draw attention to the fact that the strongest means of averting harm is seeking refuge in God, the Exalted. The name "Lord" (al-Rabb) is singled out because what is sought is protection and nurture. He attributed the Lord to himself and to them, urging them to agree with him in seeking refuge in Him, glorified is He, and in turning their spirits fully toward Him, exalted is His station, because the combined spirits of a group draw answers. This is the wisdom behind the legislation of congregation in acts of worship.

(And from every) is understood as meaning: from the evil of every one. By "arrogance" he meant refusing to submit to the truth, which is the most loathsome form of arrogance and the clearest indication of the baseness and humiliation of his soul and of the extreme injustice and oppression in him. To this was added not believing in the Day of Recompense, so that it would be even more indicative. Whoever combines arrogance, denial of the Recompense, and lack of concern for the outcome has completed the causes of harshness and audacity against God, the Exalted, and His servants, and has left no great sin without committing it. The word "al-munazzal" was chosen instead of "minhu" as a way of allusion (ta'ridh), because the statement concerns their being displayed, so they would not wear the tiger's skin when it is shown to them. This is in addition to indicating the reason for seeking refuge, and to observing the right of the accursed one's upbringing of him, peace be upon him, in general.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read «عُتُّ» with the assimilation of the dotted dhal into the ta', after converting it into a ta'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 28:

﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾. It is said that he was a Copt, a paternal cousin of Pharaoh, who held the position of heir apparent (wali al-'ahd) and of chief of police (sahib al-shurta). It is also said that he was an Israelite, and it is said that he was a stranger, not belonging to either of the two groups. His description, on these two views, as "from the family of Pharaoh" is by way of his entering their company and showing that he was of their religion and creed out of dissimulation (taqiyya, concealing one's true belief under fear) and fear. The same is said of the idafa (genitive construction) in "believer of the family of Pharaoh", which occurs in a number of reports. It is also said that ﴿from the family of Pharaoh﴾, on both views, is connected to the words of the Exalted: ﴿who concealed his faith﴾, and the fronting (of the prepositional phrase) is for restriction, meaning: a believing man who concealed his faith from the family of Pharaoh, not from Moses, peace be upon him, and those who followed him. On this view there is no problem with the time (of the statement) concerning a believer.

It has been objected that katama (to conceal) is transitive by itself without min, so one says "katamtu fulanan kadha" (I concealed such-and-such from so-and-so), not "katamtu min fulan". The Exalted said: ﴿and they do not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. The poet said:

"I concealed you by night, awake, with the thoughts,
and two concerns, one hidden and one manifest,
the whispers of the self that complain of what disturbs it,
and the coming of cares which will find no outlet."

He meant, according to al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan), "I concealed from you the whispers of the self and two concerns." It is also said that some lexicographers explicitly stated that it is transitive with min. Al-Misbah (al-Misbah al-Munir) says: katama, of the pattern qatala, is transitive to two objects, and it is permissible to add min to the first object, so one says "katamtu min Zaydin al-hadith" (I concealed the statement from Zayd), just as one says "bi'tuhu al-dar" and "bi'tuha minhu" (I sold him the house and I sold it to him). Yes, its connection to that (the verb) is contrary to the apparent meaning; rather, the apparent meaning is that it is connected to an omitted (verb) which occurs as a second attribute of "a man". On this view, the apparent meaning is that he was from the family of Pharaoh in fact. In his words, which are reported after this, there is what is apparent in that. His name is said to be Shum'an with a shin dotted, or it is said Khirbil with a kha dotted and kasra, and a ra undotted and sakin, or it is said Hizbil with a unmarked ha and a dotted zay, or it is said Habib.

Isa, Abd al-Warith, Ubayd ibn Aqil and Hamza ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Amr, read ﴿rajul﴾ with the jim sakin, and this is the dialect of Tamim and Najd. ﴿Will you kill a man﴾, meaning: do you intend to kill him? This is a metaphor in which the effect (qatl) is mentioned and the cause (intention to kill) is meant. The fact that denial does not require occurrence does not validate it without a figurative usage. ﴿Because he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, meaning: because he says that. ﴿And he has certainly brought you clear evidences﴾, those testifying to his truthfulness from among the miracles and the many proofs. The sound feminine plural (jam' al-mu'annath al-salim), although it is commonly said to indicate paucity, when the definite article (al) enters upon it, indicates abundance by the help of the context. The clause is in the state (hal) of the subject or of the object. This is a great denial from that man and a severe rebuke of them, as if he said: Will you commit the shameful act, which is the killing of a forbidden soul, while you have no justification for committing it except the word of truth which he has spoken, namely his saying: ﴿My Lord is Allah﴾, even though he has come to you with the clear evidences ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: from the one to whom Lordship is ascribed, and He is your Lord, not only his Lord. This is a gradual leading toward admission. In ﴿that he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾ up to ﴿from your Lord﴾ there is a sublime point, namely that one who says "My Lord is Allah" or "so-and-so" does not necessitate being met with killing, just as you are not met with killing when you say "Our lord is Pharaoh". How, when he has made his Lord the one who is your Lord? So it is incumbent upon you to honour him and revere him, not to forsake him and kill him.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that (an) yaqula (that he says) be construed with an omitted noun, meaning: "at the time that he says", so the adverbial (zarf, adverb of time) was omitted and the noun in the genitive became accusative as an adverbial of time, because it stands in its place. The meaning is: Will you kill him at the moment you heard from him this statement, without deliberation or thought about his matter? Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that what stands in place of the adverbial can only be a pure verbal noun (masdar sarih), like "ji'tu siyah al-dik" (I came at the crowing of the rooster), or what is with ma that is temporal (ma al-dawamiyya), not a non-pure (verbal) construction, like "ji'tu an sah al-dik" or "an yasih al-dik" (I came when the rooster crowed). In reply: Ibn Jinni, like al-Zamakhshari, explicitly stated the permissibility, and each is an imam.

Then the man took precautions for himself, fearing that the accursed one would learn the reality of his affair and attack him, so he was gentle in his argument and said: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie﴾, meaning: the consequence of his lie will not pass beyond him, so there is no need for you to kill him to avert it. ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you﴾, so at least some of what he promises you will befall you, or he promises you that. In this there is exaggeration in warning, for when he warned them of striking some of it, he implied that it is a dreadful destruction, so what of all of it? It also shows fairness and absence of partisanship. For this reason he put first the possibility of his being a liar. It is also said: what is meant is that there will strike you what he promises of the punishment of this world, which is part of his promises, as if he frightened them with what is more likely in their estimation. It is also said: ﴿some﴾ (ba'd) means ﴿all﴾ (kull), and they cited for this the verse of Amr al-Qatami:

"He who is patient may attain some of his need,
and with the hasty one there may be a slip."

Al-Zajjaj held that ﴿some﴾ (ba'd) in it is on its apparent meaning, and that the aim is to establish the proof and show the superiority of the patient over the hasty by a point the opponent cannot repel. So the verse is like the verse on the first view. They cited, for ba'd coming to mean kull, the poet's verse:

"Indeed, when afflictions have arranged matters,
without the elders, you see a flaw in some of them."

It is not restricted to this meaning, as is not hidden. It is reported from Abu Ubayda that he explained ba'd as kull too, and he cited the verse of Labid:

"Leaving places I do not like,
or the death of some souls ties it."

The verse is read as meaning: I will not cease moving through the lands until there remains no one of the servants whom I intend. The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) hold that ba'd in it is on its apparent meaning and that by it is meant itself, and the meaning is: I will not cease leaving places I do not like, except that I die. Al-Zamakhshari said:

"If the report from Abu Ubayda concerning that is sound, then what al-Mazini said in the question of al-'Alqa applies: 'He was too crude to understand what I say to him.'" And in this there is exaggeration in refutation.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar﴾. This is another argument with two aspects. The first: if he were a transgressor and a liar, Allah the Exalted would not have guided him to the clear evidences, nor would He have supported him with those miracles. The second: if he were such, Allah the Exalted would forsake him and destroy him, so there is no need for you to kill him. Perhaps he meant by it the first meaning, but he gave them the impression that he meant the second, so that their stubbornness would soften. He alluded to Pharaoh that he is a transgressor, meaning in killing and corruption, and a liar in claiming Lordship, whom Allah the Exalted does not guide to the path of right and the way of salvation. So the clause is a new sentence (mustanifa), connected in meaning to the first conditional clause, or to the second, or to both.

[p. 64]

[Page 66]

﴿O my people, the dominion is yours today, dominant﴾ — victorious and exalted — ﴿over the Children of Israel﴾ — ﴿in the land﴾, that is, in the land of Egypt, where no one opposes you at this time. ﴿Then who would help us against the might of God﴾ — against His seizing and His punishment, glorified is He — ﴿if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: do not corrupt your affair, and do not expose yourselves to the might of God Most High by killing him, for if it comes upon us, no one will be able to prevent it from us. The fa' in ﴿fa-man﴾ ("then who") is a fa' of fasiha (an exclamatory particle that signals an unstated condition), and the interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari). He attributed what pleases them, namely the dominion and dominance in the land, to them specifically, but included himself among them regarding what distresses them, namely the coming of the might of God Most High. This was to console their hearts and to signal that he is a counselor to them, striving to secure what benefits them and to repel what would ruin them, striving on behalf of his own self, so that they might be influenced by his advice.

﴿Pharaoh said﴾ after he heard that, ﴿"I only show you﴾ — that is, I only advise you ﴿what I see"﴾ — only what I see and judge to be right, namely killing him. He means: I judge nothing to be right except killing him, and what you are saying is not right. ﴿"And I guide you not﴾ by this opinion ﴿except to the path of rectitude"﴾ — the way of what is right and sound. Or it means: I do not inform you except of what I know to be right, and I withhold nothing from it, nor do I conceal from you anything contrary to what I openly say. That is, his tongue and his heart agree on what he says. But the enemy of God lied, for he was feeling a severe fear of Moses, peace be upon him, but he was restraining himself. Had he not felt it, he would not have consulted anyone.

It is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and al-Hasan that they both recited «al-rashshad» (الرَّشّادِ) with a doubled shin, taking it as fa"al (فَعّالٌ), an intensive form, either from rashida (رَشِدَ) with kasra, like ʿallam (عَلّامٍ) from ʿalima (عَلِمَ), or from rashada (رَشَدَ) with fatha, like ʿabbad (عَبّادٍ) from ʿabada (عَبَدَ).

It has also been said that it is from the augmented form arshada (أرْشَدَ), like jabbar (جَبّارٍ) from ajbara (أجْبَرَ). This was objected to on the grounds that fa"al does not come from the augmented form (mazid, the form with added letters) except in a few words, such as jabbar, darrak (دَرّاكٍ), qassar (قَصّارٍ), and sa"ar (سَآَّرٍ), and analogy is not sound based on the rare. Moreover, for some of these, the triliteral (thulathi) usage has been attested, as in jabbara-hu ʿala kadha (جَبَرَهُ عَلى كَذا) like ajbara-hu, and qassar (قَصّارٌ) like jabbar according to some, so it is not certain that it derives from the augmented form, because qasara ʿan al-shay' (قَصَرَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ) comes like aqsara ʿanhu (أقْصَرَ عَنْهُ). It is reported from al-Jawhari that al-iqsar (الإقْصارُ) is restraint with capacity, while al-qasr (القَصْرُ) is restraint with incapacity, so this does not hold on his view. As for darrak and sa"ar, they have been explained as derived by deleting the augmentation in estimation (taqdiran) but not in actual usage, as they say: abqala al-makan fa-huwa baqil (أبَقَلَ المَكانُ فَهو باقِلٌ), and awrasa al-ramth fa-huwa waris (أوْرَسَ الرَّمْثُ فَهو وارِسٌ). Ibn Jinni said: On this basis al-rashad (الرَّشادُ) is also explained, so that it comes from rashada in the sense of arshada, in estimation and not in usage, for the meaning is so. Then he said: If it is said that when the meaning is arshada, how could you permit that it be from rashida (with kasra) or from rashada (with fatha)? It is answered: the meaning returns to his being a guide (murshid), because when one is rashida, one guides (arshada), since irshad (guidance) comes from rashad (rectitude). So it is of the type of sufficing with mention of the cause over the effect (al-iktifa' bi-dhikr al-sabab ʿan al-musabbab). End of quote. It has also been said that this is permitted because intensiveness in rushd (rectitude) is achieved through giving guidance, as the scholars established in the cases of qayyum (قَيُّومٍ) and tahur (طَهُورٍ).

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: If rashida means ihtada (اهْتَدى, to be guided), then the meaning is: "I guide you only to the path of one who was guided and whose rectitude was great," and there is no need for what you have heard. It would only be needed if it were necessary that the meaning be: "I guide you only to the path of one who gives much guidance," and whence does that necessity come? It is also permitted that fa"al in this recitation indicates attribution (lil-nisba), as they say: ʿawwaj (عَوّاجٌ) for one who sells ivory (al-ʿaj, العاجِ), and battat (بَتّاتٌ) for one who sells al-batt (البَتِّ), which is a thick cloak. It is also said it is a tailasan (طَيْلَسانٌ) of silk (khazz) or wool. Some have denied that this recitation in the form fa"al belongs to the speech of Pharaoh, and that it is only in the words of the one who believed: ﴿"O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of rectitude (al-rashshad)"﴾, for Mu'adh ibn Jabal, as Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said, and Abu Hatim, used to explain ﴿the path of rectitude﴾, on his recitation, as the path of God Most High, and this cannot be applied to the speech of Pharaoh, as is not hidden. You will know, God willing, that Mu'adh recited it in the same way in the words of the believer. So perhaps the explanation as the path of God, glorified and exalted is He, was in that (the believer's speech) and not in the speech of Pharaoh. And God Most High knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 30:

﴿And the man who believed said﴾ The majority hold that he is the believing man who concealed his faith, the one who said: ﴿Will you kill a man merely because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ Allah Most High strengthened his soul and made his heart firm, so he did not fear Pharaoh and did not heed him. Then he resorted to another kind of threat and intimidation, and said: ﴿O my people, I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ to the end of the verse. Another group said: the speech of that believing man ended there, and what is meant by "the one who believed" here is Musa himself, peace be upon him, and they argued from the strength of his speech. But the first view is the one relied upon, meaning: he said, giving counsel to his people: "O my people, I fear for you, in your denial of Musa, peace be upon him, and your assailing him with evil, that there may befall you the like of what befell those who banded together against their prophets from the earlier nations." The word "day" (yawm) here means an occurrence of events (waqa'i'), and its use in this sense has become so common that it became a conventional figurative meaning, or it retains its well-known linguistic meaning. The expression is then elliptical, meaning: "the like of the occurrence of the day of the factions."

Whatever the case, the apparent reading is the plural of "day," but the plural of "factions," which is the genitive construction, together with the explanation that follows, has made the plural of "day" unnecessary, and the meaning is according to this. The singular was preferred for lightness and brevity. Al-Zajjaj said: what is meant is "the day when a faction was formed into a party," meaning that the plural of "hizb" (faction) is intended to include its individual members by way of substitution. This is an interpretation for the second reading, while what preceded is more evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 31:

﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah, and ʿAd, and Thamud﴾ That is, "like the requital of their custom," i.e., their constant habit of disbelief and harming the messengers. The genitive noun (muḍaf, "requital") is understood here because what is actually feared is the requital of the deed, not the people themselves. This construction, with the second "mithl" in the accusative, is an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to the first "mithl," because the last thing governed by the annexation is "the people of Noah." If you said, "Allah destroyed the confederates, the people of Noah, ʿAd, and Thamud," it would be nothing but an appositive to the annexation of "people" to proper names, and that ruling would then extend to the first item governed by the annexation.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a substitute (badal) for the first "mithl," and the need to posit the omitted noun remains as it is. ﴿And those after them﴾, like the people of Lot. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to His servants﴾, i.e., what He, glorified is He, did to these confederates was not injustice; rather it was justice and equity, because He, mighty and majestic, sent to them their messengers with clear proofs, but they denied them and banded together against them, and that required their destruction. This is more eloquent than His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], in that the negation there concerns the intention of injustice, because whoever is far from intending injustice is even further from injustice itself. And since injustice is indefinite, it is as if He negated that He intends any injustice at all toward His servants. Al-Zamakhshari allows that its meaning is like the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar: 7], i.e., He, glorified is He, does not will that they commit injustice for themselves, meaning that He, mighty and majestic, destroyed them because they were wrongdoers. It is not hidden that this meaning is weaker both in wording and in sense. Moreover, there is no proof in it for the Mu'tazila, since there is a distinction between "He willed it from him" and "He willed it for him." So even if it is granted that He, glorified is He, does not will that they do injustice, it does not follow that He does not will it from them, and what the People of the Sunna regard as impossible is this; thus there is no need, in their view either, to divert the verse from its apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 32:

﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling out (al-Tanad)﴾ He warned them of the otherworldly punishment after warning them of the worldly punishment. Al-tanad is a verbal noun from tanadaa al-qawm, meaning some of them called out to one another. Yawm al-tanad is the Day of Resurrection, named so because in it some of them call out to one another for help, or they cry out to one another with woe and perdition, or because of the calling between the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, as related in Surat al-A'raf, or because creation is called to the place of assembly, or because of the calling of the believer ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19] and of the disbeliever ﴿Would that I had not been given my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25].

It is related from Ibn Abbas that this calling out is the calling out that occurs among people at the blowing of the Trumpet and the blast of terror in this world, and that they flee upon their faces because of the terror that seizes them, and some of them call out to others. This was also related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that what is meant is a reminder of every call on the Day of Resurrection in which there is hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners.

A group read "al-tanad" with a sukun on the dal when pausing in recitation, treating it as if stopped upon. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, al-Za'farani and Ibn Muqsim read "al-tannad" (التَّنادِّ) with a shaddah on the dal, from nadda al-ba'ir, meaning the camel fled, i.e., the Day of fleeing and running away, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Day a man flees from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34], and in a hadith: "The people on the Day of Resurrection will be scattering, fleeing, thinking they will find a place of escape."

It was also said: what is meant by it is the Day of Gathering, from nada when it gathers, and from it comes al-nadi (the assembly).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 33:

﴿The Day you turn your backs and flee﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Calling out" (yawm al-tanad), meaning: the Day you turn away from the place of standing (al-mawqif), heading toward the Fire. It has also been said: fleeing from the Fire. It is narrated that when they hear the roar (zafir) of the Fire, they flee, but they do not reach any region of the regions except that they find angels in rows, so flight does not benefit them. This view has been preferred because it is more complete in benefit and more evidently connected to the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿You will have no protector from God﴾, meaning: He will protect you in your fleeing so that you are not punished in the Fire. This was said by al-Suddi. Qatadah said: meaning, in your rushing toward the Fire, you will have no preventer who keeps you from it, nor any helper. This is what is said according to the first meaning, "the Day you turn your backs and flee." In either case, the sentence is another circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿you turn﴾.

﴿And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, meaning, He does not guide him to the path of salvation at all. It seems that the man had despaired of their accepting his counsel, so he said this, then he rebuked them for denying the earlier messengers, and said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 34:

﴿And verily Yusuf came to you before[, Yusuf son of Ya'qub, peace be upon them both,] ﴿before﴾ i.e., before Musa, ﴿with clear proofs﴾, the manifest matters indicating his truthfulness, ﴿but you continued in doubt about what he brought you﴾ of the religion, ﴿until, when he died﴾ by death, ﴿you said: "Allah will never send after him any messenger"﴾, as an end-point to their saying.

﴿So you continued﴾ and by their saying ﴿"Allah will never send after him any messenger"﴾ they intended to deny his prophethood and the prophethood of others, i.e., there is no messenger so that He would send one. Thus, after doubt they came to a definite decision with this denial, and this is an escalation (taraqqi).

It is also possible that the doubt about his prophethood remained as it was, and their definite decision was only the denial of the prophethood of anyone else after him. It has been said: it is possible that they had displayed doubt about his life out of envy and obstinacy, and when he, peace be upon him, died, they acknowledged it and denied that Allah the Exalted would send a messenger after him, which is contrary to the apparent meaning.

As for the coming of Yusuf son of Ya'qub, peace be upon them both, to those addressed with the clear proofs, it has been said that it is from the attribution of the conditions of fathers to sons, and likewise the attribution of actions that remain to them. It has also been permitted that some of those to whom Yusuf, peace be upon him, came were literally alive. In some histories it is stated that the death of Yusuf, peace be upon him, was sixty-four years before the birth of Musa, peace be upon him, so it would be from the attribution of the condition of some to all. Al-Bahr favoured that the Pharaoh of Yusuf, peace be upon him, is the Pharaoh of Musa, peace be upon him. It is mentioned from Ashhab, from Malik, that it reached him that he lived four hundred and forty years. What most historians have mentioned is that the Pharaoh of Musa is named al-Rayyan and the Pharaoh of Yusuf is named al-Walid.

Al-Qurtubi mentioned that the first Pharaoh was of the Amalekites and this one was a Copt, and the Pharaoh of Yusuf, peace be upon him, died in his time. He preferred the view that the two are different. The matter of the coming and what accompanied it of actions is as you have heard. It has also been said: the intended Yusuf mentioned is Yusuf son of Ibrahim son of Yusuf the Truthful, whom Allah the Exalted sent as a prophet; he remained among them for twenty years, and of their affair was what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related.

Among the very strange things is what al-Naqqash and al-Mawardi related: that the Yusuf mentioned in this surah was of the jinn, whom Allah the Exalted sent as a messenger to them. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti related it in al-Itqan, and no one with even a little mastery would accept it. Yes, the view that the jinn have a prophet from among them named Yusuf also may be accepted, as is not hidden.

It was read "a-lan yab'atha" with the interrogative hamzah introduced before the particle of negation, as if some of them were confirming to others the negation of a sending.

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., like that dreadful misguidance, ﴿Allah leads astray whoever is ﴿musrif﴾ [extravagant]﴾ in disobedience, ﴿murtab﴾ [in doubt]﴾ concerning his religion, a doubter about what the clear proofs testify to, due to the dominance of illusion and immersion in blind imitation.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 35:**

﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the first relative pronoun, namely *man* (whoever), or a *bayan* (explicative apposition), or a *sifah* (qualifier) of it with respect to its meaning, as if it were said: "every extravagant doubter," or "the extravagant doubters." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative, with an implied *a'ni* (I mean). The words of the Exalted, ﴿without authority﴾, according to the aforementioned possibilities, are connected to *yujadiluna* (they dispute). His words, ﴿that has come to them﴾, are a qualifier of *sultan* (authority).
