The meaning of its "coming" is its coming from Him, glorified and exalted, either through the hands of the messengers, peace be upon them, in which case this refers to the transmitted proof (*al-dalil al-naqli*), or by way of an outpouring upon their intellects, in which case this refers to the rational proof (*al-dalil al-'aqli*). It may also be generalised, so that the meaning becomes: they dispute without any proof suitable for holding onto at all, neither rational nor transmitted.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe﴾, confirm what the speech has implied of their blameworthy condition, and in it there is a kind of wonder and magnification. The subject of *kabura* (it is great) is a pronoun referring back to the disputing (*al-jidal*), which is indicated by *yujadiluna* (they dispute), in the manner of "whoever lies, it is worse for him," i.e., the disputing about the signs of Allah without proof has become great in hatred in the sight of Allah... etc. Alternatively, it refers to the first relative pronoun, and it is kept singular in observance of its form (*lafz*). This has been objected to on the ground that it is a case of returning to the form after returning to the meaning, which the grammarians avoid.

The author of *al-Kashf* said: "This is something Ibn al-Hajib transmitted, and no one else supported him, and it is not accepted." That is, the extravagant doubter who disputes the signs of Allah without proof has become great in hatred, i.e., his hatred has grown great and magnified in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, and in the sight of the believers. ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that dreadful sealing, ﴿Allah seals upon every heart that is arrogant and tyrannical﴾, so that there issue from it the like of what was mentioned: extravagance, doubt, and disputing without right. It is also permissible for *alladhina* (those who) to be the subject (*mubtada'*) with the clause *kabura* (it is great) as its predicate, but with an omitted noun governing it, which is the real thing spoken of: i.e., the disputing of those who dispute has become great in hatred. And it is permissible for *alladhina* to be the subject with the omitted noun, and *bi-ghayri sultan* (without authority) to be the predicate of the omitted noun, i.e., the disputing of those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah, exalted is He, exists without authority. The apparent sense of some scholars' speech is that *alladhina* is a subject without an omitted noun, with *bi-ghayri sultan* as its predicate. In this there is the predication of an essence and a body by means of an adverbial phrase (*zarf*). The subject of *kabura* is likewise, according to the view of those who regard the *kaf* (in *kadhalika*) as a noun, as Al-Akhfash does, i.e., "great in hatred is the like of that disputing." In that case, the words of the Exalted, *yatba'u* (He seals)... etc., form a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) to indicate the cause that necessitates their disputing. The departure from the apparent meaning in this is not hidden. In *al-Bahr*, the preferable analysis of this sentence is that *alladhina* is the subject and *kabura* its predicate, with the subject of the verb being the pronoun of the verbal noun (*masdar*) understood from *yujadiluna*, i.e., "those who dispute, their disputing has become great in hatred." So reflect upon this.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Dhakwan, and al-A'raj, according to one of the transmissions from him, read *qalbin* with tanwin (nunation), so that what follows it is its qualifier. Describing it with arrogance and tyranny is because these are its source, like the saying "my eye saw and my ear heard." It is also permissible that this be by omitting a noun governing it, i.e., "every one with a heart that is arrogant and tyrannical." Making the two qualifiers belong to the possessor of the heart is so that the two readings agree. The reading of the remaining seven is without tanwin. It is transmitted from Muqatil that *al-mutakabbir* is the one who is obstinate in magnifying the command of Allah, exalted is He, and *al-jabbar* is the one who domineers over the creatures of Allah, exalted is He. The apparent sense is that the generality of *kull* (every) extends to *al-mutakabbir* and *al-jabbar* as well, as though the annexation of *qalb* to what follows it was first considered, and then its annexation to the whole group was considered.

[p. 69]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 36:

﴿And Pharaoh said: "O Haman, build for me a lofty tower﴾ — a building that is exposed and high, from ṣaraḥa (ṣaraḥa), meaning that a thing became manifest (idhā ẓahara). ﴿That I may reach the means﴾ — i.e., the ways (al-ṭuruq), as is related from al-Suddi. Qatada said: the doors (al-abwab). It is the plural of sabab (sabab, cause/means), and it is applied to everything by which one arrives at something. ﴿The means of the heavens﴾ — an explanation of it. In its being first left vague and then made clear there is an exaltation of its matter and an arousing of the listener's desire to know it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 37:

﴿Then that I may look upon the God of Musa﴾ With the accusative (fa-ataṭṭali‘a, "that I may look") according to the Kufans, as an answer to the optative (al-tarajji, "hoping"), for they permit the accusative after the fa' in the answer to the optative as they do for the wish (al-tamanni). The Basrans prohibited this, and they interpreted the accusative here as being in answer to a command, which is (ibn, "build"), as in his saying:

"O she-camel, proceed with a long, wide stride, to Sulayman, that we may rest."

It is also permitted that it be in coordination with the predicate of la‘alli (perhaps), on the assumption that it contains (an) because it has often come to us accompanied by it; or in coordination with (al-asbab, "the means"), in the manner of:

"The wearing of a cloak, and that my eye may be comforted."

Some have said: this hoping is in reality a wish, but the accursed one (al-La‘in) brought it out in this manner to deceive his hearers, so the accusative was in answer to a wish. Apparently the Basrans do not distinguish between one optative and another optative. Al-Jumhur read with the nominative, as a coordination with (ablugh, "I will reach"). It has been said: perhaps he intended to build for himself an observatory (rasad) in a high place from which he could observe the conditions of the stars, which are heavenly causes indicating earthly events, so that he could see whether there is in them anything indicating that God the Exalted had sent him (Musa). This indicates that he affirmed God, mighty and majestic, and he only sought what would remove his doubt concerning the message. The accursed one and the people of his age had a concern with the stars and their judgments, according to what has been said.

This possibility is, in my view, extremely remote. It has also been said: he intended to inform the people of the corruption of Musa's statement, "I am a messenger from the Lord of the heavens," by showing that if he were truly a messenger from Him, he would have to reach Him, and that is by ascending to the heaven, which is impossible; so what is founded upon it is like it. The source of this is his ignorance of God the Exalted and his supposition that He, glorified be He, resides in the heaven, and that His messengers are like the messengers of kings, who meet him and arrive at his place of settlement. He, mighty and majestic, is exalted above the attributes of created things and bodies, and does not need what the messengers of kings need; His noble messengers, upon them be prayer and peace. This is a denial of his message from God the Exalted, and there is no reference in it to denying the Creator who sent him. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: what I hold in the interpretation of the verse is that Pharaoh was among the materialists (al-dahriyya), and his purpose from this speech was to raise a doubt concerning the denial of the Creator, and its formulation is that he said: "We do not see anything about which we can judge that it is the God of the world, so it is not permissible to affirm this God." As for "we do not see Him," it is because if He existed He would be in the heaven, and we have no way to ascend the heavens, so how could we see Him? And to emphasize the impossibility he said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower﴾, which is nothing but to show that what was mentioned is not possible for anyone; and perhaps "la'alli" does not contradict that, because it is for mockery concerning this. And it is a doubt of extreme corruption, since the absence of one of the means of knowing a thing does not necessitate the absence of that thing. I have seen, from some of the Salafis, that the accursed one only said that because he heard from Musa, upon him be peace, or from one of the believers, a description of God the Exalted as being high, or that He, glorified be He, is in the heaven; so he understood it in a sense impossible for Him, exalted be He, which neither Musa, upon him be peace, nor any of the believers rejected; so he said what he said in mockery and as deception upon his people. Al-Imam has in this place a discourse by which he refuted those who say that God the Exalted is in the heaven, and he rejected their argument from what the verse implies concerning that, and he named them the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists). The discussion of this is long in scope, and the truth lies with the Salaf, may the mercy of the King, the Exalted, be upon them, and far be it from them, and then far be it from them from anthropomorphism. And his saying: ﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾ may mean that he meant by it a liar in the claim of being a messenger, and it may mean that he meant by it a liar in the claim that he has a god other than me, in accordance with his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿And thus﴾, that is, and like that extreme and excessive embellishment, ﴿the evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾, so he immersed himself in it with an immersion from which he would never by any means desist, ﴿and he was barred from the way﴾, that is, from the way of guidance. The definite article is for the known referent, and both verbs are in the passive, while the real agent is God the Exalted. He, glorified be He, did not cause either the embellishment or the barring except because Pharaoh requested it through the tongue of his readiness, and his evil choice necessitated that. This is indicated by the fact that it was read as "zayyana" in the active voice, and no one preceded it in mention except God the Exalted, not Satan.

It is also permitted that the agent be Satan, and the attribution of the act to him is through the mediation of whispering. Al-Hijaziyyan, al-Shami and Abu ‘Amr read "wa-Sadda" in the active voice, its subject being the pronoun of Pharaoh, so that the meaning is: Pharaoh barred the people from the way of guidance by such deceptions and doubts. What supports this is ﴿And the scheming of Pharaoh is nothing but in ruin﴾, meaning in loss, because it indicates that there has been a prior mention of the scheming, and this is clearer in this reading. Ibn Wathhab read "wa-Sadda" with a kasra on the sad, its origin being Sadida; the vowel was moved onto the sad after the assumption of its elision. Ibn Abi Ishaq and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read "wa-Sadda" with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal, indefinite, in coordination with (su' 'amalihi, "the evil of his deed"). It was also read "wa-Suddu" with the plural waw, meaning he and his people.

And the one who believed said: ﴿O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right guidance.﴾ He is the believer from the family of Pharaoh. It was also said that what was said about the preceding one applies here too, namely that he is Moses, peace be upon him, but this is weak, as is not hidden. ﴿O my people, follow me﴾ in what I have pointed you to. ﴿I will guide you to the path of right guidance﴾, a path by which its traveler reaches the intended goal. In this there is an indirect implication that what Pharaoh and his people follow is the path of error. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read (الرَّشادِ) with a shadda on the shin, as mentioned in al-Bahr, and the discussion of that has already passed, so do not overlook it.

O my people, indeed this worldly life is but a passing enjoyment (matāʿ), that is, a [thing of] enjoyment or a thing enjoyed, fleeting because of how quickly it vanishes; ﴿and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence﴾ because of its everlastingness and the permanence of what is in it.

ۚ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾ in this world, ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ in the Hereafter, as a justice from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been used as evidence that crimes (jinayat) are to be compensated with their like, i.e., with their equivalent, without doubling.

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those﴾ who did that ﴿will enter Paradise, being provided therein without reckoning﴾, i.e., without measurement or weighing against the deed, but rather manifold multiplications, as a grace from Him, exalted is He, and mercy. He divided the doers into male and female for emphasis and caution, to include them in full, given the possibility that women might be overlooked. He made the reward, in the matter of their deeds, a nominal sentence introduced by the demonstrative noun, together with the excellence of the reward and its detailing, giving precedence to mercy and encouraging what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He made the deed the core and pillar of the conditional proposition, and made faith a circumstantial clause (hal), to indicate that faith is a condition for the deed being taken into account, counted, and rewarded, because circumstances are restrictions and conditions for the rulings that occur in them. This includes an indication of the great nobility of this (faith) and its abundant reward. Al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Isa, and more than one of the Seven read "yudkhalun" in the passive voice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 41:

﴿And O my people, what is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ He repeated his address (nida') to awaken them from the slumber of heedlessness, to give importance to the one addressed, and as an intensification in rebuking them for the way they respond to his call. He omitted the conjunction (ʿatf) in the second address, which is ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only an enjoyment...﴾ etc., because it is an explanation (tafsir) of what was left general (ujmila) in the address before it, namely guidance to the path of right direction (al-rashad). For that is warning against inclining to the world (al-ikhlad ila al-dunya) and encouraging the preference of the Hereafter over the first life. He has fulfilled this in it in the most complete and best manner. And he did not omit it in this address, because it is not of that station. This is for the sake of balancing between the two calls: his call to the religion of God, whose fruit is salvation, and their call to taking rivals (al-andad), whose outcome is the Fire. And that is not part of explaining the guidance in any way; rather it is to establish that he is a guide and that they are misguiders, and that what he is upon is guidance and what they are upon is error. Thus it is a conjunction (ʿatf) to the first address or to the whole group. It has also been said: it is a conjunction to the second address, joining with it in explaining what was left general in the first address, both explicitly and allusively. Each has its own justification, and there is discussion regarding preference.

﴿You call me to disbelieve in God﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿you call me to the Fire﴾, or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it, on the basis that in sentences it functions as single words do. Alternatively, it is a resumed sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa) explaining that. The verb "call" (duʿaʾ) is, in its government of the particle إلى (ilā, "to") and of the lām, like "guide" (hidaya).

﴿and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾, meaning: by His being a partner to Him, exalted is He, in worship, or by ascribing to it His lordship (rububiyya) and divinity (uluhiyya). ﴿knowledge﴾: the negation of knowledge here is a metonymy (kināya) for the negation of the thing known. In his denial of calling to what he does not know, there is an indication that divinity requires a proof that necessitates knowledge of it.

﴿And I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, who combines the attributes of divinity, including perfect power and dominance, and what depends on them: knowledge, will, the ability to requite, the capacity to punish and the capacity to forgive. These two attributes were singled out for mention, although they are a metonymy for all the attributes, since they imply that, as is pointed out, because they indicate fear and hope, which are suitable to his situation and theirs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 43:

﴿There is no doubt that what you call me to has no call [to it] in this world or in the Hereafter.﴾ Its context, according to the school of the Basrans, is that there is no refutation of a preceding statement, namely what they call him to here, of disbelief in Allah, glory be to Him, and association of false deities with Him, exalted and majestic is He. [The word] "jaram" ( جَرَمَ) is a past-tense verb meaning "it became established and was true," as in the verse of the poet:

"And I indeed struck Abu 'Ubayda with a thrust that made Fazara [certain] after it that they would be angry."

And "anna" (أنَّ) with what is within its scope serves as its subject, meaning: it became established and true that there is no call to that to which you call me, of idols, to Himself at all. That is, it is the right of the One who is worshipped in truth that He call His honoured servants, such as the prophets and angels, to Himself and command them to worship Him; then the servants call one another to Him, exalted is He, and to His obedience, glory be to Him, manifesting the call of their Lord, exalted and majestic is He. As for what you call to, and to worshipping it, of idols, it does not call to that, nor does it claim lordship at all: not in this world, because it is inanimate in it and cannot do anything of calling or otherwise; nor in the Hereafter, because when Allah, exalted is He, brings it into existence there as a living being, it will disown those who call to it and its worshippers. Its sum is: it is true that your deities have no call at all, so they are not true deities. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 46:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Fire﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the clause of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, is its predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence). The clause is an explanation (*tafsir*, exegesis) of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there befell﴾ ... etc.

It is also permitted that ﴿al-nar (the Fire)﴾ be a substitute (*badal*, an apposition in grammar) for ﴿evil of the punishment﴾, and that ﴿they are exposed﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the noun it follows) from it or from ﴿the people﴾. It is also permitted that ﴿the Fire﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, which is the pronoun referring to ﴿evil of the punishment﴾, as if it were said: "What is the evil of the punishment?" And it was said: "It is the Fire." The clause ﴿they are exposed﴾ is then an explanation, as has passed. In the first construction there is a magnification of the matter of the Fire and an awesome depiction of its punishment that is absent in this construction, as the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

The source of this magnification, according to what is in al-Kashf, is the brevity (*ijmal*) and the detail (*tafsil*) regarding the manner of their punishment, and each of the two clauses conveys a kind of awe: the first is the encompassing of a punishment that deserves to be called "the evil of the punishment," and the second is "the Fire to which they are exposed morning and evening." The secret of the magnification of the Fire in this construction, rather than in the one that includes the explanation of ﴿evil of the punishment﴾ and the clarification of the manner of punishment, is that when you explain ﴿evil of the punishment﴾ as the Fire, you have exaggerated the magnitude of the evil of the punishment. Then you resume with ﴿they are exposed to it﴾ as a completion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh﴾, without the Fire being an element in what the speech is directed at. And if you bring the two clauses without regard to the two singular terms, and that one of them is an explanation of the other, then you have intended the Fire by way of independent emphasis, since you have made it the principal point of the speech, and you have brought the clause as an elucidation and clarification of the first, as if you were announcing that it is clearer because it includes what has no worse than it, namely the Fire. Moreover, one of the requirements of placing the predicated element first (*taqdim al-musnad ilayhi*) is to indicate its magnitude, with the context calling for it, and here it is so, as is not hidden. The construction also conveys specificity (*al-taqwa*, in the sense of emphasis), in the manner of "Zayd, I struck him."

From here the author of al-Kashf said: "This is the preferred construction." It is supported by the reading of the one who put ﴿al-nar﴾ in the accusative, on the basis that it is not governed by *akhussu* or *a'nі* (both meaning "I specify"), but rather by an implied verb that is explained by ﴿they are exposed﴾, like *yuslawna* (they are burned). For their being exposed to the Fire is their being burned by it, from the saying: "The captives were exposed to the sword," meaning they were killed by it. This is of the category of metaphorical (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*, an extended analogical image) metaphor, by likening their state to the state of goods displayed to one who wishes to take them. In this, the Fire is made like a seeker and eager one regarding them, because of the severity of their deserving destruction. And this exposure is of their spirits.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, and Abd ibn Humayd related, from Huzayl ibn Shurahbil, that the spirits of the people of Pharaoh are within the bellies of black birds that go out and return over the Fire, and that is their exposure.

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar from Ibn Mas'ud. These birds are forms created for them from the forms of their deeds. It has been said that this is of the category of figurative representation (*tamthil*), but this is not so.

The mention of the two times is apparent in specifying [the timing], in the sense that they are exposed to the Fire once in the morning and once in the evening, that is, at what is morning and evening in relation to us. What supports this is what Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and others related from Abu Hurayrah, that he used to have two cries every day, in the morning and in the evening. He would say at the beginning of the day: "The night has gone and the day has come, and the exposure of the people of Pharaoh to the Fire," and he would say at the beginning of the night: "The day has gone and the night has come, and the exposure of the people of Pharaoh to the Fire." So no one would hear his voice without seeking refuge with Allah, Exalted is He, from the Fire. The separation between the two times is either by the cessation of punishment or by their being punished with a kind of punishment other than the Fire.

It is also permitted that what is intended is perpetuity (*ta'bid*), being content with the two encompassing extremes as representing the whole. Whichever it is, the verse contains clear evidence for the survival of the soul and the punishment of the barzakh (the intermediate state), because after He mentioned that exposure, He, may His majesty be exalted, said:

﴿And on the day the Hour is established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment."﴾ This is clear in indicating a distinction, so it is necessary that this be in the barzakh. There is no one who makes a distinction between them and others, so the inference regarding generality is complete.

In the two Sahihs and others, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "When any one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening. If he is one of the people of Paradise, then [it is shown as] one of the people of Paradise; and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then [it is shown as] one of the people of the Fire. (*Wa yawma*, "and [mention] the day"), according to what Abu Hayyan preferred, is the object of an implied verb, and the clause is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: "And on the day the Hour is established, it will be said to the angels: 'Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment,'" that is, the punishment of Hell, for it is more severe than what they were in. Or [it means] the most severe punishment of Hell, for its punishments are of various kinds, some of which are more severe than others. And it has been said, regarding the most severe punishment, that it is the punishment of the Abyss (*al-Hawiyah*). It has also been said that ﴿wa yawma﴾ is governed by ﴿admit﴾.

"Mughnun" (bearing benefit) is from "al-ghana" with a fatha, meaning benefit. "Nasiban" (a share), meaning portion, is an object of what is indicated by the averting or bearing, or it is taken as such by including one of the two verbs, meaning "averting or bearing on our behalf a share." It may also be that "nasiban" stands in the place of the verbal noun, like "shay'an" in the Exalted's saying: ﴿Their wealth and their children will not avail them against God in anything﴾ [Al 'Imran: 116]. "Min al-nar" (of the Fire), according to this view, is connected to "mughnun," and according to the preceding view it is a fixed adverbial phrase serving as an explanation of "nasiban."

﴿Those who were arrogant will say﴾ to the weak: ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾, we and you. ﴿So how can we avail you at all? Even if we had power, we would have warded off from ourselves some of the punishment.﴾ The nominative *kull* (the whole; here, "all") is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (*ibtida'*), and it is grammatically annexed in intention, because the meaning is "all of us." *Fiha* (in it) is its predicate (*khabar*), and the whole sentence is the predicate of *inna* (indeed).

Ibn al-Sumayfa' and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *kullan* with the accusative. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari took it as an emphasis (*tawkid*) of the subject of *inna*. That *kull*, when detached from its annexation, can serve as an emphasis is justified by the fact that the meaning is understood from it. This is the view of al-Farra', and Abu Hayyan transmitted it from the Kufan grammarians. Ibn Malik rejected it in his commentary on *al-Tashil*. It was also said that it is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the pronoun hidden in the adverbial phrase (*zarf*). This was objected to on the grounds that it has the meaning of an annexed noun, which is why it may begin a sentence, so how can it be a *hal*? Even if we grant that this degree of indefiniteness suffices for it to be a *hal*, an adverbial phrase does not govern a *hal* that precedes it, as it governs an adverbial phrase that precedes it, such as in *kull yawm laka thawb* (every day you have a garment).

The question of government was answered: al-Akhfash permitted the adverbial phrase to govern a *hal* when it is placed between it and the subject, as in *Zayd qa'iman fi al-dar 'indaka* (Zayd standing in the house in your presence), and the noble verse is like this. Moreover, some permitted this even when the *hal* precedes both the subject and the adverbial phrase. Indeed, some prohibited it absolutely, but the author of the work did not follow them. Ibn al-Hajib permitted it in some of his books and prohibited it in others. It was said: this may be reconciled by saying that the prohibition applies if the adverbial phrase governs by standing in for its complement, while permission applies if the governing element is its implied complement, so that it is verbal and not merely semantic. Ibn Malik adopted this interpretation and recited for it the verse of one of the Tayy poets:

*Da'a fa-ajabna wa-huwa badi dhillatin / ladaykum fa-kana al-nasru ghayra qarib*

The verse ﴿And the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], in the reading with the accusative, has been interpreted in this way.

Abu Hayyan said: What I prefer in the analysis of this reading is that *kullan* is a substitute (*badal*) for the subject of *inna*, because *kull* is inflected in it by the inception and its abrogators (*nawasikh*) and other things. So it is as if it were said: *Inna kullan fiha* (indeed, all of them in it). And since they interpreted *hawlan aktha'a* and *yawman ajma'a* as substitutes, even though these do not directly follow governing particles, it is more appropriate to claim substitution for *kull*. Also, the indefiniteness of *kull* and its accusative as a *hal* is extremely anomalous, as in *marartu bihim kullan* (I passed by them all, i.e., entirely). He then said: If you ask, how can you make it a substitute when it is a substitute of all (*badal kull min kull*) of the pronoun of the speaker, and that is not permitted according to the majority of grammarians? I say: this is the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans, that it is permitted, and this is the correct view. Furthermore, this is not among the points on which they disagreed. Rather, when the substitute conveys comprehensiveness, it is permissible to substitute it for the pronoun of the speaker and for the pronoun of the addressee. We know of no disagreement about this, as in the verse ﴿It shall be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114], and as in your saying: *marartu bikum saghirikum wa-kabirikum* (I passed by you, your young and your old), meaning: I passed by all of you, and it shall be a festival for all of us. It has also been said: it may be for the negation of benefit only, in the sense that they will offer excuses but their excuses will not benefit them, because they are invalid. It may also be for the negation of both benefit and the excuse itself, in the sense that no excuse will occur so as to benefit. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it is said: it is possible that they will offer an excuse, but it will not benefit because it is false, and that even if they brought an excuse it would not be accepted, based on His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And it will not be permitted for them, so they will not make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. And he meant, according to what is in al-Kashf (of al-Tibi), that the non-benefit is either due to a matter returning to the excuse that exists, namely its invalidity, or due to a matter returning to the one who accepts the excuse, with no consideration given to the occurrence of the excuse. The conclusion is that what is intended by the negation is the attribute, with no regard to the thing described, whether in negation or affirmation. There is no indication in his words that he intended the negation of both together, so reflect on this. The readers other than the Kufans and Nafi' read «lā tanfaʿu» with the feminine ta' (tā' fawqiyya). Its reasoning is clear. As for the reading with the ya' (yā'), it is because al-Ma'dhira is a verbal noun (maṣdar) and its feminine marking is not real (ghayr haqiqi), and moreover it is separated from the verb by the object: ﴿and for them is the curse﴾, i.e., distance from mercy (al-bu'd min al-rahma).

﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾: it is Jahannam, and its evil (su') is what distresses them (yasu'u) within it of punishment. So its idafa (construct) is lamiyya (of the "for" type, i.e., "evil of the abode"), or it is from the idafa of the attribute to the described noun, meaning "the abode of evil" (al-dar al-su'a). The humiliation of them and the mockery (tahakkum) directed at them in the two sentences is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 53:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the guidance﴾ That by which one is guided, namely the miracles, the scriptures (ṣuḥuf) and the laws (sharaʾiʿ). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used figuratively (tajawwuz) for what has been mentioned, or it is taken to be the very essence of guidance (ʿayn al-hudā) as an intensive exaggeration (mubālagha) regarding it.

﴿And We made the Children of Israel inherit the Book﴾ We left to them after his death, peace be upon him, the Torah from among those things. So the inheritance (īrāth) is a metonymy (majāz mursal) for leaving behind (tark), or it is a subsidiary metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya) for it. It is also possible that the meaning is: We made the Children of Israel receive the Book from him, peace be upon him, without effort (bi-lā kasb), so that it includes those who were alive during his lifetime, as it is said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." This is a valid view, except that considering the period after death is more fitting for the word "inheritance," and the relation (ʿalāqa) in it is more complete. Taking the Book to mean the Torah is the apparent meaning. It has also been permitted that what is meant by it is the category of what was revealed to their prophets, so that it includes the Torah, the Psalms (Zabur) and the Gospel (Injil).

Guidance and a reminder (﴿هُدًى وذِكْرى﴾). That is, as guidance (hidayah) and as a reminder (tadhkirah), i.e., for their sake; or as one who guides and one who reminds. Thus both are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

For people of understanding (﴿لأُولِي الألْبابِ﴾), that is, for those whose intellects are sound and pure, free from the taints of illusion (wahm). They are singled out because they are the ones who benefit from it.

[Page 78]

﴿So be patient﴾: that is, once you have come to know what We have related to you, as a consolation, then be patient over what you have suffered from the harm of the polytheists. ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah﴾ to you and to the believers of victory, alluded to by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe﴾. Or it refers to all of His promises, exalted is He, and His promise of victory is included in it as a primary inclusion. ﴿is true﴾: He, glorified is He, never breaks it at all, so His victory for you and for the believers must come to pass, exalted is His station. He cited as evidence the case of Moses and those with him, and Pharaoh and those who followed him. ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾: turn to the matter of the religion and make up for what may be lapsed in, which in relation to you is considered a sin even though it is not one. Perhaps this is the concern with the matter of the enemies, by seeking forgiveness, for Allah, exalted is He, is sufficient for you in victory and in the manifestation of the affair. It has also been said: ﴿for your sin﴾ means for the sin of your community against you. It has been said that here the verbal noun (masdar) is annexed to its object (idafat al-masdar lil-maf'ul). ﴿And exalt [Allah] with the praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning﴾: that is, persist in glorifying and praising your Lord. This is so because the two extremes are mentioned and all times are intended. It is also permissible that only the two specific times are intended. By glorification (al-tasbih) is meant its literal meaning, as in the first interpretation, or prayer. Qatadah said: what is intended is the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. Al-Hasan said: what is intended is two rak'ahs in the morning and two rak'ahs in the evening. It has been said: this is because what was obligatory in Makkah was that. We have already mentioned that al-Hiss does not hold to the obligation of the five daily prayers in Makkah, so it has been said that he held to the obligation of two rak'ahs in the morning and two rak'ahs in the evening.

It has also been said that he held that what was obligatory was two rak'ahs at any time that happened to be convenient. All of these contradict the explicit and well-known report. On the interpretation of continuity, it is also permissible that by glorification is meant prayer, and by that is meant the five prayers. This was related in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, the work of Abu Hayyan) from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾: that is, His proofs, which He set up for His oneness, His revealed Books, and the miracles He manifested at the hands of His messengers. ﴿without any authority having come to them﴾: that is, without any proof from Him, Exalted is He, having come to them concerning that. The prepositional phrase is connected to *yujadiluna* (dispute). Restricting the disputing to this condition, even though it is impossible for a proof to come (for such disputants), serves to indicate that one who speaks on matters of religion must rely on a clear proof and a manifest demonstration. This applies to every false disputant, even though it was revealed concerning particular people, who, according to the more correct view, are the polytheists of Makkah.

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts except pride﴾: *in* is negating (*in* here is *in al-nafiyah*), and the predicate of *inna* is what follows it. By "breasts" (*sudur*) is meant the hearts, the term being applied to them by way of contiguity (*al-mujawarah*, closeness) and association (*al-mulabasah*, connection). Pride (*kibr*) is haughtiness and self-magnification. That is: there is in their hearts nothing but arrogance toward the truth and self-exaltation that prevents them from reflecting and learning. Or it is a metaphor for desiring leadership and preeminence in general. Or it means the desire that prophethood belong to them, that is: there is in their hearts nothing but the desire for leadership, or that prophethood belong to them rather than to you, out of envy and insolence, as they said: ﴿If only this Qur'an had been sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and they said: ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. For this reason they dispute concerning His signs, not because there is any real ground for dispute in them, nor because they possess something that might be imagined as fit to be the basis of their disputation in any respect.

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿They will not attain it﴾ is a description of *kibr* (pride). That is: they will not attain what pride requires and necessitates, namely the object of their desire in repelling the signs, or in leadership, or in prophethood. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that nothing drives them to deny you except the pride in their breasts toward you, and they will not attain what that pride demands, because Allah has humbled them. It has also been said that the sentence is independent (*mustanafah*), and the pronoun in *bi-balighihi* refers to repelling the signs, which is understood from the disputing. However, the former view is more evident.

Muqatil said: those who disputed, concerning whom the verse was revealed, were the Jews, who exalted the matter of the Dajjal (the Antichrist), and so it was revealed. Abu al-Aliyah also held this view. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted with a sound chain from him, who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and said: 'The Dajjal will come from among us at the end of time, and there will be from his affair what will be, and they exalted his affair and said: He will do such and such.' So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute...﴾" etc. This is almost explicit that the affair of the Jews was the cause of its revelation, and according to this the verse is Madinan. The discussion of this has already passed, so reflect upon it.

In another narration, the Jews used to say: "Our companion, the Messiah ibn Dawud (al-Masih ibn Dawud), will come out," intending the Dajjal, "and his authority will reach the land and the sea, and rivers will flow with him, and he is one of the signs of Allah. Then the kingdom will return to us." This was related by al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf, and then he said: Allah, Exalted is He, called their wishing for that *kibr* (pride), and He, glorified is He, denied that they would reach what they wished for. It occurs to me, on this view, that the Jews intended by exalting the affair of the Dajjal nothing but to deny that our Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is the Prophet sent at the end of time whom their prophets foretold, and they claimed that the one foretold is that accursed one. In some narrations they said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "You are not our companion," meaning the Prophet foretold by their prophets. So the attribution (*al-idafah*, "our companion") is for the slightest connection, but rather it is "the Messiah ibn Dawud, whose authority will reach the land and the sea, and rivers will flow with him." In that, by their claim, is the repelling of the signs that indicate the prophethood of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. What drove them to this was pride, envy, and love that prophethood not be taken out of the Children of Israel. So the meaning of the verse on this view is close to its meaning on the view that the disputants are the polytheists of Makkah.

Then the Jews, upon them be the curse, lied first by saying to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "You are not our companion," and second by saying: "Rather, it is the Messiah ibn Dawud," meaning the Dajjal. As for the first lie, it is evident. As for the second, it is because no prophet was sent except that he warned his community about the Dajjal and admonished them concerning him, as the reports attest. And they said: "He is our companion," meaning the one foretold to be sent at the end of time. All of that is disputing concerning the signs of Allah, Exalted is He, without any authority.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾: that is, turn to Him, Exalted is He, from the plot of one who envies you and transgresses against you. In this is an allusion that it is from the whisperings of the devils (*hamazat al-shayatin*). Abu al-Aliyah said: this is a command to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to seek refuge in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from the trial of the Dajjal. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾: that is, of your sayings and your deeds. The sentence serves as the reason for the command preceding it.

[Page 79]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾, is a confirmation of the truth and a clarification of the most famous of the things they dispute concerning the resurrection (al-ba'th), which is like monotheism in the obligation to believe in it, following the line of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Yasin: 81]. The annexation of "khalq" (creation) to what follows it is the annexation of the verbal noun (idafat al-masdar) to its object. That is, the creation of the heavens and the earth by God, exalted is He, is greater than His creation of mankind, glory be to Him, because mankind, in comparison to those great bodies, is as nothing. The meaning is that whoever is able to create that, then He, glory be to Him, is more and more able to create what is not counted as anything in comparison to it, in beginning and in return.

Abu al-Aliyah said: "Mankind" means al-Dajjal. This is based on what was narrated from him concerning the disputers. But by my life, applying this and similar verses to that is extremely far-fetched, and I do not say it. ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾, and they are the disbelievers. Since what came before was to establish the resurrection, which reason bears witness to and wisdom apparently requires, it was fitting to negate knowledge from those who disbelieve in it, because if they were among the intelligent, whose nature is to reflect and contemplate on what indicates it, their denial of it would not have come from them. He did not mention an object for "knowledge" because what suits the context is to place it in the position of an intransitive verb. It was also said: the meaning is "they do not know that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind", that is, they do not act according to the requirement of knowledge of that, by affirming the resurrection; and whoever does not act according to the requirement of his knowledge is the same as the ignorant person.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), it is said that He, may He be exalted, alerted that one should not dispute concerning the signs of God, nor should a human being be arrogant, by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿The creation...﴾ etc. That is: His creatures, exalted is He, are greater and more majestic than the creation of humans. So what is it for any of them to dispute and be arrogant toward their Creator, glory be to Him and exalted is He? ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾: they do not reflect, due to the dominance of heedlessness over them, and for this reason they disputed and were arrogant. It is not hidden that this is an interpretation of little benefit.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 58:

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not equal﴾, that is, the one heedless of knowledge of the Truth in its origin and its return, and the one who has insight into knowing both. Interpreting "the seeing" as Allah the Exalted and "the blind" as an idol is not appropriate here. ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, that is, the doers of good. For this reason it is contrasted with His saying: ﴿nor the evildoer﴾. He departed from the apparent contrast, as in "the blind and the seeing," to what is in the sublime composition (nazm), indicating that the believers are a standard of excellence (in good). "The blind" was placed first to match the blindness mentioned before it, which is the negation of knowledge. "Those who believe" was placed after it because of its proximity to "the seeing," and for their nobility. In such constructions there are methods: that each element be placed next to what suits it, as here, and that what corresponds to the first be placed first and what corresponds to the other be placed later, as in His saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not equal﴾ ﴿nor are the darkness and the light﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the heat﴾ [Fatir: 19–22]. And that the paired items be delayed, as in "the blind and the deaf," and "the hearing and the seeing." All of this is from the sphere of tafannun (variety) in eloquence and modes of speech.
[Page 80]
The purpose of negating the equality of those mentioned is to show that this disparity is something that points to resurrection, as if it were said: the heedless and the one who has insight are not equal, nor the doer of good and the doer of evil. Therefore there must be for them another state in which the difference between the two groups will appear, and that is after resurrection.

"Lā" (not) is repeated before "the evildoer" to emphasize the earlier negation, because of the separation between them by the lengthy relative clause (silah). Also, the intended negation is that the disbelieving evildoer is not equal to the believing doer of good. The mention of the blind not being equal to the seeing serves as a preparation for this. Had the negation not been repeated there, one might have overlooked it and thought it was the beginning of a new statement. If it had been said: "nor those who believe and the evildoer," it would also not have been explicit, because of the possibility that it is a subject (mubtada') and ﴿Little do you remember﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and the verb is in the plural in accordance with the meaning. This was stated by al-Khafaji. And it is the reading of the verb with the ya' of the third person. It was also said: he did not say "nor those who believe and the evildoer" because the intention is to negate the evildoer's equality with the doer of good, not to negate the doer of good's equality with him, since the purpose is to show his loss, and it is not free of turbidity. So reflect.

The relative pronoun with what is conjoined to it is conjoined to "the blind" with what is conjoined to it, in the manner of conjoining a group to a group, as in His saying: ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾ [al-Hadid: 3]. The conjunction between them was not omitted, based on the view that the first is the comparison (mushabbah bihi) and the second is what is compared (mushabbah), and that they are identical in outcome, because each of the first two attributes differs from each of the last two attributes, and the difference of attributes is like the difference of essences in the validity of conjunction. The aspect of difference is that the heedless, the one who seeks insight, the doer of good, and the doer of evil are attributes whose concepts differ, regardless of whether what they refer to is identical or not. It was also said: the difference between the first two attributes and the last two is in that the aim in the first two is knowledge, and in the last two is action. This is a view with no objection. It was also said: although they are identical in essence, they differ in consideration, since the second is explicit and the first is mentioned by way of example. This was criticized on the grounds that if mere difference of this kind were sufficient, it would be permissible to conjoin the comparison to what it is compared with, and the reverse.

﴿Little do you remember﴾, that is, you remember with little remembrance. Al-Jumhur, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Shaybah read it with the ya' of the third person, and the pronoun refers to the people or the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: the ta' (second person) is more general. The author of al-Taqrib explained this by saying that it contains the prevalence (taghlib) of address over the third person. Al-Qadi said: the ta' is for the third person, or for turning (iltifat) of address, or for the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to address them, meaning that there is an implied "say" before it. The scholar al-Tibi preferred the iltifat, because the shift from the third person to the second in a context of rebuke indicates severe harshness and emphatic denial. Thus this verse is connected to the creation of the heavens, and it is a speech with the disputants. The author of al-Kashf criticized this by saying that one may take what was mentioned as an instance of taghlib, which would then be preferable for the benefit of generality as well. Let this be understood. The apparent view is that taghlib applies on the assumption that the pronoun refers to the people, and on the assumption that it refers to the disbelievers, because some of the people or disbelievers are addressed here. The limitation (taqlil) can also be taken in its apparent sense, since among them are those who remember and are guided. Al-Jalabi said: if the pronoun refers to the people, then the limitation has its literal meaning, and the exception is the believers; and if it refers to the disbelievers, then it has the meaning of negation. Then, the apparent view is that the addressee is whoever the Prophet (ﷺ) addressed from Quraysh. As for the one who said the addressee is the Prophet (ﷺ) himself, because of His saying ﴿So be patient﴾, it is not appropriate to include him among those who do not remember, for he forgot and did not remember.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming; there is no doubt about it﴾ That is, about its coming: it is necessarily and inevitably going to come, because the evidence for its possibility is clear, and because the prophets agreed on the true promise of its occurrence. It is also possible that the meaning is that it is coming and that it is not a matter of doubt, i.e., because the evidence is clear, and so on as previously mentioned. The difference is that the object of doubt, on the first reading, is the coming (al-majī'), whereas on this reading it is the Hour (al-sā'ah). Taking it in the first sense is preferable.

﴿But most people do not believe﴾ they do not affirm it, because their outlook is limited to what they perceive through the outward senses, and illusions (al-awhām) have taken control over their intellects.
