﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, that is, worship Me, I will reward you, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and a group. It is also related from al-Thawri that he was told: "Call upon God, Most High." He said: "Leaving sins is the supplication (du'a')." He meant that supplicating with the tongue is a translation of seeking from the inner self, and that it is only valid through the soundness of orientation (tawajjuh) and the abandonment of disobedience. Whoever abandons sins has asked the Truth with the tongue of readiness (isti'dad), and this is the supplication that necessarily receives a response. Whoever does not abandon them is not a petitioner, even if he calls upon Him, glory be to Him, a thousand times.

What has been mentioned supports the interpretation of supplication as worship and confirms it, for abandoning sins is among the greatest acts of worship. And the words of the Most High fit this perfectly: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated﴾, that is, abased and debased.

It is also permissible that the meaning be: ask Me, I will give you. This is what is related from al-Suddi. Accordingly, the words of the Most High ﴿too proud to worship Me﴾ mean: too proud to supplicate to Me, because supplication is a kind of worship and one of its best kinds. Indeed, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The best worship is supplication," and then recited the verse. The threat against pride in it is because that is the habit of the affluent and extravagant, whereas the believer humbles himself before God, Most High, in all his states. And in placing "worship" in conjunction with "pride" there is an indication that supplication is a door of submission, because worship is submission. Also, the intended meaning of "worship" is supplication, and pride is only directed at something that, if one did it, one would not be proud. Al-Kashshaf says: "This interpretation is more apparent according to the wording and more fitting to the context, because when He made disputing about the signs of God a form of pride, He made supplication and submission to His signs a form of humility, since one who calls upon the Most High and seeks refuge in Him, Mighty and Majestic, does not dispute His signs without any authority from Him whatsoever." The conjunction in the words of the Most High (Wa qala) is the conjunction of a whole narrative to another whole narrative, because the two share the same purpose. For this reason, when He completed this narrative, namely His words, glory be to Him, ﴿And your Lord says﴾ up to His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:117 and elsewhere], He stated the purpose in His words, ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute about the signs of God?﴾, just as He first built the narrative upon it in His words, blessed and exalted be He, ﴿Indeed, those who dispute about the signs of God without authority﴾ [Ghafir 40:35]. If one truly reflects on this noble surah, one finds that most of its discourse is built on refuting those who dispute about the signs of God, which include monotheism and resurrection, and clarifying the manner of refutation in that through various arts. Then consider how what the surah concludes with corresponds to what it began with, His words, glory be to Him, ﴿So let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir 40:4], and how it finally stated explicitly what it had alluded to at the beginning, so that you may be amazed. This is the reason for the conjunction. End of quotation.

What he mentioned about this interpretation being more apparent according to the wording is very clear, because the first interpretation involves departing from the apparent meaning without need in two places: in "supplication," where it is used figuratively for worship, either because it includes it or because it is a specific form of worship and the general is intended by it; and in "response," where the reward for worship is called a response by figurative usage or by mushakalah (correspondence of terms), because it follows it as a response. By contrast, the second interpretation involves departing from the apparent meaning in only one place, namely ﴿from My worship﴾, and even that is after the need arises, so it is not like removing the sock before reaching the water. Indeed, it has been said that there is no need for figurative usage there at all, because the idafah (construct) is intended to refer to a known (covenanted) matter here, and so it conveys what was previously stated. But that it is more fitting to the context as well is not established in my view. In any case, ﴿astajib﴾ is in the jussive as the answer to the imperative, meaning: if you call upon Me, I will respond to you. Response on both interpretations is conditioned by God's will, according to what our principles require. He has explicitly stated this regarding the response to supplication, glory be to Him: ﴿He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills﴾ [al-An'am 6:41]. And pride in worshipping God, Most High, whether in supplication or otherwise, is disbelief, and it entails what is mentioned in the noble verse.

As for abandoning this not out of pride, the detailed discussion of it is not hidden. As for the circumstances of abandoning supplication, it has been said that they vary. Sometimes it is not good, as indicated by the saying of the Prophet, may God, Most High, bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever does not call upon God, Most High, He will be angry with him." Related by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Hakim from Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' report. And sometimes it is good, as indicated by what is related about the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him, leaving supplication on the day he was thrown into the fire, and his saying: "His knowledge of my state suffices me from asking." It may perhaps be said: leaving supplication out of reliance on God's knowledge, Mighty and Majestic, is itself a form of supplication. And God, Most High, knows best.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu Ja'far read "sa-yudkhalūna" (they will be made to enter), in the passive voice from the causative (al-idkhal). The transmission from 'Asim and Abu 'Amr differs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 61:

﴿Allah is the One who made the night for you that you might rest therein﴾ — that you might rest in it, by which He, glorified is He, caused the sun to set in it, so that He, exalted is His majesty, made it cold and dark; and He, mighty and majestic, made its coldness a cause for the weakening of the moving faculties, and its darkness a cause for the stilling of the outward senses, and [He made these] into other things which He made causes of tranquility and repose. ﴿And the day to see by﴾ — in which one sees, or by which one sees. So the day is either a temporal container for seeing, or a cause of it.

Whichever it is, the attribution of seeing to it, by making it "seeing" (mubsiran), is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi) on account of the connection between the two. In it there is hyperbole (mubalaghah), and that seeing has reached a degree that pervades the day of the one who sees. For this reason He did not say "that you might see therein" in the manner of what occurred in its counterpart. If it is said: Why did He not say "He made the night for you still (sakinan), so that the hyperbole mentioned would be in it, and the two parallel phrases would come out in one manner of hyperbole?" I say: it has been answered that the blessing of the day is more complete and greater than the blessing of the night, so He took the path of hyperbole with regard to it, and the other was left on its apparent sense as an alert to this. It has also been said that the two blessings are like two horses in a race, so the priority of the first is indicated by its being placed first, and the excellence of the second by the hyperbole; and it is as you see. It has also been said that He did not say that because the night is described in its literal sense as still, so it is said "a still night," meaning there is no wind in it; and it is not far-fetched that stillness in this sense is a conventional literal meaning. So if it were said "still," the intended meaning would not be distinguished when considering the absolute usage, though it would be distinguished when considering the contextual indication of contrast.

The preference for this style is because the clear, self-evidently precise speech is, from the outset, the original, especially in an address that came in the context of favour to the elite and the common people alike, who vary in understanding and in complete and deficient insight. And in the disclosure: since seeing was not in itself a final cause, but the cause is seeking the bounty, as is explicitly stated in Surah al-Qasas, in contrast to stillness and rest at night, He stated that explicitly in the first and alluded to it in the second, along with conveying a subtle point in the metaphorical attribution.

Al-Jalabi said: If the verse is taken as ihtibak (elliptical balancing), it is said that the meaning is: He made the night dark for you that you might rest in it, and the day seeing that you might disperse in it and seek of the bounty of Allah, the Exalted. So something was omitted from the first by the indication of the second, and from the second by the indication of the first. It does not need what was mentioned in explaining the omission of hyperbole in the first counterpart. This is the well-known view regarding the verse, and Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty﴾ — no bounty equals His bounty; and for the purpose of conveying this, he did not say "the one bestowing bounty." ﴿upon mankind﴾ — its righteous and its wicked alike. ﴿but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ — due to their ignorance of the Benefactor and their neglect of the places of blessings. The repetition of "mankind" is to specify the ingratitude to them, and this is from placing their clear, explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, which indicates that it is among their characteristics and особенно of their distinguishing traits in most cases.

﴿That﴾, the one characterized by the aforementioned attributes that entail divinity (ulūhiyya) and lordship (rubūbiyya), ﴿Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no god but He﴾. These are successive predicates (akhbār mutarādifa): each subsequent one specifies the preceding one and reduces the sharing of its meaning, given the original lexical sense, and confirms it. Some of them permit being treated as an adjective (wasfiyya) or an appositive (badaliyya). The phrase (Creator of every thing) is placed after ﴿there is no god but He﴾ in verse 106 of Surah al-An'am [6:106], whereas here it is placed first, because the purpose here, as has been said, is to refute those who deny the resurrection, so it is fitting to foreground what indicates this, namely that the origin of every thing is from Him, glorified and exalted be He, and likewise its return.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "خالِقَ" (Khāliqa) in the accusative, as a specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), meaning "I mean" or "I specify" the Creator of every thing. Then ﴿there is no god but He﴾ becomes a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) that functions as a kind of conclusion from the attributes mentioned. It is as if it were said: Allah, exalted be He, is characterized by the attributes mentioned, and there is no god except the one characterized by them; therefore there is no god but He. ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾ meaning: how, and from what direction, are you turned away from worshipping Him, glorified be He, to worshipping other than Him, exalted and majestic be He.

Talha, in one transmission, read "يُؤْفَكُونَ" (yu'fakūn) with the third-person (yā' al-ghayba) prefix.

Thus are those turned away who used to deny the signs of Allah. (Qur'an 40:63)

That is, like that wondrous delusion which has no basis and no justification whatsoever, every one who denies the signs of the Exalted, whatever sign it may be, is turned away. It is not some other delusion that has a basis and some justification at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 64:

﴿Allah is the One Who made the earth for you a dwelling-place﴾, i.e., a place of settlement (mustaqarr). ﴿And the sky a canopy﴾, i.e., a dome (qubbah). From this comes the word abniyat al-Arab (the dwellings of the Arabs), referring to their tents (qibab) that are pitched. The application of this term to the sky is by way of analogy (tashbih), and it is an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), and it contains an indication of its roundness (kuriyyatuha). This is an explanation of His favour, exalted is He, related to place, after the explanation of His favour related to time. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And He shaped you and perfected your shapes﴾ is an explanation of His favour, exalted is He, related to yourselves. The fa' in (fa-ahsana) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), so the meaning is: He shaped you in the finest shaping, in that He created each of you upright in stature, with clear skin, with proportionate limbs and features, prepared for practicing crafts and acquiring perfections. Al-A'mash and Abu Ruzayn read «siwarakum» with a kasrah on the sad, to avoid the dammah before the waw. The pattern fu'lah with a damma on the fa' forming a plural on the pattern fi'l with a kasra is irregular (shadh), and from it comes quwwah and qiwa, with a kasra on the qaf in the plural. A group read «suwarakum» with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the waw, on the pattern of busrah and busr. ﴿And provided for you from the good things﴾, i.e., the delightful things in taste, clothing and other things; it was also said: the lawful. ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾: the one described with the sublime attributes mentioned, Allah, your Lord, are two predicates for "that" (dhalikum). ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, exalted is He in His essence, ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., their Owner and their Nourisher. All of them, under His dominion, are in need of Him, exalted is He, in their essence, their existence and all their conditions, such that if His overflowing grace (fayd), exalted is His majesty, were cut off from them for a single moment, they would perish entirely.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 65:**

﴿He is the Ever-Living﴾, the One alone possessing true, essential life, ﴿there is no god except Him﴾, since no existent being comes near Him in His essence, His attributes, or His acts, exalted and majestic is He. ﴿So call upon Him﴾, i.e., worship Him alone, because what necessitates this belongs exclusively to Him, may He be exalted.

Interpreting "supplication" (du'a') as "worship" ('ibada) is what the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿sincere in obedience to Him in religion﴾ require, i.e., free from both hidden and manifest shirk (associating partners with God). This interpretation also best fits the consequence of the attributes of lordship (rububiyya) and divinity (uluhiyya) that were mentioned. The word "supplication" was used because what is fitting is worship carried out with humility, lowliness, and submission. ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., saying this.

[Page 84]

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat (The Divine Names and Attributes) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Whoever says, 'There is no god but God,' let him then say, right after it, 'All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds.'" This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So call upon Him, sincere in obedience...﴾ etc. Abd ibn Humayd narrated something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. According to this view, ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ etc. is part of the speech of those commanded to worship, mentioned before it. It has also been allowed that it is part of the speech of God, exalted is He, as an inshā' (performative utterance) of the praise of His own essence, glorified is He, by His own essence, majestic is His affair.

from the proofs (ḥujaj) and the signs (āyāt), or from the signs, because they confirm the proofs of reason and call attention to them, since the revealed signs (al-āyāt al-tanzīliyyah) clarify the created signs (al-āyāt al-takwīniyyah), both the outer (al-āfāqiyyah) and the inner (al-anfusiyyah). ﴿And I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, to submit myself to Him, exalted is He, and to devote my religion sincerely to Him, mighty and majestic is He.

He it is Who created you from dust, as part of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from it, as its verification has already passed. Then from a drop (nutfah), that is, then He created you in a detailed creation from a drop, that is, from seminal fluid (maniyy). Then from a clinging clot (alaqah), a piece of congealed blood. Then He brings you out as a child (tifl), that is, as children (atfal). It is a collective noun (ism jins) that applies to the few and the many.

In al-Misbah, Ibn al-Anbari said: "The word tifl is used in one form for the masculine, the feminine, and the plural, and agreement (mutabaqah) with it is also permissible." It has been said that it is singular in form but is interpreted as a plural: He created every individual of this kind, then He brings out each individual of it as a child.

Then that you may reach your maturity (ashuddakum). The lam in li-tablughu is connected to an omitted element, whose estimated sense is: then He keeps you alive so that you may reach. That omitted element is coordinated with (yukhrijukum). It is also permitted that li-tablughu be coordinated with an implied cause for "li-yukhrijakum," as if it were said: then He brings you out so that you grow gradually, then so that you reach your maturity (ashuddakum) and your completeness in strength and intellect. The same applies to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then that you may become elders﴾ (li-takunu shuyukhan), and it is permissible to coordinate it with (li-tablughu).

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Bakr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read «shuyukhan» with a kasra on the shin. It has also been read «shaykhan». This is like His words: ﴿children, and among you is one who is taken in death before⦆ (tifl, wa-minkum man yutawaffa min qablu), that is, before the state of old age, after reaching maturity or even before it. Then ﴿and that you may reach﴾ (wa-li-tablughu) is connected to a verb omitted after it, that is, and that you may reach ﴿a specified term﴾ (ajalan musamma). This is the Day of Resurrection, by bringing about that creation from dust and the stages that follow it. It is coordinated with (khalaqakum). By the Day of Resurrection is meant what it contains of recompense, for people were created only to worship, and then they reach the recompense. The interpretation of the specified term as this was related from al-Hasan. Some said it is the day of death. This was objected to on the grounds that the time of death is understood from the mention of being taken in death before it, so it is better to interpret it as what has already been mentioned. The apparent practice of al-Zamakhshari favours this view, as explained in al-Kashshaf. ﴿And perhaps you will reason﴾ (wa-la'allakum ta'qilun), and so that you may understand what is in that transition through the stages of wisdoms and lessons of many kinds.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "That is, and perhaps you will reason about your Lord, that He gives you life as He caused you to die."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 68:**

﴿He is the One who gives life﴾ to the dead, ﴿and causes death﴾ to the living. Or it means: He is the One who does giving life and causing death. ﴿So when He decrees a matter﴾ means He intends a matter of the matters to come forth into external existence. ﴿He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ without depending on anything among things at all.

This, according to the later scholars (al-Khalaf), is an illustration of the effect of His power over what is willed, when His will attaches to it, and a depiction of the speed with which created things follow His creating, without there being a commander and a commanded. The discussion of this has already passed. The first fa' (فَ)

[Page 85]

is to indicate that what follows it is a result of what precedes it, insofar as it requires an essential power not dependent on number or material. It has also been permitted that it be explanatory (تَفْصِيلِيَّة) and causal (تَعْلِيلِيَّة) as well, so reflect on this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 69:

﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of God? How are they turned away?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their shameful states and their feeble opinions, and a preface to what follows of the explanation of their denial of the whole Qur'an and of all the other books and laws, and the arrangement of the threat upon that. Likewise, what preceded in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute...﴾ (the verse beginning "Indeed, those who dispute") and so on, is an explanation that their disputation is founded upon a corrupt basis which can hardly enter into existence, so there is no repetition in it. Thus it is in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary).

And al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: The repetition of the mention of disputation is due to the multiplicity of the disputants, in that there are one people here and other people there; or the disputation is about different matters, in that in each it is taken in a suitable sense, so what passed concerns the resurrection and here concerns monotheism; or it is for emphasis, out of concern for the matter. He chose what is in Irshad, that is: look at these arrogant people who dispute His clear signs, which necessitate belief in them and restrain from disputing about them, how they are turned away from them, despite the converging motives to turn towards them and the complete absence of anything that diverts from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied the Book﴾ — that is, the whole of the Qur'an, or the genus of the heavenly books, for denying it is denying them. It is in the genitive case (majrur) as a substitute (badal) for the first relative pronoun, or as an explanatory apposition (bayan), or as an adjective (sifa) of it; or it is in the accusative case (mansub) by way of censure (dhamm); or in the nominative case (marfu') as a deleted predicate (khabar mahdhuf), or as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿then they will come to know﴾. The second relative clause was connected with denial (al-takdhib) rather than disputation (al-mujadala) because it is customary for disputation to occur in some matters but not in all. The use of the past tense (sighat al-madi) indicates certainty (al-tahqiq), just as the use of the present tense (sighat al-mudari') in the first relative clause indicates the renewal and repetition of the disputation. ﴿And with that with which We sent Our messengers﴾ — from among all the other books, according to the first interpretation of "the Book" (al-Kitab), or the general revelation and laws (al-shara'i'), according to the second interpretation.

﴿Then they will come to know﴾ the reality (kunh) of what they did of disputation and denial when they witness its punishments.

﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ is a temporal adverbial complement (*zarf*) governing "they will know" (*ya'lamun*). The meaning is future-oriented (*al-istiqbal*). The past tense is used to indicate that the event is certain to occur, so it is as if it had already happened in reality. Therefore there is no incompatibility between *sawfa* (سَوْفَ, "soon") and *idh* (إذْ, "when").

﴿and the chains﴾ is conjoined (*'atf*) to "the shackles." The prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wa-al-majrur*) is, in intention, postponed, as if it were said: "when the shackles and the chains are around their necks."

Allah's words ﴿they are dragged﴾ mean: *yajurrun*, i.e., they are pulled along.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 72:**

﴿in scalding water﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a grammatical state) relating either to the pronoun in (يَعْلَمُونَ, *ya'lamūna*, "they know") or to the pronoun in (في أعْناقِهِمْ, *fī a'nāqihim*, "around their necks"). It may also be a resumed independent sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa) explaining their condition after that. It is also permitted for (اَلسَّلاسِلُ, *al-salāsil*, "the chains") to be the subject (mubtada'), with the sentence (يُسْحَبُونَ, *yusḥabūna*, "they are dragged") as its predicate, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "they are dragged with them."

It is also permitted for (اَلْأغْلالُ, *al-aghlāl*, "the yokes") to be the subject, with ﴿and the chains﴾ coordinated to it, and the sentence being the predicate of the subject; (وفي أعْناقِهِمْ, *wa-fī a'nāqihim*, "and around their necks") is then in the position of a circumstantial clause. Its status is not hidden.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Wathhab read (وَالسَّلاسِلَ يَسْحَبُونَ, *wal-salāsila yusḥabūna*), with (السَّلاسِلَ, *al-salāsila*) in the accusative and (يَسْحَبُونَ, *yusḥabūna*) in the active voice. Thus (السَّلاسِلَ, *al-salāsila*) is a fronted direct object of (يَسْحَبُونَ, *yusḥabūna*), and the sentence is coordinated to what precedes it. There is no harm in the alternation between a nominal and a verbal sentence.

A group, including Ibn 'Abbas in one transmission, read (وَالسَّلاسِلِ, *wal-salāsili*) in the genitive. Al-Zajjaj explained this as a genitive by means of an omitted preposition, as in the line of poetry:

*Kulayb pointed with the palms and the fingers*

That is, "and with the chains," as it was read; or "in the chains," as in the codex of Ubayy. Al-Farra' explained it as coordination according to meaning, since the yokes around their necks means their necks in the yokes. A parallel is the line:

*Ill-omened men, who do not reform their tribe, nor is there a crier except with the separation of its crow.*

This is called in non-Qur'anic usage ʿaṭf al-tawahhum (coordination by apparent assumption, where the case is governed by a supposed alternative construction). Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya took this explanation, as did Ibn al-Anbari. After weakening al-Zajjaj's explanation, Ibn al-Anbari explained the reading according to what al-Farra' said. He said: "This is like saying: ʿAbd Allah quarrelled with Zayd, the two wise men (al-ʿāqilayn), with the accusative and with the nominative of (al-ʿāqilayn), because when one of them quarrels with his companion, the other has quarrelled too." This construction is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians. He transmitted its permissibility from Muhammad ibn Sa'dan al-Kufi, who said: "Because each of them is both agent and object."

﴿then in the Fire they are kindled﴾ means they are burned outwardly and inwardly. (سَجَرَ, *sajara*, "to kindle") is from "he kindled the oven" when he filled it with fire. It can also mean filling it with firewood so as to heat it. From this comes (السَّجِيرُ, *al-sajīr*, "the intimate friend"), as if he has been filled with love (سُجِرَ بِالحُبِّ, *sujira bil-ḥubb*), that is, filled. It is understood from the Qamus that (السَّجْرُ, *al-sajr*) is among the words with opposite meanings (al-aḍdād). Both derivations fit al-sajīr: "filled with your love," or "emptied of others in favour of you." The first is more apparent.

What is meant by this and by what precedes it is that they are tormented with various kinds of punishment: being dragged on their faces into the blazing Fire, then the Fire being let loose upon their insides, and that they are tormented outwardly and inwardly. Therefore there is no contrast (istidrāk) in mentioning this after what has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verses 73–74:

﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with God?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "They have strayed from us."﴾ That is, it will be said to them and they will say. The past tense is used to indicate that the event is certain to occur. The question is for rebuke. Their straying from them means their absence, as in "his mount strayed" when he does not know where it is. This does not contradict what suggests that their gods are bound together with them in the Fire, because the Fire has levels, and they have different positions in it. So it is possible for them to be absent from them in some of these and joined with them in others. It is also possible that their straying is a metaphor (isti'ara) for the lack of benefit, so that their presence is like their absence. It is then mentioned in its literal sense in one place and in its figurative sense (majaz) in another. ﴿Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before.﴾ That is, rather, it has become clear to us today that we did not used to worship anything of worth in the world. This is a turning away from the claim that the false gods do not exist for them or do not benefit them, to the claim that they are not anything of worth.

In this there is an acknowledgment of their error and remorse over their ugly deed, at a time when that will not benefit them. Al-Jalabi regarded this verse as similar to His saying, ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], where they resort to lying out of their confusion and agitation. The meaning of His saying, ﴿Thus God leads astray the disbelievers﴾, is that He, exalted is He, bewilders them in their affair until they resort to lying, even though they know it will not benefit them. Perhaps what has been mentioned before is the one that fits the context.

The meaning of this is: in the same way of misguidance, God leads astray the disbelievers in this world, to the extent that they make claims in it which turn out to be nothing. Or it is like the straying of their gods from them in the Hereafter: We lead them astray from their gods there, so that even if they seek the gods and the gods seek them, some of them will not meet others. Or in the same kind of straying and lack of benefit, God leads the disbelievers astray so that they do not find their way in this world to what would benefit them in the Hereafter. In al-Majma' it says: just as God caused these people's deeds to go astray and nullified what they had hoped for, so He does with the deeds of all who adopt disbelief as their religion, so that they gain nothing from them. Thus the leading astray of the disbelievers means the leading astray of their deeds, that is, their nullification. This is reported from al-Hasan, and other meanings have been given for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 75:

[Page 87 marker from the source]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their being dragged in chains and shackles, being set ablaze in the Fire, and being reproached with questioning. It was also permitted, on some interpretations, that it refers to Allah the Exalted leading the disbelievers astray. Ibn 'Atiyya took the first view, meaning: that is the punishment you are in, ﴿because you used to exult in the earth﴾, meaning you were insolent and boastful, as Mujahid said, ﴿without right﴾, meaning through shirk and disobedience, or without any entitlement to that. In the phrase ( الْأرْضِ ), "the earth," there is an added emphasis on the awfulness of insolence. ﴿And because you used to revel﴾, meaning you used to extend yourselves in exultation. It was also said that the meaning is: because you used to rejoice at what befell the prophets of Allah the Exalted and His friends of hardship, and because you used to extend yourselves in rejoicing at what you were given, to the point that you forgot the Hereafter because of it and became preoccupied with the blessing rather than the Bestower. In a hadith: "Allah the Exalted dislikes the arrogant and exultant, and loves every sorrowful heart." Between al-farah (exultation) and al-maraḥ (revelry) there is a fine paronomasia. The shift to direct address serves to intensify the reproach, because blaming a person to his face is a public exposure of him. This is why it was said: "Advising someone in front of a crowd is a rebuke."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 76:

﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾, that is, the gates allotted to you, ﴿abiding therein﴾, expecting to abide forever. ﴿Evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾ from the truth: Hell.

The sublime structure of the discourse, given that it begins with "Enter" (ud-khulu), would require that it say: "Evil is the entrance of the arrogant," so that the beginning and the end correspond. But since entering qualified by abiding (al-khulud) is the cause of lingering, He expressed it with "abode" (al-matwa), and the correspondence is valid in meaning. This matter, as al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) inferred, is said to them after the preceding exchange while they are in the Fire, and the aim of consideration in it is abiding; so it is a command qualified by abiding, not by entering in general. It is also permissible to say: after entering it, they were commanded to enter the gates allotted to them, so it was a command to enter, qualified by the division into each gate. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is said to them before this exchange, at the very beginning of the matter: "Enter."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 77:

﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah﴾ — that He will punish your disbelieving enemies — ﴿is true﴾, existing without doubt. ﴿And whether We show you﴾ — its original form is "fa-in narayanka", so "má" was added to emphasize the conditional "in" (in). For this reason it was permissible for the verb to take the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid), as has been said. Al-Mubarrad went to the necessary combination of má and the energetic nun after the conditional in, and al-Zajjaj [held that]: according to both of them, it is not permissible to add má without attaching a nun, nor to attach a nun without adding má. It is transmitted in the verse of the poet:

*"Fa-imma tarayanni wa li lummatun, fa-inna al-hawadetha awda bihа"*

Abu Hayyan attributed to Sibawayh a statement in which both usages are permitted. The prevailing view, as stated by more than one scholar, is that when "in" is emphasized by "má", the verb after it takes the energetic nun. ﴿Some of what We promise them﴾ — namely, killing and capture — ﴿or We take you in death﴾ before that — ﴿then to Us they will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, when We will recompense them for their deeds. This is the response to "natawaffayannaka", and the response to "nurayannaka" is omitted, being like "fa-dhaka" (that). It is also permitted that it be a response to both, meaning: whether We punish them during your life or do not punish them, We punish them in the Hereafter with the most severe punishment; and the restriction to mentioning the return in this context indicates its severity. Al-Zamakhshari preferred, in this verse, what was mentioned first, and in the parallel verse in [al-Ra'd: 40], namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you [in death], then upon you is only the conveyance﴾, [there is] what indicates that the clause joined with "fa" is a response under both assumptions. He said in al-Kashf: The difference is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ [al-Rum: 60; Ghafir: 55, 77] is a promise of fulfillment and victory, and that is what the concern of the Prayer and peace be upon him was centered on, and the concern of the believers is bound to it according to the requirement of this context; so it is fitting that "fa-dhaka" be estimated there. Then the second estimate was introduced to refute their mockery and [to affirm] that he is victorious in every state, and to complete the consolation. As for the context of "alladhi" in al-Ra'd, it does not ask for the delivery to be answered, and that there is nothing upon him other than that, however the matter turns out. So whoever goes to attach what is here to what is in al-Ra'd has missed the point of al-Zamakhshari. End. So reflect and do not be heedless.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub read ﴿yurja'un﴾ with a fatha on the ya', and Talha ibn Musarrif and Ya'qub in the transmission of al-Walid ibn Hassan read it with a fatha on the ta' of address (tā' al-khitāb).

And We certainly sent messengers ﴿before you﴾, of distinction and great number, ﴿before your sending﴾.

﴿Of them are those We have related﴾, that is, We have told you their news and their traces, ﴿to you﴾, such as Noah, Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them.

﴿And of them are those We have not related to you﴾. They are the majority of the messengers, peace be upon them. Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how many prophets are there?' He said, 'One hundred and twenty-four thousand. Of them, the messengers are three hundred and fifteen, a great multitude.'" The apparent meaning is that the term "messenger" in the verse refers to something more specific than "prophet." However, the Qadi's practice may give the impression that it refers to something equivalent to "prophet."

Whatever the case, there is no indication in the verse that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not know the number of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, as some people have imagined. The report of Imam Ahmad has been rejected on this basis, and there has been the dispute between us and him that has taken place. This is because what is negated is the relating (qasas), and you have known its meaning. Therefore, the negation of relating does not necessitate the negation of mentioning their names. Even if we grant it, the negation of mentioning names does not necessitate the negation of mentioning that their number is such-and-such without referring to their names. Moreover, the negation with lam (لَمْ), which according to the correct view turns the present tense into the past, means that relating is negated in the past, and this does not necessitate that the negation continues. So it is possible that they were all related to him (ﷺ) after that, and that this was not revealed as Qur'an.

More evident in indicating that the negation does not continue is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you﴾ [An-Nisa: 164]. This is because the mind immediately understands from it that what is meant is: We have not related them to you before this, for a place where ﴿We have related them to you before﴾. In sum, to use the verse as evidence that he (ﷺ) did not know the number of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, nor came to know it afterward, is a great ignorance, indeed a grave abandonment. We seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, from that.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And of them are those We have not related to you﴾, that he said: "Allah, the Exalted, sent an Abyssinian slave as a prophet, so he is among those who were not related to Muhammad (ﷺ)." And from Ibn Abbas, with the wording: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, sent a black prophet among the Abyssinians, so he is among those who were not related to him, peace be upon him." What is meant by this, in the manner already mentioned, is that his stories and traces were not mentioned to him (ﷺ), and his circumstances and reports were not presented to him, as was the case regarding Moses, Jesus and others among the messengers, peace be upon them. It cannot be said that what is meant is that the sending of a person described by this was not mentioned to him (ﷺ), since the wording does not support this. Also, even if what has been mentioned were intended, from where did Ali, may Allah honour his face, or Ibn Abbas know that? Would the gate of the city of knowledge speak about knowledge that was not poured into him from that city? Far be it from him, and then far be it. Likewise his cousin Ibn Abbas, Abdullah.

This report has been objected to on the basis that it contains the sending of a slave, and they have said that a slave cannot be a messenger. It has been answered that "slave" in it does not mean a owned person, who cannot be a messenger because of his lack of freedom of action and because souls recoil from following him. Rather, it means one of the "slaves" in the sense of black people by custom. Even if it were said that a slave in this sense also cannot be a messenger, because souls recoil from following him, just as they recoil from following an owned person, we say: granting that there is recoiling, it is only when the sending is to people other than black people. As for when the sending is to black people, there is no recoiling at all. The apparent wording of Ibn Abbas is that this black man was sent only among the Abyssinians. Committing to the view that no messenger may come from the blacks, the descendants of Ham, is not supported by the evidence. For if recoiling were what prevents sending, it is not realized when the sending is to his own kind. And if the obstacle is that there is no one among the descendants of Ham who is qualified for sending because of the deficiency of their intellects and the scarcity of their perfection, then claiming this is ignorance. Allah, the Exalted, knows best where He places His message. How many among the descendants of Ham have we seen who are more intelligent and more perfect than many of the descendants of Sam and Yafith? Even if a decisive statement has come from our Prophet (ﷺ) that no messenger will come from those people, then let it be mentioned, and how could it be? Moreover, the matter of prophethood concerning those mentioned is easier than the matter of messengerhood, as is not hidden. Perhaps on the basis of all that we have mentioned, al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "There is doubt about the soundness of the report."

﴿And it was not for a messenger﴾, that is, it was not valid or proper for a messenger from those messengers, ﴿to bring a sign﴾, that is, a miracle, ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾. The miracles, despite the diversity of their kinds, are gifts from Allah, the Exalted, which He distributed among them as His will required, which is founded on profound wisdoms, like the rest of the distribution. They have no choice in preferring some of them or in independently bringing what is demanded of them. ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾, with punishment in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿it will be judged with truth﴾, by saving the one who is in the right and rewarding him, and destroying the falsifier and punishing him. ﴿And the falsifiers will lose there﴾, that is, at the time the command of Allah, the Exalted, comes. "There" is a noun of place used for time. ﴿The falsifiers﴾ are those who hold to falsehood absolutely, so the obstinate and those who demand signs enter among them in the first place. Some of the exegetes explained "the falsifiers" as referring to them, and explained "the command of Allah" as the Resurrection, and some explained it as the killing on the day of Badr. What we have mentioned is more appropriate.

The most distant of what we have seen regarding the verse is that the meaning is: when Allah, the Exalted, wills to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decrees and executes that with truth, every falsifier loses, and he attains the corruption of his Hereafter.

God is the One who made the livestock (al-an'am) for you﴾. By it is meant specifically the camels, as related from al-Zajjaj and chosen by the author of al-Kashshaf. The lam (ﻝ, "ل") here indicates purpose (ta'lil), not exclusivity (ikhtisas), since that is the well-known sense in the parallel verses. That is, He created them for your sake and for your benefit. And the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿that you may ride upon some of them﴾ and so on, are an elaboration of what the statement indicated in general terms. For this reason some have made it a badal (substitution, apposition) of what precedes it, a badal mufassal min mujmal (a detailed substitution of a general term), by repeating the preposition. The min (ﻣِﻦ, "من") is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning the beginning of the connection of riding to them, or it is partitive (tab'idiyyah). The same applies to the min in His words ﴿and from them you eat﴾. Yet, on the partitive reading, the intended meaning is not that riding and eating are each restricted to a specific part of them, such that one cannot be connected to what the other is connected to. Rather, each part of them is suitable for each of the two. Indeed, they often count the noble camels for riding. According to what al-Jalabi held, the clause is a conjunction on the level of meaning (atf 'ala al-ma'na), for His words ﴿that you may ride upon some of them﴾ carry the meaning of "from them you ride," or "from them you eat" carries the meaning of "that you may eat from them," but it was not expressed in that form for a particular reason.

Al-Allamah al-Taftazani said: this clause is a circumstantial clause (hal), but its apparent reading entails the conjunction of a circumstantial phrase upon an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and there is no escape from it except by positing an implied conjunct, meaning: He created for you the livestock, [and] from them you eat, so that it becomes a conjunction of one clause upon another clause.

Al-Khafaji responded to this by saying: It has not become clear to me why this waw (واو) should be taken as a conjunctive waw requiring the aforementioned supposition, while the apparent reading is that it is a circumstantial waw, whether we say it is a circumstantial phrase relating to the subject (al-fa'il) or to the object (al-maf'ul). What comes to my mind is conjunction according to meaning, and perhaps considering it on the side of the conjoined element is easier, so it is taken into account also in

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 80:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in them you have benefits﴾, i.e., other than riding and eating, such as milk, wool and hides. It is also said that it means "and that you may benefit from benefits in them," or something similar. ﴿And that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾, i.e., a matter of importance that concerns you, such as carrying loads from one land to another. This is a conjunction with "that you may ride of them" and it came in its pattern. The apparent expectation was to pair the benefits derived from the livestock, by bringing the lam (li-, "that") with all of them or omitting it throughout; but it deviated to what is in the sublime composition for a particular reason.

The author of al-Kashf said: Since here the livestock refers specifically to camels, riding and reaching a need were made the most complete purpose of them, because among their benefits are riding and being carried upon them. As for eating from them and benefiting from their wool and milk, in relation to those two matters they are a small and meagre amount. So the lam was introduced before both of them and they were placed flanking what lies between them, as an indication that these too are suitable for being a reason, but fall short of those two. As for the specification derived from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And from them you eat﴾, it is because they are among what is intended for riding and prepared for eating, so it is not contradicted by horses according to the view of one who permits their meat, nor by cattle.

The author of al-Fara'id said: It was said ﴿And from them you eat﴾ and ﴿And in them you have benefits﴾, and it did not say "that you may eat from them" and "that you may reach benefits," because they are at present eating and taking benefits. As for riding and reaching a need, these are two matters awaited, so a form indicating the future was used for them. It was objected that all of them are future with respect to the time of creation.

Al-Qadi said: The change of structure in eating is because it falls within the scope of necessity. It was also said in its explanation: that is, the object of the purpose need not necessarily result from the act, so the change to the form of a nominal circumstantial clause together with the use of the continuous form serves to draw attention to its distinction from riding, in that it is among the necessities of man. This explanation applies also to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in them you have benefits﴾, because the intended benefit is the benefit of drinking and clothing, and this is among the necessities, and it does no harm. Yes, there is in it a subtle point that is not hidden.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Riding and reaching a need may be the purpose of the Wise, exalted is His majesty, because of the religious benefits in them, such as establishing a religion and seeking obligatory or recommended knowledge; therefore the lam was introduced before them, unlike eating and obtaining benefits, for these are of the kind of permissible things that cannot be the purpose of the Wise. This is built upon his doctrine of linking command and will, and it is not correct either, because permissible things which are a blessing may, according to them, be the purpose of the Wise, exalted is His majesty. Alas, I wonder what he would say concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾ [Yunus: 67]. Yes, if it were mentioned that it is due to its containing the religious purpose, it would be more fitting for the entry of the lam, and it would be a valid view, if it were sound.

It was also said: the change of the sublime structure in eating is for the sake of observing the fawasil (verse-endings), just as the fronting of the prepositional phrase is for that reason. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in them you have benefits﴾, it is like a follower of eating, so it was given its treatment; and this, as you see, is weak. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And upon them﴾ is a preparation for His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And upon the ships you are carried﴾, so as to combine the land-vessels and the sea-vessels; it is as if it were said: "And upon them on land and upon the ships at sea you are carried," so there is no repetition. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, it is said: perhaps the intended carrying here is the carrying of women and children upon them in the howdah, and this is the secret of separating it from riding. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is said to be for the sake of observing the fawasil, like its fronting earlier.

It was also said that the fronting here and in what preceded is for emphasis. It was said: "upon the ship" (ʿalā al-fulk) rather than "in the ship" (fī al-fulk), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Carry therein of every kind two pairs﴾ [Hud: 40], because the sense of being in a vessel and of being upon it both exist in it, so either expression is correct; and what favours ʿalā here is the harmony of the passage (al-mushakala).

Some have held that by the livestock is meant the eight pairs, so that riding and eating from them relate to the whole, yet not in the sense that each of them is restricted to a particular part of them such that the one may not be related to what the other relates to; rather, some of them are related to by eating alone, such as sheep, and some are related to by both, such as camels. Some counted cattle too, and their riding is customary among some people of tents; and some included horses, mules and all other animals benefited from among the livestock, and this is weak.

The view that the intended meaning is the eight pairs has been preferred over the view reported from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is camels alone, on the ground that the context is one of favour, and this requires generality, and the apparent meaning is that. But that the context is one of favour is not granted; rather it is a context of argument, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17], as the context indicates. And the mention of benefits does not contradict this, for it is incidental.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 81:

﴿And He shows you His signs⦆ That is, His proofs which indicate the perfection of His affairs, exalted is His majesty. ﴿So which of Allah's signs will you deny?⦆ That is, which one of those signs will you deny? For each of them is so manifest that no one who has any intellect at all would dare to deny it. Here "ayy" (which, what) is an interrogative of rebuke, and it is in the accusative case governed by "tunkiroon" (you deny). The idafah (annexation) of "al-ayat" (the signs) to the Exalted Name is to instil awe and to magnify the gravity of denying them. The masculine form of "ayy" in such a usage as mentioned is the common and widespread one, and the feminine is rare, and from it is the verse of poetry:

"Bi-ayyi kitabin am bi-ayyati sunnatin
Tara hubbahum ara'an 'alayya wa-tahsabu"

Al-Zamakhshari said: Because the differentiation between masculine and feminine in nouns that are not adjectives, such as "himar" (male donkey) and "himara" (female donkey), is rare, and it is even rarer in the case of "ayy", because it is an interrogative noun about something that is vague and unknown to the questioner, and the differentiation contradicts what was mentioned, because it requires distinguishing between what is feminine and what is masculine, so that it would be known to him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 82:

﴿Had they not travelled﴾ on the earth, that they might see how was the end of those before them? That is, they sat and did not travel, according to one of the two opinions: ﴿on the earth, so that they might see how was the end of those who were before them﴾ from the destroyed nations. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They were more numerous than them, and mightier in strength and in monuments left upon the earth﴾... etc. is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), similar to what passed in its counterpart at the beginning of the surah; indeed, most of the discourse there applies here too. ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾. The first "ma" is either a negative particle or an interrogative in the sense of negation, in a place of nasb (accusative) governed by "aghnā" (did avail). The second "ma" is a relative pronoun in a place of raf' (nominative) as its subject, or it is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and the verbal noun resulting from the interpretation is likewise in the nominative as its subject. That is: "it did not avail them," or "what thing availed them? That which they earned," or "their earning."

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 83:**

﴿When their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾ (al-bayyinat): the miracles, or the manifest signs that comprise all of that. ﴿they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾. Six interpretations have been mentioned for this.

The first: the intended meaning of "knowledge" is their deviant beliefs and their refuted doubts concerning the Origin, the Return and other matters, or their beliefs concerning the conditions of the Hereafter, as is the apparent meaning of al-Kashshaf's words. Describing these beliefs as "knowledge" is according to their own claim, for mockery, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has overtaken them concerning the Hereafter﴾ [an-Naml: 66]. The meaning is that they rejoiced in this, belittled the knowledge of the messengers, peace be upon them, and repelled the clear proofs by means of it.

The second: the intended meaning is the knowledge of the philosophers and the materialists from the sons of Yunan (Greece), in its various kinds. So when they heard of the revelation of God, exalted is He, they rejected it and belittled the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them, in comparison with what they themselves possessed of such knowledge. It is related from Suqrat (Socrates) that he heard of Musa, peace be upon him, and he was told: "If you were to emigrate to him?" He said: "We are a people who are refined, so we have no need of one who refines us." The times are similar; we have seen one who abandoned following the Seal of the Messengers (ﷺ), and disdained to be affiliated with the law of any of them, rejoicing in what he had licked up from the leftovers of the philosophers, and said: "Knowledge is that, and not what the messengers brought, may the blessings and peace of God, exalted is He, be upon them all."

The third: the original sense is: ﴿When their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, they did not rejoice in the knowledge that came to them; so they were placed in its position, and they rejoiced in what they had of ignorance. Then that ignorance was called "knowledge" because of their elation with it and their placing it in the position of the elation that was due to them over the knowledge that had come to them. In this there is mockery of the extent of their ignorance and an exaggeration of their being devoid of knowledge. The pronoun in (they rejoiced) and (what they had) on these interpretations refers to the disbelievers spoken of.

The fourth: the pronoun in (they rejoiced) may be taken to refer to the disbelievers, and the pronoun in (what they had) to the messengers, peace be upon them. The intended "knowledge" is the truth that the messengers brought, i.e., they rejoiced over what the messengers had of knowledge, a rejoicing of laughter at it and mockery of it. Its summary is that they mocked the clear proofs and what the messengers brought of the knowledge of revelation. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾.

The fifth: the two pronouns may be taken to refer to the messengers, peace be upon them. The meaning is that when the messengers saw the persistent ignorance of the disbelievers and their mockery of the truth, and knew the evil of their end and the punishment that would reach them for their ignorance and mockery, they rejoiced in what they had been given of knowledge and thanked God, exalted is He. And there befell the disbelievers the requital of their ignorance and their mockery. This is reported from al-Jubba'i.

The sixth: the two pronouns may be taken to refer to the disbelievers, and the intended meaning of "what they had of knowledge" is their knowledge of worldly affairs and their understanding of managing them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [ar-Rum: 7], and ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾ [an-Najm: 30]. So when the messengers came to them with the knowledge of religions, which is the farthest thing from their knowledge because it calls to renouncing the world and abstaining from pleasures and desires, they did not turn to it, belittled it, mocked it, and believed that there was no knowledge more beneficial or more productive of advantages than their own; so they rejoiced in it. The author of al-Kashf said: "Of these six interpretations, the most preferable is the third, for it contains the mockery and the exaggeration of their being devoid of knowledge, and includes what the first includes and more; it is free from the lack of correspondence with reality that is in the second, from the insufficiency of expression for conveying the meaning that is in the fourth, and from the disjunction of the pronouns that is in the fifth. The sixth is close, but it falls short of the benefits of the third." End of quotation. So consider it very carefully.

Abu Hayyan approved the sixth interpretation, and objected to the third, saying: "A positive clause is not expressed by a negated clause except in a few instances of speech, such as 'an evil that bares its fang' (sharr aharru dhā nāb), though there is disagreement about this. And since its matter reverts to a restricted affirmation, it is permissible. But as for the verse, it should not be interpreted as an exception to the rule, because that mixes up the meanings of distinct sentences, and nothing from them can be relied upon. And you know that there is no difference in meaning between 'they did not rejoice in what had come to them of knowledge' and ﴿they rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾, as has been established." Yet this interpretation, in my view, despite its merit, is not free from remoteness, and the words of the author of al-Kashf are not free from some uneasiness.

**Page 92**

﴿Fa-lamma ra'aw ba'sana﴾ (when they saw Our might), meaning the severity of Our punishment. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with a painful punishment﴾ [al-A'raf: 165]. ﴿They said: "We believe in Allah alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him."﴾ They mean the idols, or all their other false deities.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 40, verse 85:**

﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment.﴾ That is, at the moment of seeing Our punishment, because divine wisdom decreed that such faith should not be accepted. ("Their faith," *iymanuhum*, is raised as the subject of *yakun* (was), or as the agent of *yanfa'uhum* (benefit them). In *yakun* there is a dummy pronoun (*damir al-sha'n*), according to the disputed question of the same kind as in *kana yaqumu Zaydun* (it was that Zayd stood).) The negative particle entered on the verb "to be" (*al-kawn*) and not on "benefit" (*al-naf'*), in order to convey the meaning of negating validity. It is as if their faith was not valid and was not proper, given the wisdom that their faith should benefit them at the sight of the punishment.

Here there are four *fa'*s: the *fa'* of ﴿so what they had gathered did not avail them﴾, the *fa'* of ﴿so when their messengers came to them﴾, the *fa'* of ﴿so when they saw Our punishment﴾, and the *fa'* of ﴿so it did not benefit them﴾. The first *fa'* is like in your saying: "Wealth was given, so he withheld charity," and what follows it is a financial result of what they had been engaged in: the rivalry in wealth, children, and enjoying fortresses and the like. The second is explanatory, like in your saying: "He did not show kindness to the poor afterwards, so withholding charity..." In the example, what follows up to His, exalted be He, saying ﴿and what they used to mock surrounded them﴾ is an elaboration of that summary, and how the matter ended for them in the opposite of what they had hoped, and how they gathered, massed and exerted themselves to extinguish the light of God, and how the evil plot encompassed its own people. In His, glorified be He, saying ﴿what did their gathering avail them﴾ there is a hint that they strove to make it avail them. The third *fa'* indicates sequence, and makes what follows it a consequence of what precedes it and occurring right after it. ﴿So when they saw Our punishment﴾ is dependent on His, exalted be He, saying ﴿So when their messengers came to them﴾... etc. It follows it, because it is in the position of "so they disbelieved." However, ﴿So when their messengers came to them﴾ is a detailed explanation of disbelief, comprising their evil treatment and their ingratitude for the greatest blessing of God, the Book and the Messenger. It is as if it was said: "They disbelieved; then when they saw Our punishment, they believed." The fourth *fa'* is similar: what follows it is conjoined to "they believed," indicating that the non-benefit of their faith and its rejection by them is a consequence of faith at the sight of punishment. It is as if it was said: "When they saw Our punishment they believed; so their faith did not benefit them, since the faith that benefits is faith given by choice."

﴿The way of God that has already passed among His servants﴾: that is, God has established this, namely the non-benefit of faith at the sight of violence, as a practice that is established in the past, a long-standing precedent. It is among the emphatic infinitive nouns, like "the promise of God" and "the dye of God." It has also been permitted that it be in the accusative as a warning, meaning: "Beware, O people of Mecca, of the practice of God toward the enemies of the Messengers."

﴿And there the disbelievers lost﴾: that is, at the time of their seeing the violence, taking "there" as a place-noun that has been used metaphorically for time, as has been mentioned just before. This ruling is specific to faith at the moment of violence. As for repentance at the moment of violence, it is accepted and beneficial by the grace and generosity of God, exalted be He, and the difference is clear. It is reported from some of the great scholars that the faith at the moment of violence is also accepted. The meaning of ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ is that their faith itself did not benefit them, but God, exalted be He, benefited them through it in reality. The condition of this interpretation and what belongs to this type is not hidden from you. And God knows best.

* * *

"From the door of allusion (*ishara*) in some verses," according to what some of the masters have pointed to: ﴿Ha Mim﴾ is an allusion to what was poured upon the heart of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, from the All-Merciful, for the *ha'* and the *mim* are from the middle of the two noble names. In this there is also a secret that is not permissible to disclose. And since the surah began with what points to mercy, and that it is the attribute of the one called to and the caller, there is mentioned afterwards, of the attributes of the One called to, namely God, the Mighty and Majestic, what indicates the greatness of mercy and its precedence. In this there is what there is of good tidings to the one called.

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believed﴾ ... etc. In it is an allusion to the nobility of faith and the exaltedness of the rank of believers, and that it is fitting for believers among the children of Adam to ask forgiveness for one another. In this there is also, of the confirmation of the indication of the greatness of God's mercy, exalted and majestic, what is not hidden. ﴿So call upon God, making religion sincerely His﴾, by being unmixed with anything of the aims of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. It has been said: in the unrestricted use of "Spirit" there is an allusion to the spirit of prophethood, which is cast upon the prophets; and the spirit of guardianship (*wilaya*), which is cast upon the knowers (*'arifin*); and the spirit of understanding, which is cast upon the believing, devout worshippers. ﴿That he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. It has been said: the "meeting" is with God, exalted be He, and there is no existence for other than Him, and this is the station of annihilation (*fana'*) alluded to by His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿the Day they come forth, nothing of them being hidden from God﴾, from the acceptance of their existence, not ... ﴿"Whose is the Kingdom today?" "To God, the One, the Subduer"﴾, since there is no one in the abode except Him, a dwelling. ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed﴾ from the manifestation (*tajalli*) ﴿for what it earned﴾ in expending existence for the One worshipped, ﴿with no injustice today﴾, so every soul will obtain from the manifestation according to the measure of its expenditure of existence, no less than that.

﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day, when the hearts rise up to the throats, choking﴾. This is the common people's resurrection, which is postponed, and it alludes to the elite's resurrection, which is hastened for them. It has been said: for them, in every breath, there is a resurrection of reproach, punishment, reward, distance and nearness, and what did not exist for them in reckoning. The pounding of the heart speaks, the emaciation informs, the color reveals, and the lover conceals, but the affliction appears. When the annihilation of attributes draws near, the hearts reach the throats and the eyes witness what the inner consciences conceal. ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾: the treachery of the eyes of lovers is their approval of deliberately looking at other than the Beloved with approval and delight, and what the breasts conceal is the desires of souls, the pleasing things of hearts, and the longings of spirits.

﴿And your Lord said: "Call upon Me; I will respond to you"﴾. It has been said: that is, ask Me, and I will answer you, and you will find Me, and whoever finds Me finds everything. So the supplication that is not rejected is this supplication. In some reports: "Whoever seeks Me finds Me." ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾, to supplicate to Me and seek Me, ﴿will enter Hell﴾, deprivation ...

[Page 93]

and distance from Me, ﴿humbled﴾: abased and humiliated. ﴿God is the One who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by﴾. In it is an allusion to the night of humanity and the day of spirituality. It has been mentioned that people's rest at the known night is of categories: the heedless rest in the ease of souls and bodies; the people of desire rest in their like and kinds among men and women; the people of obedience rest in the sweetness of their deeds and the strength of their hopes; the people of love rest in the moaning of souls, the yearning of hearts, the humility of secrets, and the kindling of spirits with longings, which are hotter than fire. ﴿God is the One who made the earth a settled place for you﴾: it alludes to the fact that He, exalted be He, made the earth of humanity a dwelling place for the spirit, and the heaven a building, that is, the heaven of spirituality is built upon it. ﴿And shaped you and perfected your forms﴾: by making you mirrors of His beauty and majesty. In a report: "God created Adam in His image." In this there is an allusion to the rejection of "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" [Al-Baqarah: 30]. And to God there is one who said:

*"The slanderers did not diminish your rank with me, nor did the backbiter harm you."*

*"As if they praised you, not knowing that I, regarding you, know what they blame."*

As for the disbeliever, due to the evil of his choice, he joined the devils and became one manifesting the attributes of subjugation from the Lord of the worlds. "God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves." The discourse on the surah of the Believer is complete, and praise belongs to God, first and last, inward and outward.
